title: How Bitcoin works: one real transaction from Alice's wallet to the blockchain, every figure recomputed

nodes.label: Transaction
nodes.body: A transaction is the unit of action in Bitcoin: a message telling the network that the owner of certain bitcoins has authorized the transfer of that value to another owner. The new owner can in turn spend the value by creating another transaction, and so on, which gives a chain of ownership. This first branch of the chapter follows one such transaction, Alice's payment for a podcast episode in Bob's online store, from the moment it is conceived to the moment it is spent onward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A transaction is the unit of action in Bitcoin: a message telling the network that the owner of certain bitcoins has authorized the transfer of that value to another owner. The new owner can in turn spend the value by creating another transaction, and so on, which gives a chain of ownership. This first branch of the chapter follows one such transaction, Alice's payment for a podcast episode in Bob's online store, from the moment it is conceived to the moment it is spent onward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Everything else in Bitcoin exists to carry transactions safely. The network propagates them, miners gather them into blocks and the blockchain records them, so a student who knows what a transaction contains, and how transactions refer to one another, has the vocabulary for the rest of the course. The book adds a point that is easy to miss: bitcoins do not exist physically or as digital data that could be emailed. What exists is a database on every full node that says who controls how many bitcoins, and a transaction is the data that convinces the nodes to update that database (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In the chapter Alice scans a payment request in Bob's store, her wallet builds a transaction, the network relays it and a miner records it in a block. The same object is met in every wallet, every block explorer and every node, because all of them read and write the same kind of data. Later chapters open it up: the keys and signatures that authorize it, the format in which it is sent, and the fees that pay for it.

The branch is organised around the questions a learner asks in order. What parts does a transaction have? Who is allowed to spend an output, and how is that proved? How do transactions link to one another, and what forms do they commonly take? In which units is value counted? How does a wallet construct a transaction, and how does the payment begin with a request? Each question is a group of concepts below, and later groups rely on the words defined in earlier ones.

Two cautions apply from the start. A transaction does not move coins from one place to another: it changes who may spend certain outputs, because the book says there are no physical coins or even individual digital coins and that the coins are implied in transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And this chapter simplifies on purpose: it names the signature, the script and the identifier without opening them, so each is given a concept here and a full treatment in a later chapter.

nodes.label: Transaction part
nodes.body: A transaction part is one of the pieces a transaction is assembled from. The chapter names the two sides, the inputs that spend funds and the outputs that receive them, and the small difference between them that pays the miner. To describe them exactly this group also explains the unspent output, the identifier by which a transaction is referred to, the size that a transaction occupies, the fee rate by which miners compare fees, and the ledger image that gives the whole structure its meaning (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A transaction part is one of the pieces a transaction is assembled from. The chapter names the two sides, the inputs that spend funds and the outputs that receive them, and the small difference between them that pays the miner. To describe them exactly this group also explains the unspent output, the identifier by which a transaction is referred to, the size that a transaction occupies, the fee rate by which miners compare fees, and the ledger image that gives the whole structure its meaning (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Reading a transaction correctly means knowing which part does which job. An input says what is being spent and who allows it, an output says what is created and who may spend it next, and the fee is whatever remains. Confusing these parts leads to the classic misunderstandings, such as believing that a payment is a single amount sent from one address to another.

The parts are met in every block explorer, which retrieves a transaction and shows what it spends and what it creates, and in every wallet that has to assemble them. The chapter's own illustration shows Alice's payment to Bob's store as one transaction whose input is an earlier output and whose two outputs are the payment and the change. The same transaction is printed byte by byte in the book's chapter on transactions, which lets this course check every figure in its description.

The parts work as a single balance that the protocol never writes down. An input does not carry an amount: it carries a reference to an earlier output, and the amount is whatever that output said. An output does carry an amount, together with the condition under which it may be spent next. So the value of a transaction is fixed entirely by what it points back to, and the fee is not a field at all but the gap between the inputs it consumes and the outputs it creates - for the chapter's own payment, 100000 satoshis in against 75000 and 20000 out, leaving 5000. Because a miner's room in a block is measured in weight rather than in value, that gap only becomes a price once it is divided by the transaction's virtual size, which is its weight divided by four and rounded up: 569 weight units give 143 virtual bytes and a fee rate of 34.97 satoshis for each of them. The identifier and the outpoint are what make the references possible, since an input has to name both a transaction and which of its outputs is meant (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Double-entry ledger
nodes.body: A ledger is a book of record in which each movement of value is written down as an entry, and double-entry bookkeeping is the practice of recording every movement from two sides: what leaves one account and what arrives in another. The chapter uses this picture directly. It says that transactions are like lines in a double-entry bookkeeping ledger, with one or more inputs, which spend funds, on one side and one or more outputs, which receive funds, on the other (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A ledger is a book of record in which each movement of value is written down as an entry, and double-entry bookkeeping is the practice of recording every movement from two sides: what leaves one account and what arrives in another. The chapter uses this picture directly. It says that transactions are like lines in a double-entry bookkeeping ledger, with one or more inputs, which spend funds, on one side and one or more outputs, which receive funds, on the other (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The image gives a student a first mental model for something that has no physical form. Instead of thinking of coins travelling between wallets, one thinks of entries in a shared book, each entry saying which earlier entries it consumes and which new ones it creates. The same image explains why the blockchain is described as the authoritative journal of all transactions: a journal is the chronological book in which such entries are first written down (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The picture appears in the chapter's figure of a transaction as a bookkeeping line, in the discussion of the transaction fee, and in the very first overview of Bitcoin, where the system is said to consist of users with wallets, transactions that are propagated across the network, and miners who produce the consensus blockchain, the authoritative journal of all transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nakamoto's paper speaks of a record that cannot be changed without redoing the proof of work (Nakamoto, 2008).

In an ordinary ledger the two sides of an entry balance exactly. In Bitcoin they balance only once the fee is counted: the outputs add up to slightly less than the inputs, and the difference is an implied fee collected by the miner (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For Alice's payment the inputs total 100000 satoshis, the outputs 75000 and 20000, and the fee 5000, so that outputs plus fee equal inputs. The check sum([75000, 20000, 5000]) == 100000 evaluates to True, and the same total follows when the two output amounts are read out of the transaction's own bytes.

The analogy is a teaching device and has limits. A bookkeeper's ledger names accounts and their owners, while a Bitcoin transaction names no person: it refers to earlier outputs and to conditions for spending the new ones. The transaction data also has no field for a running balance per owner. A balance is computed by a wallet, which adds up the unspent outputs it can spend.

nodes.label: Input
nodes.body: An input is the part of a transaction that spends funds. It does not contain coins; it points to an earlier transaction's output, and it carries the proof that the person spending is entitled to do so. In the chapter's figure, the input of Alice's payment is labelled Tx1:0, meaning the output of her earlier transaction in which Joe sold her bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An input is the part of a transaction that spends funds. It does not contain coins; it points to an earlier transaction's output, and it carries the proof that the person spending is entitled to do so. In the chapter's figure, the input of Alice's payment is labelled Tx1:0, meaning the output of her earlier transaction in which Joe sold her bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Inputs are what turn separate transactions into a connected history. Because every input names the output it consumes, anyone can follow a payment backward through the chain of ownership, and anyone can see whether the same output is being spent twice. The proof of ownership in the input, a digital signature that can be independently validated by anyone, is what lets strangers accept a payment without knowing who the payer is (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Inputs are found in every transaction. A simple payment has one input, a consolidation has many, and a miner's reward transaction has a special input that spends nothing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). When a wallet constructs a transaction, choosing the inputs is its first task, as the concepts on coin selection and on getting the right inputs explain.

The book's chapter on transactions calls the reference that an input contains an outpoint. It consists of the 32-byte identifier of the transaction in which the funds were received and an output index, a 4-byte unsigned integer counted from zero that picks one output of that transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A full node uses the outpoint to find the earlier output, and from it learns the amount and the conditions for spending it. Real transactions do not state the value of their inputs; software must look up the output that is referenced, which for Alice's real transaction is an output of 100,000 satoshis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Reading the bytes of that transaction shows one small difference from the figure: the output index stored in the input is 1, whereas the simplified figure labels the reference Tx1:0. The identifier inside the input is also stored in the opposite byte order to the one used when it is displayed: reversing the bytes eb3ae38f... of the stored form gives 4ac54180..., the form that Bitcoin Core's commands accept (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

An input cannot be partly spent, in the same way that a banknote cannot be torn in two: the whole of the referenced output is consumed, and any surplus must be sent back to the payer as change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word input also invites a misreading. It does not mean money entering an account, but an earlier output being used up. And a figure is a simplification: when a detail matters, such as which output of the earlier transaction is meant, read it from the transaction itself.

nodes.definition: An input spends funds by referring to an earlier transaction's output and proving ownership with a digital signature.

nodes.label: Output
nodes.body: An output is the part of a transaction that receives funds. It consists of an amount, counted in satoshis, and a script, the condition that must be satisfied to spend that amount later. In Alice's payment one output carries 75000 satoshis for Bob's store and another carries 20000 satoshis back to Alice, so the outputs together add up to 95000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An output is the part of a transaction that receives funds. It consists of an amount, counted in satoshis, and a script, the condition that must be satisfied to spend that amount later. In Alice's payment one output carries 75000 satoshis for Bob's store and another carries 20000 satoshis back to Alice, so the outputs together add up to 95000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Outputs are where ownership is created. The chapter explains that an output is created with a script saying, in effect, that it is paid to whoever can present a signature from the key corresponding to Bob's public address. Because only Bob's wallet holds that key, only Bob can later spend the output. The book calls this encumbering the output with a demand for a signature from Bob (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Outputs are met in every transaction. They are also what a wallet counts when it reports a balance: the balance is the sum of the outputs that the wallet's keys can spend and that nobody has spent yet. Each output that is still unspent is a coin-like unit that a later transaction can take as an input. The book notes that an output can hold as little as zero and as much as 21 million bitcoins, a limit explained under the concept of consensus rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A transaction can have several outputs, and they are numbered from zero in the order in which they appear, which is what the second half of an outpoint refers to. In the bytes of Alice's real transaction the output at position 0 carries 20000 satoshis, her change, and the output at position 1 carries 75000 satoshis for Bob's store; the later figure of the chain accordingly shows Bob spending the output Tx2:1. The sum of all outputs is at most the sum of all inputs, and what is left over is the fee: sum([75000, 20000]) evaluates to 95000, and the 5000 satoshis missing from the 100000 that Alice spent form the fee.

Outputs are all-or-nothing in the same way as inputs: a later transaction takes a whole output or leaves it alone. An output also never expires. It stays unspent, and is counted in every full node's database, until a valid transaction spends it, which is why the book warns that outputs of very small value can become uneconomical to spend and are a burden on the nodes that must keep track of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Transaction fee
nodes.body: The transaction fee is a small payment to the miner who includes a transaction in a block. It is never written in the transaction as a separate number. It is implied by the difference between the value of the inputs and the value of the outputs, so any value that the outputs do not claim goes to the miner (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The transaction fee is a small payment to the miner who includes a transaction in a block. It is never written in the transaction as a separate number. It is implied by the difference between the value of the inputs and the value of the outputs, so any value that the outputs do not claim goes to the miner (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The fee is how a user asks the network to process a payment in a timely fashion. The chapter on fees explains that it is not a fee in the usual sense: it is not an amount set by the protocol or by any miner, but much more like a bid in an auction for the limited space in a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is one of two payments that reward a miner, the other being the newly created bitcoins of the block reward. Nakamoto's paper already described it: if the output value of a transaction is less than its input value, the difference is a fee added to the incentive of the block containing the transaction (Nakamoto, 2008).

The wallet adds the fee when it constructs the transaction; Alice only has to choose a destination, an amount and a fee. The fee can always be read as the difference between the sum of the inputs and the sum of the outputs, and a miner's reward transaction collects the sum of all fees in its block.

For Alice's payment the arithmetic is simple. Her input is Tx1's output of 100000 satoshis, the two outputs total 95000 satoshis, and so 100000 - sum([75000, 20000]) evaluates to 5000: the fee is 5000 satoshis. The figure is derived from the amounts that the book prints, and it is the miner, not Bob, who receives it. The book's own diagram of the chain lists the same fee of 5000 for the transaction to Bob's store and a fee of 8000 for Bob's onward transaction.

Because the fee is implied, a wallet that mistakes the amounts can send an enormous fee without any warning from the format, since there is no field to check. Wallets should therefore make it hard to pay an excessive fee by accident, while still allowing it on purpose, as the chapter on fees advises (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Fees also do not depend on the value being sent, but on how much space the transaction takes, which the concepts of size and fee rate explain.

nodes.definition: The fee is implied: the difference between the inputs and the outputs, collected by the miner who includes the transaction.

nodes.label: Transaction size
nodes.body: The size of a transaction is the room that it takes up in a block. Because every block can hold only a limited amount of transaction data, software needs a measure for it. The book names the modern unit weight, and an alternative expression of the same measure, the virtual byte or vbyte, of which one equals four units of weight; a vbyte is thus easy to compare with the plain byte, the unit of eight bits, that older blocks used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The size of a transaction is the room that it takes up in a block. Because every block can hold only a limited amount of transaction data, software needs a measure for it. The book names the modern unit weight, and an alternative expression of the same measure, the virtual byte or vbyte, of which one equals four units of weight; a vbyte is thus easy to compare with the plain byte, the unit of eight bits, that older blocks used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Size is what makes block space a scarce good. A block is limited to 4 million units of weight, so the number of transactions that fit depends on how large each one is, not on how much value it moves (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A payment of a million bitcoins and one of a single satoshi may occupy the same room, and a miner who has to choose between them looks at the fee that each pays for that room, which is the idea behind the fee rate.

Size appears whenever a wallet shows how much a payment costs, and in the figures that block explorers and Bitcoin Core report for a transaction. Alice's real transaction is reported by Bitcoin Core as 194 bytes in size, 143 vbytes and 569 units of weight (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's consensus code defines the block limit as MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT of 4,000,000 and the factor between the weight and the old byte as WITNESS_SCALE_FACTOR of 4 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The weight of a transaction is the sum of the weights of its fields, each field's serialized size in bytes being multiplied by a factor (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The factors are chosen so that the part of a transaction that holds its proofs counts for less than the rest, which keeps the cost of spending an output low. Reading the 194 bytes of Alice's transaction and counting the proof part once and everything else four times gives 569 units of weight, and 569 divided by four, rounded up, gives 143 vbytes, as (569 + 3) // 4 evaluates to 143 in whole numbers. A block of 4,000,000 units of weight is therefore a block of at most one million vbytes.

The three numbers answer different questions. The size in bytes is the length of the serialized data, the weight is what the block limit counts, and the virtual byte is the weight expressed in a familiar unit. Mixing them up is a common reason for fee figures that do not match between two tools. The factors themselves belong to a later chapter on transactions, and a student should treat the number 4 as a fixed part of today's rules, not a law of nature.

nodes.example: Alice's payment: 194 bytes, weight 569, 143 vbytes
nodes.definition: A block has limited room; transactions are measured in weight units, four of which make one virtual byte (vbyte), and a miner compares them by fee per unit.

nodes.label: Fee rate
nodes.body: The fee rate is the fee a transaction pays for each unit of the space it takes in a block. Miners do not compare transactions by their total fee alone; they divide the fee by the size of the transaction, as a shopper divides the price of a bag of rice by its weight to find the best deal. The most common unit today is the satoshi per virtual byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The fee rate is the fee a transaction pays for each unit of the space it takes in a block. Miners do not compare transactions by their total fee alone; they divide the fee by the size of the transaction, as a shopper divides the price of a bag of rice by its weight to find the best deal. The most common unit today is the satoshi per virtual byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Block space is scarce, and the fee rate is the price at which it is sold. A transaction pays a single fee however large it is, but a larger transaction leaves room for fewer others in the block, so a miner who wants the most revenue from a block fills it with the transactions that pay the highest fee per unit of space. The chapter says accordingly that transactions are added to a new block prioritized by the highest fee rate first (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Fee rates matter whenever a wallet lets a user choose how quickly a payment should be processed. A user who wants a payment confirmed sooner chooses a higher fee rate; one who can wait chooses a lower one. The book lists several units in which a fee rate is written, among them satoshis per virtual byte, which it calls the most commonly used today, and bitcoin per kilo-vbyte, which Bitcoin Core mainly uses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The calculation is a plain division. Alice's payment paid 5000 satoshis and takes up 143 virtual bytes, so its fee rate is 5000 / 143, which rounds to 34.97 satoshis per virtual byte. A miner sorts the candidate transactions by this ratio and takes them from the top until the block is full. The size of 143 comes from the transaction's own bytes, as the concept of transaction size shows, and the fee of 5000 from the amounts in the chapter.

The units are a source of expensive mistakes. The book warns that a fee rate copied from a field with one denominator into a field with another can lead to paying a thousand times too much, and that switching the numerator could mean a hundred million times too much (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fee rate is also a market price, not a rule of the protocol, so what counts as a good rate changes with demand for block space; the figure of 34.97 describes one payment, not a recommendation.

nodes.example: fee divided by size
nodes.definition: A miner compares transactions by their fee for the space they use, the fee rate, usually quoted in satoshis per virtual byte.

nodes.label: Unspent transaction output
nodes.body: An unspent transaction output, abbreviated UTXO, is a transaction output that has not yet been used as an input by any later transaction. The glossary defines it as an unspent transaction output that can be spent as an input in a new transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet's bitcoins are, in this sense, nothing other than the unspent outputs it can unlock.

paras.text: An unspent transaction output, abbreviated UTXO, is a transaction output that has not yet been used as an input by any later transaction. The glossary defines it as an unspent transaction output that can be spent as an input in a new transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet's bitcoins are, in this sense, nothing other than the unspent outputs it can unlock.

The idea explains how Bitcoin keeps track of ownership without accounts. A full node holds a copy of every confirmed transaction's unspent outputs, and a valid new transaction may spend only outputs that are in that set. Each time a new block arrives, the outputs that its transactions spend are removed from the database and the outputs they create are added, so the set of unspent outputs is the current state of the whole system, and a double-spend is simply an attempt to use an output that is already gone (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter meets UTXOs when it describes how Alice's wallet gets the right inputs. A wallet that runs on a full node holds every unspent output, while many user wallets run as lightweight clients that track only their own (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The network chapter adds that some implementations keep a database of all unspent outputs, which holds millions of entries and, unlike the mempool, does not usually differ between nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Mark each output with a flag that says whether it has been spent. Starting from the outputs of Alice's chain, the expression that lists the outputs whose flag is false returns Tx2:0 and Tx2:1, because Tx1:0 was consumed by Alice's payment. A node that receives a new transaction performs the same filter at scale: for each outpoint it looks the output up in its set, rejects the transaction if the output is missing or already spent, and otherwise treats it as valid in this respect.

Two misreadings are common. An unspent output is not an account balance, and a wallet's total is the sum of many separate outputs, each of which is spent whole. And an unspent output is still tied to a condition: it counts as spendable only for the party that can satisfy its script. Wallets therefore track UTXOs for their own keys and ignore the rest.

nodes.example: an output nobody has spent
nodes.definition: An unspent transaction output (UTXO) is an output that no later transaction has consumed; full nodes keep the set of all of them.

nodes.label: Transaction identifier
nodes.body: The transaction identifier, or txid, is the 32-byte name of a transaction. It is derived from the transaction's own data by a hash function, so it is not assigned by anyone, and two different transactions cannot sensibly share one. In the chapter the txid is what an input uses to refer to the transaction in which funds were received (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The transaction identifier, or txid, is the 32-byte name of a transaction. It is derived from the transaction's own data by a hash function, so it is not assigned by anyone, and two different transactions cannot sensibly share one. In the chapter the txid is what an input uses to refer to the transaction in which funds were received (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Names make references possible. Because a txid summarizes the transaction it identifies, a reference to it cannot be redirected to different content, and anyone holding the transaction can recompute the name and confirm it. This is also what makes a chain of transactions auditable: every link is a txid plus a position, and both can be checked independently by any node.

The txid is the search key in every block explorer: the chapter says that explorers accept a Bitcoin address, a transaction hash, a block number or a block hash. The book prints the identifier of Alice's payment to Bob as 466200308696215bbc949d5141a49a4138ecdfdfaa2a8029c1f9bcecd1f96177, which is 64 hexadecimal characters, since the book notes that it takes 64 hexadecimal characters to display 32 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Bitcoin Core computes the identifier by hashing the serialized transaction without its proof data (Bitcoin Core, 2026); hashing means applying the double SHA-256 construction that the concept of the hash function shows, and the result is shown with its bytes reversed. Doing exactly that to the 194 bytes of Alice's real transaction reproduces the printed identifier. The reversal is the byte-order trap the book describes: a hash is displayed to users in one byte order but used internally in another, so the identifier that the transaction's input stores, eb3ae38f..., is the earlier transaction's identifier read the other way round, and reversing its bytes gives 4ac54180... (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A txid belongs to the transaction as it was built, and it is not proof that the transaction has been confirmed: a payment can have a txid and still wait in the mempool. The byte-order difference is a frequent source of confusion for programmers: pasting the stored form into a block explorer, or the displayed form into a program that expects the stored one, finds nothing, because the hash is the same and only its reading differs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a 32-byte name for Alice's payment
nodes.definition: The transaction identifier, or txid, is a 32-byte value derived from the transaction's data; an input points to an earlier output by txid and position.

nodes.label: Script
nodes.body: A script is a small program written in Bitcoin's own scripting language, called Script. The book describes it as a Forth-like, stack-based language and says that both the script placed in an output and the legacy input script used in a spending transaction are written in it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). An output script specifies the conditions that must be met to spend the output in the future, such as who is authorized to spend it and how they will be authenticated; an input script satisfies those conditions and allows the output to be spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A script is a small program written in Bitcoin's own scripting language, called Script. The book describes it as a Forth-like, stack-based language and says that both the script placed in an output and the legacy input script used in a spending transaction are written in it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). An output script specifies the conditions that must be met to spend the output in the future, such as who is authorized to spend it and how they will be authenticated; an input script satisfies those conditions and allows the output to be spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Scripts are what make spending conditions flexible without making the rules of the network complicated. The first version of Bitcoin did not simply attach a public key to an output; it let payments go to an output script and let the spender answer with an input script, so that conditions such as needing two signatures out of two keys could be expressed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's chapter on keys states the idea in one sentence: bitcoins are received to an output script that acts like a public key, and spending is authorized by an input script that acts like a signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In the chapter, the script is the thing Alice's wallet puts in the output when it encumbers the payment with a demand for a signature from Bob (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every full node runs the scripts of every transaction it validates. The most common form in the early years was a payment to the hash of a public key; Alice's real transaction uses newer forms of output, and its two output scripts have different lengths, 34 bytes for the change and 22 bytes for the payment, as the bytes of the printed transaction show (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Script is a stack-based language: it reads items from left to right, pushes numbers onto a stack, and operators remove items from the stack, act on them and may push a result back. The book's first example is the script 2 3 OP_ADD 5 OP_EQUAL. The numbers 2 and 3 are pushed, OP_ADD replaces them by their sum 5, the number 5 is pushed, and OP_EQUAL replaces the two top items by TRUE if they are equal. A small interpreter that follows these rules ends with the stack [True] (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A transaction is valid when the script ends with a true value on top of the stack, and the input script and the output script are executed separately with the stack handed from one to the other (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Script is deliberately limited. It has no loops and only conditional flow control, so it is not Turing complete, which guarantees predictable execution times; and it is stateless, so a script behaves the same way on every system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's arithmetic example is also a warning: an output with the script 3 OP_ADD 5 OP_EQUAL can be spent by anyone who knows that the number 2 satisfies it, because a script grants authority to whoever can satisfy it, not to a named person (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 2 3 OP_ADD 5 OP_EQUAL
nodes.definition: A script is a short program in Bitcoin's stack-based language; an output carries the conditions for spending it, and the spender supplies data that makes the program end with TRUE.

io.code: (lambda s: [s.append(s.pop() + s.pop()) if t == 'OP_ADD' else s.append(s.pop() == s.pop()) if t == 'OP_EQUAL' else s.append(int(t)) for t in '2 3 OP_ADD 5 OP_EQUAL'.split()] and s)([])

nodes.label: Serialization
nodes.body: Serialization is the writing of a structured object as a flat sequence of bytes, in an order and a format on which sender and receiver agree, so that the receiver can rebuild the same structure. A transaction in a wallet is a structure of inputs, outputs and amounts; a transaction on the network is a string of bytes. The book names this form directly, calling serialized Bitcoin transactions the data format that software uses for sending transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Serialization is the writing of a structured object as a flat sequence of bytes, in an order and a format on which sender and receiver agree, so that the receiver can rebuild the same structure. A transaction in a wallet is a structure of inputs, outputs and amounts; a transaction on the network is a string of bytes. The book names this form directly, calling serialized Bitcoin transactions the data format that software uses for sending transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Everything exact in this chapter depends on the serialized form. The identifier of a transaction is a hash of its bytes, so the bytes must be defined to the last detail; the size that a fee pays for is the length of those bytes; and the signature commits to them. If two programs serialized the same transaction differently they would compute different identifiers and the network would not work. This is why the description of the format belongs to the consensus-critical part of Bitcoin and not to a matter of taste.

The reader meets the serialized form as a long hexadecimal string. The book prints Alice's real transaction in that form in its chapters on Bitcoin Core and on transactions, and the same string appears in both; it is 194 bytes long, and every number this course quotes about that transaction was read out of it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Wallets exchange this form when a transaction is signed on one device and sent from another, and block explorers offer it for download.

The format is a sequence of fixed and variable fields. Amounts are eight-byte integers written with the least significant byte first, so the change output's 20,000 satoshis appear in the bytes as 204e000000000000, and reading those eight bytes back as a little-endian integer gives 20000, as the calculation above shows. Counts, such as the number of inputs, are written in a compact form that uses one byte for small values and more for larger ones. Reading the whole string field by field recovers the one input, the two outputs and the witness, which is how the checks of this chapter obtain the amounts without trusting any figure in the text.

A serialized transaction is not readable by eye, and it is not encrypted either: it is simply a precise encoding, and anyone with the format can decode it. Two cautions follow. First, the identifier is computed from the serialization without the witness data, so the same payment has two byte-lengths and two hashes, which the concepts of the identifier and of the size explain. Second, the hexadecimal string is a printing of the bytes, not the bytes themselves, so a program must decode the text before hashing it.

nodes.example: the 194 bytes of Alice's payment
nodes.definition: Serialization is the writing of a structure as a flat sequence of bytes in a fixed order, which is the form in which a transaction is sent, hashed and stored.

nodes.label: Byte order
nodes.body: Byte order, also called endianness, is the direction in which the individual bytes of a multi-byte value are written down. Writing the most significant byte first is called big-endian and is what people do when they write ordinary numbers; writing the least significant byte first is called little-endian and is what most processors do internally. Both orders describe the same value, and a reader must know which one is meant, because the two printings look like completely different numbers.

paras.text: Byte order, also called endianness, is the direction in which the individual bytes of a multi-byte value are written down. Writing the most significant byte first is called big-endian and is what people do when they write ordinary numbers; writing the least significant byte first is called little-endian and is what most processors do internally. Both orders describe the same value, and a reader must know which one is meant, because the two printings look like completely different numbers.

Bitcoin uses both orders, and the mismatch is a standing source of confusion that the book itself warns about: hash digests are displayed to users in one byte order but are used internally in a different byte order (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student who does not know this will conclude that the identifier stored inside Alice's input is a different transaction from the one her wallet shows, and a programmer who does not know it will search a block explorer for a hash that exists and find nothing.

The clearest example is in this chapter's own data. The identifier of the transaction in which Joe paid Alice is printed by the book and accepted by Bitcoin Core as 4ac54180...8fe33aeb, while the bytes stored inside Alice's input, read in the order in which they appear, spell eb3ae38f...8041c54a (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The amounts in a serialized transaction are stored little-endian, and so are the four-byte fields of a block header, while a hash is displayed big-endian; both forms occur within the same 194 bytes.

Reversing a sequence of bytes converts between the two readings. Taking the displayed identifier, decoding it from hexadecimal into 32 bytes, reversing them and printing them again gives the stored form, whose first eight bytes are eb3ae38f27191aa5, as the calculation above shows; doing it a second time returns the original. The reversal is on whole bytes, not on hexadecimal characters: reversing the characters of the string would exchange the two halves of every byte and give a different value altogether.

Three practical rules follow. Reverse bytes, never characters. Reverse only values that the convention requires, which in this chapter means transaction and block hashes, not the witness or the output scripts. And when a tool reports something that does not match, try the other order before concluding that the data is wrong, because the book's note about the two byte orders applies to almost every hash a reader will paste from one program into another (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the identifier read both ways
nodes.definition: Byte order is the direction in which the bytes of a value are written; Bitcoin displays hashes in one direction and stores them in the other, so the same value looks like two.

nodes.label: Outpoint
nodes.body: An outpoint is the exact name of one transaction output: the identifier of the transaction that created it together with the position of that output within the transaction. The book's chapter on transactions uses the word for the field inside an input and states its shape, an outpoint containing a 32-byte transaction identifier followed by an output index that is a four-byte unsigned integer starting from zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's figures write an outpoint in the short form Tx1:0, a transaction label and a position separated by a colon.

paras.text: An outpoint is the exact name of one transaction output: the identifier of the transaction that created it together with the position of that output within the transaction. The book's chapter on transactions uses the word for the field inside an input and states its shape, an outpoint containing a 32-byte transaction identifier followed by an output index that is a four-byte unsigned integer starting from zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's figures write an outpoint in the short form Tx1:0, a transaction label and a position separated by a colon.

The outpoint is the link that makes the whole structure of Bitcoin work. Because an input names one and only one earlier output, a node can look it up, learn the amount and the spending condition, and check whether it is still unspent; and because the identifier is a hash, the reference cannot be redirected to other content. The set of unspent outputs that a full node keeps is in effect a table indexed by outpoints, so the double-spend check is a lookup of one outpoint.

The reader meets outpoints in block explorers, where every input is shown with the transaction it spends and the position within it, and in the chapter's two figures of transaction chains, where arrows join an output to the input that consumes it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Alice's real transaction the outpoint names the transaction 4ac54180...8fe33aeb and the output at index 1, and Bob's later transaction, the chapter says, spends Tx2:1, the output of 75,000 satoshis.

An outpoint is formed by putting the two parts together, as the small example does by joining an abbreviated identifier and the index with a colon. In the serialized bytes the two parts sit next to each other: 32 bytes of hash, stored in the reversed order that the concept of byte order describes, then four bytes holding the index as a little-endian integer. Nothing else is needed, because the amount and the conditions are not repeated in the input; the book stresses that transactions do not explicitly include the value of their inputs and that software must find the previous output (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two warnings. The index counts from zero, so the first output of a transaction is output 0 and the familiar off-by-one error here means spending the wrong output or none at all. And an outpoint is not an address and not an owner: it identifies a position in the ledger, and who may spend it is decided by the script in the output it names, which is why a chain of outpoints can be followed without learning anybody's identity.

nodes.example: txid 4ac54180... index 1
nodes.definition: An outpoint is the pair of a transaction identifier and an output index that names exactly one output; an input consists of an outpoint and the data that satisfies it.

nodes.label: Witness
nodes.body: The witness of an input is the data that proves the input may be spent. The book gives the word its general sense, saying that an abstract name for the data held by an input script is a witness, and then names the arrangement that this chapter's transaction uses: the idea of separating the rest of the data in a transaction from its witness for the purpose of generating a transaction identifier is called segregated witness, or segwit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The field that holds the separated data is called the witness structure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The witness of an input is the data that proves the input may be spent. The book gives the word its general sense, saying that an abstract name for the data held by an input script is a witness, and then names the arrangement that this chapter's transaction uses: the idea of separating the rest of the data in a transaction from its witness for the purpose of generating a transaction identifier is called segregated witness, or segwit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The field that holds the separated data is called the witness structure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The separation matters for two reasons that this chapter has already met. The first is the identifier: because the witness is left out of the data that is hashed, the identifier of a transaction no longer changes when the proof changes, which removes a family of problems the book lists as circular dependence and third-party and second-party malleability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is size: the witness bytes are counted once in the weight while the rest are counted four times, which is why spending an output is cheaper than it would otherwise be and why the three size figures of a transaction differ.

The reader meets the witness in the bytes of Alice's transaction, which is written in the newer format. Two extra fields at the front mark that format, which the book calls the extended serialization: a marker that must be zero and a flag that in the current protocol is one, and the book notes that a transaction with no witness must instead use the older, legacy serialization, which has neither those two fields nor the witness structure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The witness in Alice's transaction holds one item of 65 bytes, the signature and its hash-type byte, as the digital-signature concept explains.

The figures can be read out of the transaction. Its full serialization is 194 bytes and the part without the witness is 125, so 69 bytes belong to the witness and the two marker bytes; the weight is the stripped part counted four times plus the witness part once, which the expression computes as 125 times three plus 194, that is 569, the figure Bitcoin Core reports, and dividing by four and rounding up gives the 143 virtual bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The transaction identifier is the double hash of the 125-byte stripped form, which is what Bitcoin Core's source does when it hashes the serialization without witness data (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Do not read the separation as hiding: the witness is public, it is sent to every node and it is committed to by the block, so nothing about it is secret. Note also that the word has two uses that the book keeps apart, the witness as the abstract name for authorizing data and the witness structure as the field that carries it, and that the course's later chapters on authorization open both. Finally, a transaction with no witness at all is serialized in the older format, so a program that assumes the two marker bytes are always present will misread such a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 69 of Alice's 194 bytes
nodes.definition: The witness is the data that proves an input may be spent, kept in its own structure outside the part that the transaction identifier is computed from; this separation is called segregated witness.

nodes.label: Cryptographic foundations
nodes.body: A transaction asks every computer on the network to believe something without trusting anyone: that the person spending certain bitcoins is entitled to spend them. Mathematics alone makes that possible, and this group collects the mathematical tools on which the rest of the chapter silently relies. They are the hash function, which condenses any data into a short fingerprint; the key pair and the public-key cryptography behind it; the elliptic curve on which Bitcoin's keys live; the digital signature that proves entitlement; and the checksum that protects a string from typing errors. The chapter itself only names these tools in passing, so each is given a plain explanation here (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A transaction asks every computer on the network to believe something without trusting anyone: that the person spending certain bitcoins is entitled to spend them. Mathematics alone makes that possible, and this group collects the mathematical tools on which the rest of the chapter silently relies. They are the hash function, which condenses any data into a short fingerprint; the key pair and the public-key cryptography behind it; the elliptic curve on which Bitcoin's keys live; the digital signature that proves entitlement; and the checksum that protects a string from typing errors. The chapter itself only names these tools in passing, so each is given a plain explanation here (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Almost every later concept of the chapter is built from these tools. A transaction identifier is a hash, a block is identified by a hash, mining is a search for a hash with a special property, and an input is accepted only when it carries a signature that was made with the right private key. A reader who does not know what a hash or a signature guarantees cannot judge what the network can and cannot promise. The book's own chapter on keys says it will examine public keys, private keys, signatures and hash functions and then use all of them together to describe addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

These tools are met far beyond Bitcoin. Hash functions protect stored passwords and verify downloaded files, public-key cryptography secures every encrypted web connection, and checksums guard credit card numbers and bank account numbers against typing mistakes. The book notes that public-key cryptography was invented in the 1970s and is a mathematical foundation for modern computer and information security (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin chooses among such tools and combines them in a particular way, and the combination is what is new.

These tools work by turning a long thing into a short thing in a way that cannot be undone, and by turning a secret into a proof that can be checked without it. A hash function reads its input in blocks and stirs each one into a small internal state, so that the result depends on every bit of the input, has the same length whatever the input was, and shares nothing visible with the result of a nearly identical input - about half the bits of a 256-bit output change when one character of the input does. Public-key cryptography supplies the second move: a private key is a number, the public key is what that number reaches on the curve, and computing forward is cheap while computing backward has no known shortcut. A digital signature combines the two, because what is signed is not the transaction but a hash of it, which is why a signature cannot be lifted onto a different transaction. A checksum is the same hashing used for a humbler purpose, detecting a copying mistake rather than resisting an attacker (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Nakamoto, 2008).

Two warnings are in order. First, these tools are quite different in what they promise: a hash function provides no secrecy, a signature provides no secrecy either, and neither is the same thing as encryption. Second, a clever tool is only as safe as its use. The book warns that anything less than completely random when a private key is chosen can significantly reduce the security of the key and of the bitcoins it controls (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Read each concept below with the question what exactly does this guarantee, and what does it leave open?

nodes.label: Hash function
nodes.body: A hash function is a procedure that takes data of any length, however long or short, scrambles it thoroughly and outputs a value of fixed length, which is called the hash or the digest of the data. The book describes it as a function that takes a potentially large amount of data, scrambles it, and outputs a fixed amount of data, and it points out two properties. The same input always gives the same output, and a secure function makes it impractical for anybody to choose a different input that produces an output seen before (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A hash function is a procedure that takes data of any length, however long or short, scrambles it thoroughly and outputs a value of fixed length, which is called the hash or the digest of the data. The book describes it as a function that takes a potentially large amount of data, scrambles it, and outputs a fixed amount of data, and it points out two properties. The same input always gives the same output, and a secure function makes it impractical for anybody to choose a different input that produces an output seen before (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Because of these two properties a digest works as a commitment: it is a promise that, in practice, only one input produces it. This lets Bitcoin refer to large objects by a short name that nobody can redirect to something else. A hash is also the raw material of mining, since the network's lottery is a search for an input whose hash falls below a threshold, and nobody can find such an input except by trying one after another (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Without hash functions Bitcoin would need a central party to say what a transaction or a block is.

Bitcoin uses the function called SHA-256, whose output is always 256 bits long, that is, 64 hexadecimal digits, whatever the size of the input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The identifier of a transaction, the identifier of a block, each node of a merkle tree and the proof of work are all results of applying SHA-256 twice in a row, which the book calls double-SHA256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Outside Bitcoin the same family of functions checks the integrity of downloaded software and stores passwords in a form that cannot be read back.

You can try it directly. Hashing the phrase Hello, world! followed by a line break with SHA-256 gives d9014c46...f72ff5, the value printed in the book, and the result has 64 hexadecimal digits, that is 256 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Changing a single character changes the whole result: hashing the same phrase with a question mark in place of the exclamation mark produces a digest that differs from the first in 61 of its 64 digits. Nobody can predict how a digest will change, and this unpredictability, together with the fixed length, is what makes searching for a special hash a pure matter of trial.

A hash function is not encryption. It has no key and no way back, so you cannot recover the input from the digest, but if the possible inputs are few, anyone can simply hash all of them and compare. A digest also says nothing about who made the data: anyone can compute it. And the guarantee that two different inputs will not give the same digest is a statement about the effort needed to find such a pair, not an absolute impossibility, because a function with a fixed-length output must map many inputs to the same output; the book calls such a pair a collision and says finding one is computationally infeasible (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a fixed-size fingerprint of any data
nodes.definition: A hash function turns data of any length into a fixed-length value that is easy to compute, always the same for the same input, and impractical to steer toward a chosen result.

nodes.label: Key pair
nodes.body: A key pair consists of two numbers that belong together: a private key and a public key. In Bitcoin the private key is a number, usually derived from a number picked at random, and the public key is calculated from it by a mathematical operation that is easy in one direction and impractical in the other. The book states that a Bitcoin wallet contains a collection of key pairs, each consisting of a private key and a public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A key pair consists of two numbers that belong together: a private key and a public key. In Bitcoin the private key is a number, usually derived from a number picked at random, and the public key is calculated from it by a mathematical operation that is easy in one direction and impractical in the other. The book states that a Bitcoin wallet contains a collection of key pairs, each consisting of a private key and a public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The pair separates two abilities that ordinary passwords combine. Anyone may be told the public key, and with it can receive funds or check a signature, but only the holder of the private key can produce a valid signature. The book says that control over the private key is the root of user control over all funds associated with the corresponding public key, and that revealing the private key to third parties is equivalent to giving them control over the bitcoins it secures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same text adds that a lost private key cannot be recovered, and the funds it secured are lost forever.

Every wallet manages key pairs, as the chapter's wallets for Alice and Bob do, although the chapter itself never shows one. The private key is usually written as 64 hexadecimal digits, that is, 256 bits, and the book gives 1E99423A...A526AEDD as an example of a randomly generated private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Outside Bitcoin, key pairs are what secure shell logins, signed software updates and encrypted email use as their basis.

The private key can be any number from 0 up to n minus 1, where n is a constant slightly smaller than 2 to the power 256, defined as the order of the elliptic curve that Bitcoin uses; to create one, software picks a random 256-bit number and checks that it is below n (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The public key K is then obtained by multiplying a fixed point G on the curve by the private key k, so that K equals k times G. The book prints the public key of its example key as the coordinates x = F028892B...DC341A and y = 07CF33DA...2E505BDB, and an implementation of the multiplication in the Python standard library reproduces both numbers from the private key.

The private key is a number, not a file or a word, and its secrecy depends entirely on how it was chosen. The book advises against writing one's own random number generator and recommends a cryptographically secure generator seeded with enough entropy, because a process that is less than completely random can significantly reduce the security of the key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The public key cannot be turned back into the private key by the known mathematics, but this is a statement about today's computers and algorithms, not a proof that it can never be done.

nodes.example: a secret number and the public value made from it
nodes.definition: A key pair is a private key, a secret 256-bit number, together with the public key calculated from it; the public key can be shared, the private key must not be.

nodes.label: Public-key cryptography
nodes.body: Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is a branch of cryptography in which each participant has two related keys instead of one shared secret. One key can be made public and the other must stay private. It rests on mathematical functions that are easy to calculate in one direction and infeasible to calculate in the opposite direction with the computers and algorithms available today. The book names two such functions, prime number exponentiation and elliptic curve multiplication, and says that Bitcoin uses elliptic curve addition and multiplication (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is a branch of cryptography in which each participant has two related keys instead of one shared secret. One key can be made public and the other must stay private. It rests on mathematical functions that are easy to calculate in one direction and infeasible to calculate in the opposite direction with the computers and algorithms available today. The book names two such functions, prime number exponentiation and elliptic curve multiplication, and says that Bitcoin uses elliptic curve addition and multiplication (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Before this invention, two parties who wanted to protect a message needed to share a secret in advance, which does not scale to a network of strangers. Public-key cryptography removes that need. The book explains that in Bitcoin it is not used to encrypt transactions, because transactions are public. Its useful property is the ability to generate digital signatures: a private key can be applied to a transaction to produce a signature that only someone who knows the private key could have made, yet anyone with the public key and the transaction can verify it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

You use it every time a browser opens a secure web page, and wallets use it every time they spend. The book says that public-key cryptography was invented in the 1970s and is a mathematical foundation for modern computer and information security (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Bitcoin, the public key is used to receive funds and the private key is used to sign the transactions that spend them, and a node verifies the signatures without ever learning a private key.

A tiny example shows the idea of a one-way function. In arithmetic with remainders modulo 17, the power 3 to the 7th gives 2187, which leaves the remainder 11 when divided by 17, and computing this takes a few multiplications. Going backward means asking which exponent gives remainder 11; with so small a modulus one can simply try all exponents and find that the answer is 7. With numbers of 256 bits the same search is hopeless, and that gap between forward and backward effort is what the cryptography relies on. Bitcoin uses the elliptic-curve version of this problem, which the concept of the elliptic curve describes.

The security is conditional. It depends on the assumption that no efficient method of reversing the function is known, and on the keys having been chosen at random; the book says that the private key must stay secret at all times and be protected from accidental loss (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word public must not be misread: the public key may be shared, but the private key must never be. Note, too, that signing is not encrypting, so a Bitcoin transaction is readable by everyone, and its privacy rests on other things, such as the fact that addresses name no person.

nodes.example: easy forward, impractical backward
nodes.definition: Public-key cryptography uses a pair of related keys and a mathematical function that is easy to compute in one direction and infeasible to reverse, which makes unforgeable digital signatures possible.

io.code: [k for k in range(1, 17) if pow(3, k, 17) == 11]

nodes.label: Elliptic curve
nodes.body: An elliptic curve is the set of points whose two coordinates satisfy a certain cubic equation. Bitcoin uses one particular curve, defined in a standard called secp256k1, whose equation is the very simple y squared equals x cubed plus 7. The calculation is done not with ordinary real numbers but modulo a very large prime number p, that is, over a finite field, so that the curve becomes a scattered pattern of points rather than a smooth line (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An elliptic curve is the set of points whose two coordinates satisfy a certain cubic equation. Bitcoin uses one particular curve, defined in a standard called secp256k1, whose equation is the very simple y squared equals x cubed plus 7. The calculation is done not with ordinary real numbers but modulo a very large prime number p, that is, over a finite field, so that the curve becomes a scattered pattern of points rather than a smooth line (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Points on an elliptic curve can be added to each other by a geometric rule, and adding a point to itself repeatedly gives multiplication of a point by a whole number. This multiplication is easy to carry out but, when the numbers are large, practically impossible to undo: given the result, finding the number is the discrete logarithm problem. The book calls this a trap door function and says it is the basis for unforgeable and secure digital signatures that prove control over bitcoin funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin's choice of this particular curve and its constants is part of the protocol, so every implementation must use exactly the same ones.

The curve appears wherever Bitcoin software derives a public key from a private key or checks a signature. The book notes that many implementations use the libsecp256k1 library for the curve mathematics (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and Bitcoin Core carries a copy of it in its source tree. Elliptic curves are also used in other protocols, such as secure web connections, because they give strong security with short keys.

The curve secp256k1 is fixed by the constants p, the generator point G and the order n. The prime is p = 2^256 - 2^32 - 977, which the book writes as 2^256 minus 2^32 minus 2^9 minus 2^8 minus 2^7 minus 2^6 minus 2^4 minus 1; the two forms are equal, because the powers from 2^9 down to 2^4 and the 1 add up to 977 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The generator point is the same for everybody, and a check with exact integer arithmetic shows that its two coordinates satisfy the curve equation modulo p, since the remainder of y squared minus x cubed minus 7 is 0. Over a toy field of only 17 elements the same equation has just 17 pairs of coordinates, which is why a picture of such a curve is only an illustration.

The picture of a smooth curve in textbooks is misleading for Bitcoin. With a finite field the curve is a cloud of points in a very large grid, and the geometric rule of tangent lines and reflections is only an analogy for the algebra that is actually computed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Writing your own implementation of the mathematics is also dangerous: simple code like that in the examples of this course is not protected against timing attacks, and real wallets use carefully reviewed libraries.

nodes.example: the curve y squared equals x cubed plus 7
nodes.definition: Bitcoin's keys are points on the curve secp256k1, y squared = x cubed + 7 over a finite field of prime order p; multiplying a point by a number is easy and the reverse is infeasible.

nodes.label: Digital signature
nodes.body: A digital signature is a number, or a pair of numbers, calculated from a message and a private key, which anyone can check against the corresponding public key. The book explains that a signature consists of two parts: an algorithm for creating a signature for a message using a private key, and an algorithm that allows anyone to verify the signature given the message and the public key. In Bitcoin the message is the transaction, or more exactly a hash of a specific part of the transaction data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A digital signature is a number, or a pair of numbers, calculated from a message and a private key, which anyone can check against the corresponding public key. The book explains that a signature consists of two parts: an algorithm for creating a signature for a message using a private key, and an algorithm that allows anyone to verify the signature given the message and the public key. In Bitcoin the message is the transaction, or more exactly a hash of a specific part of the transaction data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter says that a transaction contains proof of ownership for each amount being spent, in the form of a digital signature from the owner that can be independently validated by anyone (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The later chapter on signatures lists three purposes: the signature proves that the controller of the private key has authorized the spending, the proof cannot be denied afterwards, and the authorized transaction cannot be changed by unauthenticated third parties (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Together these replace the bank's signature card and the clerk's judgement with a calculation that thousands of independent nodes can repeat.

Two signature algorithms are used in Bitcoin today, the Schnorr signature algorithm and the elliptic curve digital signature algorithm, ECDSA (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's real transaction carries one witness item of 65 bytes, which is the length that the book gives for a Schnorr signature of 64 bytes followed by one byte that names the signature-hash type; its last byte is 01, the code of the type that signs almost the whole transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Outside Bitcoin, digital signatures are used to sign software updates, contracts and web certificates.

The mechanism can be run with the textbook ECDSA formulas on the curve of the previous concept. Using the book's example private key, the program signs the message pay Bob 75000 and obtains two numbers r and s; checking them against the public key returns True. If the message is changed to pay Bob 95000, the same pair fails the check and returns False, which is the integrity guarantee in miniature. The program fixes the secret nonce k for the sake of a repeatable output, which a real signer must never do: the book describes the nonce as private, and notes that the extra complexity of ECDSA has in some cases resulted in software accidentally leaking private keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A signature is tied to what was signed. Bitcoin lets a signer choose, with a flag called SIGHASH, which part of the transaction the signature commits to, so a signature is not simply a stamp on the whole document (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The signature also does not identify a person: it shows only that someone controlling the private key authorized this transaction. Finally, forging a signature without the private key is believed infeasible, not proven impossible, and a stolen private key lets a thief sign validly, with no way for the network to tell.

nodes.example: a proof made with the private key
nodes.definition: A digital signature is a value computed from a message and a private key that anyone can check against the public key, proving authorization, preventing denial and detecting changes.

nodes.label: Checksum
nodes.body: A checksum is a short piece of data calculated from a longer piece and attached to it, so that a recipient can recompute it and see whether the longer piece was damaged on the way. The book describes the checksum in the old base58check address format as an additional four bytes added to the end of the data, derived from the hash of the encoded data, which can therefore be used to detect transcription and typing errors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The newer bech32 format has a stronger checksum of its own.

paras.text: A checksum is a short piece of data calculated from a longer piece and attached to it, so that a recipient can recompute it and see whether the longer piece was damaged on the way. The book describes the checksum in the old base58check address format as an additional four bytes added to the end of the data, derived from the hash of the encoded data, which can therefore be used to detect transcription and typing errors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The newer bech32 format has a stronger checksum of its own.

Addresses are typed, spoken, copied and photographed by people, and a single wrong character could send funds to an address that nobody controls. A checksum turns that silent loss into an immediate error message. The book says that it prevents a mistyped Bitcoin address from being accepted by the wallet software as a valid destination, an error that would otherwise result in loss of funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bech32 goes further: in an address of the expected length it is guaranteed to detect any error affecting four characters or fewer, and for an address typed with a few errors it can tell the user where the errors are (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Every Bitcoin address has a checksum, and Bob's address in the chapter's payment request, bc1qk2g6u8..., is a bech32 address. The same idea protects credit card numbers, bank account numbers and ISBNs. In Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 173 the checksum of bech32 is defined by a polynomial calculation over the characters, with a final value that must equal a fixed constant for the address to be valid (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

The older method is easy to run. The checksum of the data is the first four bytes of the double-SHA256 hash of the data. For the word bitcoin that gives f1ef1bf1, and changing a letter of the word produces four entirely different bytes, so an altered text is detected with overwhelming probability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bob's bech32 address can be verified with the procedure in BIP 173: running the specified calculation over the address gives the value 1 for the address in the payment request, and for the same address with one character changed the result is different from 1, so the wallet refuses it (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

A checksum detects accidents, not attacks. An adversary who changes the data can simply compute a new matching checksum, so a checksum protects against a mistyped character but not against a malicious substitution, for which one needs a signature. The guarantee of bech32 also holds only if the length is unchanged: the book reports that in the original bech32 design it was easy to add or remove letters q before a final p without invalidating the checksum, a weakness that the later bech32m variant was made to remove (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a few bytes of hash that catch typing errors
nodes.definition: A checksum is a short value derived from data and appended to it so that a transcription or typing error can be detected; Bitcoin addresses carry one.

nodes.label: Bit and byte
nodes.body: A bit is the smallest unit of digital information: a single binary digit that is either 0 or 1. A byte is a group of eight bits, and it is the unit in which computers normally measure the length of data. The two units describe the same thing at different granularities, so one length can always be converted into the other by multiplying or dividing by eight. Every size that this chapter quotes, from the 32 bytes of a transaction identifier to the 256 bits of a private key, is a statement in one of these two units.

paras.text: A bit is the smallest unit of digital information: a single binary digit that is either 0 or 1. A byte is a group of eight bits, and it is the unit in which computers normally measure the length of data. The two units describe the same thing at different granularities, so one length can always be converted into the other by multiplying or dividing by eight. Every size that this chapter quotes, from the 32 bytes of a transaction identifier to the 256 bits of a private key, is a statement in one of these two units.

The chapter cannot be read without them. The book says that the output of SHA256 is always 256 bits long whatever the size of the input, that an input refers to an earlier transaction by a 32-byte identifier, and that output indexes are 4-byte unsigned integers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). These are the same kind of statement, and a reader who cannot move between the two units will think that a 256-bit hash and a 32-byte hash are different objects. Precise sizes also matter for a different reason: the room a transaction takes in a block is counted in bytes, and that is what its fee buys.

You meet both units in every tool. Bitcoin Core reports the size of Alice's transaction as 194, counting bytes; the book describes a key as a 256-bit number; a block header is 80 bytes, which is 640 bits; and the chapter's figures for the first synchronization of a node are given in gigabytes, which are multiples of the byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Outside Bitcoin the same units measure files, memory and network speeds, where the bit is traditional for transmission rates and the byte for storage.

The conversion is a multiplication by eight. The identifier of the first block's only transaction is 32 bytes of data, and reading it with the standard library and multiplying its length by eight gives 256, so the two descriptions agree. A byte written in hexadecimal takes exactly two characters, because one hexadecimal digit stands for four bits, which is why a 32-byte value is printed as 64 characters, as the book notes when it says that it takes 64 hexadecimal characters to display 32 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Watch the capital letter and the prefix. A lowercase b usually means bit and a capital B means byte, so 1 MB and 1 Mb differ by a factor of eight. Prefixes are also ambiguous: a kilobyte may mean 1,000 or 1,024 bytes depending on the author, which is one reason the book quotes the block limit as a weight of 4,000,000 rather than in megabytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And a byte is not a character: text becomes bytes only after an encoding is chosen, which is why the standard for payment requests has to say that each octet of the UTF-8 sequence is percent-encoded (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

nodes.example: 32 bytes are 256 bits
nodes.definition: A bit is one binary digit; eight bits make a byte. Sizes in Bitcoin are quoted in both, and 32 bytes are 256 bits.
