nodes.label: Hexadecimal notation
nodes.body: Hexadecimal notation writes numbers in base sixteen, using the ten digits 0 to 9 and then the letters a to f for the values ten to fifteen. Because sixteen is two to the fourth power, one hexadecimal digit corresponds exactly to four bits and two digits to one byte. This makes hexadecimal the usual way to print binary data for human eyes: it is far shorter than writing out bits and, unlike decimal, it lines up exactly with byte boundaries.

paras.text: Hexadecimal notation writes numbers in base sixteen, using the ten digits 0 to 9 and then the letters a to f for the values ten to fifteen. Because sixteen is two to the fourth power, one hexadecimal digit corresponds exactly to four bits and two digits to one byte. This makes hexadecimal the usual way to print binary data for human eyes: it is far shorter than writing out bits and, unlike decimal, it lines up exactly with byte boundaries.

Almost every value this chapter quotes is written in hexadecimal: the transaction identifier, the block hash, the private key, the address's underlying program, the compact form of the mining target. Without the notation these would have to be printed as enormous decimal numbers in which no part corresponds to a field. The notation is also what lets a reader check a length at a glance, since the book's remark that 64 hexadecimal characters display 32 bytes is just the statement that two digits make a byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The identifier of Alice's payment, 46620030...d1f96177, is 64 hexadecimal characters. The compact encoding of the first block's mining target is printed as 1d00ffff, and the same block's hash begins with a long run of zeros, which is only visible because the hash is written in hexadecimal. Outside Bitcoin, colours in web pages, memory addresses in debuggers and bytes in network traces are all written the same way.

Converting is a matter of weighted digits. The two-digit value ff stands for fifteen sixteens plus fifteen, that is 255, the largest value a byte can hold; the four-byte value 1d00ffff read as one number is 486,604,799. Python's standard library converts in both directions, with int(text, 16) reading a hexadecimal string and hex(number) writing one, and the small program above shows all three results together. Hexadecimal is case-insensitive as a notation, although Bitcoin's newer address format deliberately forbids mixing cases for a different reason, its checksum (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

Two traps are worth naming. The first is that hexadecimal is only a notation: the identifier of a transaction is 32 bytes of data, not 64 characters of text, and a program that hashes the printed form instead of the bytes gets a completely different answer. The second is the order in which the bytes are written down, which Bitcoin does differently in different places; the concept of byte order explains that trap in detail.

nodes.example: the digits 0-9 and a-f
nodes.definition: Hexadecimal writes a number in base 16 with the digits 0 to 9 and a to f; each digit stands for four bits, so one byte is exactly two hexadecimal digits.

nodes.label: Entropy
nodes.body: Entropy, in the sense used in cryptography, is a measure of how unpredictable a value is to someone who does not know it. It is counted in bits: a value drawn uniformly at random from two equally likely possibilities has one bit of entropy, from four possibilities two bits, and from two to the power 256 possibilities 256 bits. Entropy is therefore not a property of the number itself but of the process that produced it; the same number may be unguessable if it was drawn at random and worthless if it was the year of someone's birth.

paras.text: Entropy, in the sense used in cryptography, is a measure of how unpredictable a value is to someone who does not know it. It is counted in bits: a value drawn uniformly at random from two equally likely possibilities has one bit of entropy, from four possibilities two bits, and from two to the power 256 possibilities 256 bits. Entropy is therefore not a property of the number itself but of the process that produced it; the same number may be unguessable if it was drawn at random and worthless if it was the year of someone's birth.

Every guarantee in this chapter that rests on a secret rests on entropy. A private key is only safe because an attacker would have to search an unimaginably large space, and that space is large only if the key was really chosen at random. The book makes the point sharply: it advises the reader not to write their own code to create a random number, to use a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator seeded with sufficient entropy, and it warns that any process that is less than completely random can significantly reduce the security of the private key and of the bitcoins it controls (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

You meet entropy wherever a secret is generated: when a wallet creates a key, when a browser sets up an encrypted connection, when a system picks a password salt. The book compares the size of Bitcoin's private key space, two to the power 256, with the number of atoms in the visible universe, and says that picking a private key is in effect picking a number between 1 and two to the power 256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same chapter notes that the private key must be less than the order of the curve, a number only slightly smaller than that bound.

Counting entropy is counting possibilities. If a value is chosen uniformly from N equally likely possibilities it has the base-two logarithm of N bits of entropy, so a uniform 256-bit number has 256 bits, which the small calculation above confirms by taking the bit length of two to the power 256 and subtracting one. Weak choices collapse this number: a key derived from a six-letter lowercase word has at most the entropy of twenty-six to the sixth power, about twenty-eight bits, and a modern computer can try every one of those in seconds. The gap between twenty-eight and 256 bits is the whole difference between a secret and a formality.

Entropy cannot be judged by looking at a value. A key full of apparently random digits may have been produced by a predictable generator, and the result will look exactly as unguessable as a real one. Nor does more entropy help anywhere else: the chapter's hashes, identifiers and addresses are public values, and adding randomness to them changes nothing. Entropy matters only for the values that must stay secret, which in this chapter means the private key behind the signature.

nodes.example: how unpredictable a secret is
nodes.definition: Entropy measures how unpredictable a value is, counted in bits; a key chosen from 2**256 equally likely values has 256 bits of it, and a key chosen badly has far less.

nodes.label: Nonce
nodes.body: A nonce is a value that is varied in order to change the output of a cryptographic function without changing the data that is really being protected. The word is a contraction of number used once. The book introduces it in exactly this role: a variable used to vary the output of a cryptographic function, in that case to vary the output of the SHA256 commitment to a phrase (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Two very different nonces appear in this chapter, and keeping them apart matters: the secret nonce used when a signature is made, and the public nonce in a block header that a miner changes while searching for a proof of work.

paras.text: A nonce is a value that is varied in order to change the output of a cryptographic function without changing the data that is really being protected. The word is a contraction of number used once. The book introduces it in exactly this role: a variable used to vary the output of a cryptographic function, in that case to vary the output of the SHA256 commitment to a phrase (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Two very different nonces appear in this chapter, and keeping them apart matters: the secret nonce used when a signature is made, and the public nonce in a block header that a miner changes while searching for a proof of work.

A nonce is what turns a fixed, deterministic function into something that can be searched. A hash function always gives the same output for the same input, so a miner who wants a different output must change the input, and the nonce is the field reserved for that purpose. In signing, the nonce serves the opposite purpose: it makes two signatures over the same message different, which is necessary for the mathematics of the signature scheme to stay secure. The book describes the signing step as first generating a private nonce, and warns that the extra complexity of handling it has in some cases resulted in software accidentally leaking private keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mining nonce is a field of the block header, four bytes wide, described by the book's glossary as a 32-bit field whose value is set so that the hash of the block will contain a run of leading zeros, while the rest of the fields may not be changed because they have a defined meaning (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's own description of mining is the same idea in words: if the output does not match the template, the miner makes a small change to the candidate block and tries again (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The signing nonce is not stored anywhere: it is used once and discarded.

The book's own miniature example can be run. Setting the goal that the hexadecimal hash of the phrase Hello, world! followed by a number should begin with a zero, and trying the numbers in order, the first that succeeds is 32, giving the digest 09cb91f8...ccbec314, exactly the value and the nonce that the book prints (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). One hash verifies the answer, while thirty-two were needed to find it, and that asymmetry is the whole of proof of work. The mining nonce has only about four billion possible values, so real miners exhaust it and then change another field, which the book calls the extra nonce solution (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The two nonces must never be confused, because their rules are opposite. The mining nonce is public and may be anything; the signing nonce must be secret and must never be reused, since reusing one with the same key allows the private key to be recovered. A nonce is also not a password or a key: in mining it is simply the part of the input that the searcher is allowed to change, and in signing it is a one-time random value that is thrown away as soon as the signature exists.

nodes.example: a number used once to vary a result
nodes.definition: A nonce is a value, often a counter, that is changed to make a cryptographic function produce a different output; signing uses a secret one and mining a public one in the block header.

nodes.label: Encryption
nodes.body: Encryption is the transformation of data into a form that cannot be read without a key, together with the matching transformation that turns it back. Its purpose is secrecy. It is one of several things that cryptography can provide, and this chapter mentions it mainly in order to say what Bitcoin does not do with it. The term is needed because two of the tools explained here, the hash function and the digital signature, are regularly mistaken for encryption, and the mistake leads to wrong expectations about what the system protects.

paras.text: Encryption is the transformation of data into a form that cannot be read without a key, together with the matching transformation that turns it back. Its purpose is secrecy. It is one of several things that cryptography can provide, and this chapter mentions it mainly in order to say what Bitcoin does not do with it. The term is needed because two of the tools explained here, the hash function and the digital signature, are regularly mistaken for encryption, and the mistake leads to wrong expectations about what the system protects.

The distinction decides what is private on a blockchain. The book states plainly that public-key cryptography in Bitcoin is not used to encrypt, that is, to make secret, the transactions, and that its useful property is instead the ability to generate digital signatures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every transaction in this chapter, including Alice's, is therefore readable by anyone: the amounts, the conditions on the outputs and the signature itself are public. What a reader cannot do is forge a signature, and that is a guarantee about authorship, not about secrecy.

Encryption is met all around Bitcoin even though it is not inside a transaction. A browser connecting to Bob's shop uses it, a wallet file on disk may be encrypted with a passphrase, and the book's network chapter describes encrypted and authenticated connections between nodes, so that an observer of the wire cannot read what two peers exchange (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The course notes for this chapter make the same separation when they describe the key as what unlocks a previous output rather than as something that hides data (Altunel, 2021).

The simplest possible illustration is a reversible operation with a key. Combining each byte of the words pay Bob with the key value 0x5a by the exclusive-or operation gives the unreadable bytes 2a3b237a183538, and applying the very same operation again with the same key returns the original text, as the program above shows. Real encryption uses far stronger constructions, but the shape is this: one operation forward with a key, one back with a key. A hash function has no such backward step and no key, and a signature does not hide the message it is attached to.

Do not expect encryption to give privacy on the blockchain, and do not expect signatures to give secrecy. The book's chapter on keys lists the private key's requirement as remaining secret at all times, which is a matter of storage and not of encrypting transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Note also that encrypting a payment would defeat the system's purpose: nodes must read a transaction in order to verify it, which is why the data is public and the privacy of a user rests on other things, such as the fact that an address names no person.

nodes.example: making data unreadable without a key
nodes.definition: Encryption transforms data so that only a holder of the right key can read it again; Bitcoin's public-key cryptography is used for signatures, not for encrypting transactions.

io.code: (lambda k, m: (bytes(c ^ k for c in m).hex(), bytes(c ^ k for c in bytes(c ^ k for c in m)).decode()))(0x5a, b'pay Bob')

nodes.label: Linkage
nodes.body: A single transaction is only the beginning of the story, because bitcoins are never created in a vacuum: each is spent from something that existed before and gives rise to something that will exist afterwards. This group deals with the links between transactions. It explains the chain that results when each transaction spends the outputs of an earlier one, the change that a spender receives back because an output cannot be partly spent, and the choice that a wallet makes among the outputs it could spend, which is called coin selection.

paras.text: A single transaction is only the beginning of the story, because bitcoins are never created in a vacuum: each is spent from something that existed before and gives rise to something that will exist afterwards. This group deals with the links between transactions. It explains the chain that results when each transaction spends the outputs of an earlier one, the change that a spender receives back because an output cannot be partly spent, and the choice that a wallet makes among the outputs it could spend, which is called coin selection.

The links are what turn individual transactions into a history, and the history is what lets any node decide whether a payment is genuine. If Alice's payment spends an output created by Joe's transaction, and that output has not been spent before, the payment is valid in this respect; if it has been spent, the payment is a double spend. The three concepts of the group show how the requirement is met in practice, and also how wallet design decisions leave traces that others can read.

The chapter makes the links visible in two illustrations: a chain of three transactions in which the output of one is the input of the next, and the later chain from Joe through Alice and Bob to Gopesh, Bob's web designer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The idea is met in block explorers, which show for every input the transaction it spends, and in every wallet, which has to remember which outputs it can still use.

The links work because an output can be spent once and only once. Each input names one earlier output, and a node that has already seen that output spent rejects the second attempt, so the history of a coin is a chain in which every step consumes the step before it. Change falls out of the same rule: an output cannot be spent in part, so a payer who holds an output larger than the amount owed must consume all of it and create a second output back to herself. That is why the chapter's payment has two outputs rather than one, and why its amounts have to be read as a whole - 100000 consumed, 75000 to the payee, 20000 returned and 5000 left for the miner. Coin selection is the wallet's side of the same arithmetic: it must choose a set of outputs whose total is at least the amount plus the fee, and every choice it makes changes the size of the transaction and therefore the fee it has to leave (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Links are public, and public links can be followed by anybody. A chain of transactions is a record of where each output came from, so the choices that a wallet makes in building the links affect the privacy of its owner. Keep this in mind while reading the concepts: the same facts that make Bitcoin auditable also make it traceable.

nodes.label: Transaction chain
nodes.body: A transaction chain is the sequence of transactions that arises when each transaction spends outputs created by an earlier one. In the chapter, Alice's payment to Bob's store uses the output of a previous transaction as its input: the one in which her friend Joe gave her bitcoins in return for cash. The book labels that earlier transaction Tx1 and Alice's payment Tx2, and its figure shows Tx2 referring to Tx1 by an arrow and by the label Tx1:0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A transaction chain is the sequence of transactions that arises when each transaction spends outputs created by an earlier one. In the chapter, Alice's payment to Bob's store uses the output of a previous transaction as its input: the one in which her friend Joe gave her bitcoins in return for cash. The book labels that earlier transaction Tx1 and Alice's payment Tx2, and its figure shows Tx2 referring to Tx1 by an arrow and by the label Tx1:0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chain is the answer to the question of where bitcoins come from and where they have gone. Because each input names the output it consumes, anyone can follow a payment back through the chain of ownership, and the owner of an output can be changed only by a transaction that spends it. When Bob spends the output he received, he extends the chain; the chapter's last illustration shows Alice's transaction as part of a chain from Joe to Gopesh (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same structure underlies the idea of provenance, which the final concepts of this chapter take up.

The book describes the reference in an actual transaction as the 32-byte transaction identifier of the transaction in which Alice received the money from Joe, followed by a colon and a number that gives the position of the output, counted from zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Software cannot read the value of an input from the input itself: the book stresses that actual Bitcoin transactions do not explicitly include the value of their inputs, so software has to find the previous transaction output being spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The numbers in the book's illustration make the chain concrete. Tx1 sent 100,000 satoshis to an output locked by Alice's key. Tx2 spends it and creates two outputs, 75,000 satoshis for the podcast and 20,000 satoshis back to Alice, and the 5,000 satoshis that are left over form its fee, as the calculation 100000 - 75000 - 20000 gives. Bob then spends the 75,000 output, which is Tx2:1, in Tx3, which pays 67,000 satoshis in a single output, so that the fee of Tx3 is 75000 - 67000, or 8,000 satoshis, as the figure states (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each link is simply a pair of a transaction identifier and an output position.

The figure is a simplification, and the real transaction differs from it in a detail. In the figure Alice's input is labelled Tx1:0, which is the output of 100,000 satoshis, the first of the two outputs drawn for Tx1; but in the bytes of the real transaction the output index stored in the input is 1. The order of Tx2's outputs, by contrast, agrees with the figure: the change of 20,000 satoshis is at position 0 and Bob's 75,000 satoshis at position 1, which is why Tx3 spends Tx2:1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Remember also that a chain of transactions links outputs, not people: it does not say who the owners are, only which outputs were spent to create which others.

nodes.example: Alice's payment spending Joe's output
nodes.definition: Each transaction's inputs spend earlier outputs, so transactions form chains back through history.

nodes.label: Making change
nodes.body: Making change is the practice of adding to a transaction an output that returns the surplus to the person who is paying. The book explains the need with money in a shop: if you buy a five-dollar item with a twenty-dollar bill you expect fifteen dollars back, and in the same way a transaction input, like a currency note, cannot be partly spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). If a purchase costs 5 bitcoins and you only have an input worth 20, you send one output of 5 to the store owner and one of 15 back to yourself, not counting the fee (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Making change is the practice of adding to a transaction an output that returns the surplus to the person who is paying. The book explains the need with money in a shop: if you buy a five-dollar item with a twenty-dollar bill you expect fifteen dollars back, and in the same way a transaction input, like a currency note, cannot be partly spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). If a purchase costs 5 bitcoins and you only have an input worth 20, you send one output of 5 to the store owner and one of 15 back to yourself, not counting the fee (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Without change, every payment would have to match an available output exactly, or the surplus would be given to the miner as an enormous fee. The change output lets a wallet spend any output, whatever its size, and keep the remainder. It also explains why most payments have the same shape: one input and two outputs, one for the receiver and one for the sender (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the sender, the change output is simply a new output that can be spent in a later transaction.

Alice's payment is the example. Her single input of 100,000 satoshis cannot be divided, so her wallet creates a payment output of 75,000 satoshis for Bob's store and a change output of 20,000 satoshis for herself, and the remaining 5,000 satoshis are the fee (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book adds that, at the level of the protocol, there is no difference between a change output and a payment output, and it calls the address the change goes to a change address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The wallet's arithmetic is a subtraction. With an input worth 100000 satoshis, a payment of 75000 and a fee of 5000, the change is 100000 - 75000 - 5000, which is 20000. The result matches the first output that the real transaction contains. A transaction without a change output is possible too; the book calls it a changeless transaction, says it can have only a single output, and shows Bob creating one as Tx3. It is practical only when the amount to spend is about the same as the inputs minus the fee (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book hopes that payment and change look identical on the blockchain, since the change address is often a new address of the sender's wallet, for privacy reasons, and a third party could not then tell which output is the change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's real transaction does not fully achieve that ideal: its two output scripts have different lengths, 34 and 22 bytes, so an observer can tell them apart. And the change is not extra money: it is an ordinary output that nobody can use unless the wallet keeps the key, so a wallet that loses the change key loses the change.

nodes.definition: An output larger than the payment returns the rest as change to a new address of the payer, because an input cannot be partly spent.

nodes.label: Coin selection
nodes.body: Coin selection is the process by which a wallet decides which of its unspent outputs to use as inputs in a payment. Different wallets use different strategies. The book says they might aggregate many small inputs, or use one that is equal to or larger than the desired payment, and that unless the wallet can match the payment plus the fee exactly, it will need to generate change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Coin selection is the process by which a wallet decides which of its unspent outputs to use as inputs in a payment. Different wallets use different strategies. The book says they might aggregate many small inputs, or use one that is equal to or larger than the desired payment, and that unless the wallet can match the payment plus the fee exactly, it will need to generate change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The choice has consequences that last. The book compares it with handling cash: if you always use the largest bill in your pocket you end up with a pocket full of loose change, and if you only use the loose change you will often be left with only big bills. People subconsciously find a balance between these extremes, and Bitcoin wallet developers strive to program this balance (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet that always picks small outputs builds large transactions that cost more in fees; one that always picks large outputs creates many small outputs that may later be too small to be worth spending.

In the chapter the choice is trivial, because Alice's wallet holds one output that is sufficient to pay for the podcast; had it not been, her wallet might have had to combine several smaller outputs, like picking coins from a purse, until it could find enough (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Real wallets perform coin selection on every payment, and some let the user choose the outputs by hand.

A simple strategy can be programmed in a few lines. Suppose a wallet holds outputs of 60000, 30000 and 25000 satoshis and must pay 75000 plus a fee of 5000, a need of 80000. Taking outputs from the largest down until the sum reaches the need picks 60000 and 30000, whose sum 90000 leaves a change of 10000. This is only one of many strategies, and its trade-offs differ from those of, for example, preferring the smallest sufficient set or the set that gives no change at all.

The selection is visible to the outside world. Spending several outputs in one transaction shows that one party probably controls all of them, which weakens privacy. And every input costs space and therefore fee, so the cheapest set now is not always the best for later. Treat coin selection as a design decision with several competing aims, and remember that the book presents it as a balance, not as a single correct method.

nodes.example: choosing which inputs to spend
nodes.definition: Wallets choose which inputs to spend, balancing many small inputs against few large ones, much as people handle cash.

nodes.label: Form
nodes.body: Transactions come in a few typical shapes, which this group calls forms. A form is described by how many inputs and outputs a transaction has and by what it is used for. The chapter names three: the simple payment, with one input and two outputs; the consolidation, which spends several inputs into a single output; and payment batching, which pays several recipients with a single transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Transactions come in a few typical shapes, which this group calls forms. A form is described by how many inputs and outputs a transaction has and by what it is used for. The chapter names three: the simple payment, with one input and two outputs; the consolidation, which spends several inputs into a single output; and payment batching, which pays several recipients with a single transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Recognizing the forms helps a reader to interpret what a block explorer displays and to guess what the sender intended. A transaction with many inputs and one output is probably a tidy-up of small amounts, one with many outputs is probably a business paying many people, and one with one input and two outputs is probably an ordinary payment with change. The forms also show that nothing in the format limits a transaction to one payer and one payee.

The forms are met first in the three illustrations of the chapter: the most common transaction, the consolidation that aggregates funds, and the batch that distributes them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They are then met in the world. Ordinary wallets create simple payments all day; wallets and businesses create consolidations as housekeeping, usually when fees are low; and services that owe money to many people create batches on a schedule. A reader who opens almost any block in an explorer will find all three among its transactions, and being able to name them makes a block readable instead of a wall of numbers.

The forms differ only in how many references go in and how many conditions come out, and the same rule governs all of them: the outputs may not total more than the inputs, and the difference is the miner's. From that one rule the economics of each form follow. A payment with one input and two outputs, the chapter's own case, is the ordinary shape because a payer usually has one suitable output and needs change. Consolidation reverses the proportions, spending many small outputs into one, which costs a large transaction once in order to make later transactions small - and is therefore done when fee rates are low. Batching spreads one input over many outputs, which lets a business pay many people for little more than the cost of paying one, because the expensive part of a transaction is its inputs rather than its outputs. Each form is therefore a different answer to the same question about size and fee, not a different kind of transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A form is a description of a typical shape and not a rule of the protocol, which sees only a list of inputs and a list of outputs and checks the same conditions whatever the shape. The names used here are the conventions of the course and of the book, so another text may count the forms differently. A transaction can also combine the features, for example by consolidating many inputs while paying two recipients and returning change, in which case no single name fits. Finally, a form says nothing about who built the transaction or why: the shape is a hint about intention, never evidence of it, and reading too much into it is the mistake that the privacy remarks of this branch warn against.

nodes.label: Simple payment
nodes.body: A simple payment is the most common form of transaction. It has one input and two outputs: the first output pays the receiver and the second returns the change to the sender (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the shape of Alice's payment to Bob's store, and the form that most people have in mind when they speak of sending bitcoin.

paras.text: A simple payment is the most common form of transaction. It has one input and two outputs: the first output pays the receiver and the second returns the change to the sender (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the shape of Alice's payment to Bob's store, and the form that most people have in mind when they speak of sending bitcoin.

The form is common because it is the natural result of how outputs behave. A person usually owns an output that is larger than the item to be bought, an output cannot be partly spent, and so the wallet writes one output for the seller and one back for the buyer. Understanding it explains why Alice's balance after paying Bob is not simply her earlier balance minus 75,000 satoshis in a single step: the old output disappears and a new, smaller one takes its place.

The shape is the one in the chapter's figure of the most common transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is also what the real transaction contains: a program that reads the bytes of Alice's transaction finds one input and two outputs, so the pair (1, 2) is exactly what the form prescribes. The same shape can be seen in the large majority of everyday payments on a block explorer.

Counting is all that is needed. If the number of inputs is one and the number of outputs is two, and the amounts are 100000 for the input, 75000 and 20000 for the outputs, then the fee is the 5000 that remains. The order of the outputs is not fixed by the form: in Alice's real transaction the change comes first and the payment second, which is why the book's later figure refers to the output Tx2:1 when Bob spends his payment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A simple payment is a description, not a promise. Some payments have a single input and a single output, the changeless transactions, and some have a second output that is not change, for instance a donation. The two-output pattern also invites a privacy question: when the outputs have different amounts, an observer may guess that the larger one is the change, or the smaller; the guess is only a guess.

nodes.example: one input, two outputs
nodes.definition: The most common form: one input, and two outputs - the payment and the change.

nodes.label: Consolidation
nodes.body: A consolidation transaction spends several inputs into a single output. The book offers a picture from everyday money: it is the real-world equivalent of exchanging a pile of coins and currency notes for a single larger note (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Wallets and businesses create such transactions to clean up lots of smaller amounts.

paras.text: A consolidation transaction spends several inputs into a single output. The book offers a picture from everyday money: it is the real-world equivalent of exchanging a pile of coins and currency notes for a single larger note (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Wallets and businesses create such transactions to clean up lots of smaller amounts.

Many small outputs are inconvenient. Each needs a separate input when it is spent, and every input adds to the size and therefore to the fee of a later transaction. A wallet or business that has received many small payments can combine them in one transaction, at a time when fees are low, and later pay with a single large output. Because the chapter on coin selection explains that wallets balance small and large outputs, the consolidation can be seen as the inverse of an ordinary payment.

The form is shown in the chapter's illustration of a consolidation transaction aggregating funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Exchanges and shops that receive many small payments run consolidations regularly, and block explorers show them as transactions with many inputs and a single output. The book does not give a fixed number of inputs: it says only that the transaction spends several inputs into a single output.

The arithmetic is unchanged: the single output is the sum of the inputs minus the fee. As an illustration, three outputs of 30000, 25000 and 20000 satoshis consolidated with a fee of 1500 give one output of 73500 satoshis. The numbers are invented for the example, and the fee is assumed. What matters is the shape, many inputs and one output.

Consolidation has costs that the picture of a single note hides. All the inputs are spent together, and so a watcher can conclude that they probably belong to the same owner, which is a loss of privacy. It must also be paid for now: spending many inputs makes a large transaction, and a large transaction pays a larger total fee than a small one at the same fee rate.

nodes.example: many inputs, one output
nodes.definition: Many inputs spent into a single output, like exchanging a pile of coins for one note.

nodes.label: Payment batching
nodes.body: Payment batching is the form in which one transaction pays to multiple outputs representing multiple recipients. The book says that it is seen often on the blockchain and that commercial entities use it to distribute funds, for example when processing payroll payments to multiple employees (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The transaction has few inputs, often one, and many outputs.

paras.text: Payment batching is the form in which one transaction pays to multiple outputs representing multiple recipients. The book says that it is seen often on the blockchain and that commercial entities use it to distribute funds, for example when processing payroll payments to multiple employees (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The transaction has few inputs, often one, and many outputs.

A business that pays many people would otherwise create a separate transaction for each, and every one of those transactions would carry its own overhead. A batch gathers the payments in one transaction. It is the counterpart of the consolidation: instead of many inputs flowing into one output, one flow of funds is spread to many outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A batch also makes the payer's own accounting simpler, as a single transaction records the whole payroll.

The chapter shows the form in its illustration of a batch transaction distributing funds, drawn as one input flowing into several outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In practice the businesses that use it are those that owe money to many people at once: exchanges paying withdrawals, payroll services paying salaries, mining pools paying their members. A reader meets such a transaction in a block explorer as a short list of inputs above a long list of outputs, each with its own address and amount, and can usually tell at a glance that one party built it. The same shape also appears whenever a service combines the payments of many customers to save fees, which is why a batch is not always the work of a single payer.

The arithmetic is again the same: the inputs equal the outputs plus the fee. Suppose a single input of 200000 satoshis is used to pay four employees 60000, 55000, 50000 and 32000 satoshis, a total of 197000, and a fee of 3000 is paid. Then 200000 - 197000 - 3000 equals 0, so there is no change; the batch is also a changeless transaction in the sense of the previous concepts. The amounts are invented for the illustration.

The recipients of a batch can see the other outputs and their amounts, because the transaction is public, so a payroll batch discloses the full list of salaries paid in one transaction to anyone who looks. A batch also depends on a single set of inputs and a single signature step, and a mistake in building it affects every recipient at once.

nodes.example: one transaction, many recipients
nodes.definition: Payment batching pays several recipients with one transaction that has many outputs, as a payroll does.

nodes.label: Unit
nodes.body: A unit is a standard quantity in which value is counted, and a currency usually has several of them: one for everyday prices, smaller ones for small change, and sometimes a very small one in which the accounts are actually kept. Bitcoin's unit of account is the bitcoin, but the protocol itself counts in a far smaller unit, so that every amount in a transaction is a whole number and no rounding is ever needed. This group introduces that unit, the satoshi, together with the fractions of a bitcoin that are built on it, and it explains the convention by which the course writes amounts down (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A unit is a standard quantity in which value is counted, and a currency usually has several of them: one for everyday prices, smaller ones for small change, and sometimes a very small one in which the accounts are actually kept. Bitcoin's unit of account is the bitcoin, but the protocol itself counts in a far smaller unit, so that every amount in a transaction is a whole number and no rounding is ever needed. This group introduces that unit, the satoshi, together with the fractions of a bitcoin that are built on it, and it explains the convention by which the course writes amounts down (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader who does not know the units cannot read a transaction or a fee, because the same payment is described by three different numbers depending on the unit chosen. The prices in Bob's store are quoted in dollars and in bitcoin, while the figures in the diagram of the transaction chain are satoshis, because that is what the protocol itself uses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A mistake of the unit is therefore not a small error but a factor of one hundred million, and the chapter on fees warns that confusing the denominator or the numerator of a fee rate can mean overpaying by a thousand or by a hundred million times (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Stating the unit beside every figure is the cheapest possible protection against that class of mistake.

Units are met wherever an amount is displayed. A wallet usually shows a balance in bitcoin with up to eight decimal places, and many wallets offer a setting that switches the whole display to satoshis instead. A fee is almost always quoted as a rate in satoshis per virtual byte, which mixes the smallest unit of value with a unit of size. A block explorer shows both forms side by side for the same transaction. And the figures of this chapter, 100,000 satoshis in and 75,000 and 20,000 out, are the protocol's own unit, while the invoice that started the payment asks for 0.01577764 bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group has a single concept, the satoshi, because every other unit is a plain multiple of it. The relation to the bitcoin is a fixed number and the division is exact: a bitcoin is exactly 100,000,000 satoshis, so a whole number of satoshis can describe any amount that can be sent, and the total supply of 21 million bitcoins is 2.1 quadrillion satoshis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The intermediate names follow the same arithmetic, so a millibitcoin is a thousandth of a bitcoin and therefore 100,000 satoshis, the figure the chapter gives for the output that Joe's transaction created for Alice (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because the protocol stores amounts as integers of satoshis, the sums in a transaction never carry a rounding error.

Do not mix units in a calculation, and do not trust a number that arrives without one. Many defects and many costly payments have come from treating a figure in one unit as a figure in another, which is why this course states the unit next to every number it writes down. Two further cautions belong here. The names of the fractions are conventions and not protocol rules, so a wallet may offer units that another wallet has never heard of; and converting a decimal amount in bitcoin into satoshis with ordinary floating-point arithmetic can introduce a small error, which is one reason the protocol counts in whole satoshis in the first place.

nodes.label: Satoshi
nodes.body: The satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin that can be recorded in a transaction: one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin, or 0.00000001. The book says the Bitcoin network can transact in fractional values, from the millibitcoin, one thousandth of a bitcoin, down to 1/100,000,000th of a bitcoin, which is known as a satoshi (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In a serialized transaction the amount of an output is stored as a whole number of satoshis.

paras.text: The satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin that can be recorded in a transaction: one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin, or 0.00000001. The book says the Bitcoin network can transact in fractional values, from the millibitcoin, one thousandth of a bitcoin, down to 1/100,000,000th of a bitcoin, which is known as a satoshi (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In a serialized transaction the amount of an output is stored as a whole number of satoshis.

The name has a short history. When Bitcoin was first created, the smallest unit had no name and some developers called it the base unit; later many users began calling it a satoshi in honor of Bitcoin's creator, who published the whitepaper under the name Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The practical importance is that integer arithmetic is exact: the protocol counts whole satoshis and never needs fractions, so there are no rounding errors in the totals of a transaction.

Satoshis are met in the figures of the chapter, where Tx1 sends 100,000 satoshis, which are 0.001 bitcoin, and Alice's payments are 75,000 and 20,000 satoshis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They are also the unit of the fee rate, satoshis per virtual byte. The consensus rules cap the total at 21 million bitcoins, which is 2.1 quadrillion satoshis, and Bitcoin Core defines one bitcoin as COIN = 100,000,000 and the maximum amount as 21,000,000 times that (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The conversions are plain division and multiplication. A millibitcoin is 10**8 // 1000 satoshis, which is 100000, exactly the 100,000 satoshis, or 0.001 bitcoin, that the book gives for the output of Tx1. A bitcoin amount from a payment request, such as 0.01577764, converts to 1,577,764 satoshis when it is multiplied by 10**8 with exact decimal arithmetic. Doing the conversion with ordinary floating point numbers invites small errors, which is one reason why the protocol itself counts in whole satoshis.

The book states a convention that students often overlook: it uses the same pluralization rules as for dollars, so the text speaks of 10 bitcoins and 0.001 bitcoins, and of millibitcoins and satoshis in the same way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Another caution concerns display: wallets may show amounts in bitcoin or in satoshis, and a user who reads 100000 where 0.001 was expected has made a mistake of a factor of one hundred million in the other direction.

nodes.example: one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin
nodes.definition: The smallest unit: a bitcoin divides into 100,000,000 satoshis.

nodes.label: Payment request
nodes.body: A payment request is the message through which a seller tells a buyer what to pay, to whom and why. In the chapter the request is created automatically by Bob's e-commerce system as a QR code that holds an invoice, and Alice's wallet reads it so that she never has to type an address or an amount. This group explains the pieces: the address-bearing web link called a URI, the QR code that carries it, the improvement proposal that defines its format, and the invoice itself (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A payment request is the message through which a seller tells a buyer what to pay, to whom and why. In the chapter the request is created automatically by Bob's e-commerce system as a QR code that holds an invoice, and Alice's wallet reads it so that she never has to type an address or an amount. This group explains the pieces: the address-bearing web link called a URI, the QR code that carries it, the improvement proposal that defines its format, and the invoice itself (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Typing a long address by hand is slow and error-prone, and an address typed wrongly can lose the payment. A payment request puts the address, the amount and a description into one object that a wallet can read in one step. The book notes that, unlike a QR code that simply contains a destination address, the invoice is a QR-encoded URI that contains a destination address, a payment amount and a description, so that the wallet application can prefill the information and show a human-readable description to the user (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The request is met in every online and shop payment with Bitcoin: on the checkout page, in an invoice, on a receipt. In the chapter, Alice scans the code on display with her smartphone, sees a payment for the correct amount to Bob's Store, and selects Send to authorize it; within a few seconds Bob sees the transaction on the register (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The course notes of this chapter, written for the second edition, show the same flow with an older style of address (Altunel, 2021).

The group begins with the URI, the general kind of web address that the request uses. The QR code is then described as the carrier. The improvement proposal is explained next, since the format is defined in one; and finally the invoice of the chapter, the Bitcoin URI of BIP 21, is dissected piece by piece and executed.

The request itself is not a transaction. Nothing is sent to the network when a code is displayed or scanned, and the buyer can decline. The format is also only a convenience: a wallet must still ask the user to approve the payment, and the standard itself says that clients must not act on such a URI without getting the user's authorization (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

nodes.label: Uniform resource identifier
nodes.body: A uniform resource identifier, URI, is a string of characters that names or locates something according to a general format. It begins with a scheme, such as http or bitcoin, followed by a colon, and then a path and optionally a query that carries additional parameters after a question mark, separated by ampersands. The standard BIP 21 says that Bitcoin URIs follow the general format for URIs as set forth in RFC 3986, that the path component consists of a bitcoin address, and that the query component provides additional payment options (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

paras.text: A uniform resource identifier, URI, is a string of characters that names or locates something according to a general format. It begins with a scheme, such as http or bitcoin, followed by a colon, and then a path and optionally a query that carries additional parameters after a question mark, separated by ampersands. The standard BIP 21 says that Bitcoin URIs follow the general format for URIs as set forth in RFC 3986, that the path component consists of a bitcoin address, and that the query component provides additional payment options (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

A common format lets different programs cooperate without knowing about each other. A web page or a QR code can carry a link, the operating system can recognize the scheme, and the wallet that registered itself for it can open it. The standard says the purpose of the scheme is to enable users to easily make payments by simply clicking links on webpages or scanning QR codes, and recommends that graphical bitcoin clients register themselves as the handler for the bitcoin: scheme (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

Everyone who uses the web has seen URIs: web addresses are URIs with the scheme http or https. The glossary of the book says, in its entry for the improvement proposal BIP21, that it proposes an improvement of the bitcoin uniform resource identifier scheme (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the chapter the URI is the content of Bob's QR code.

Python's standard library splits a URI into its parts. Applying urlsplit to the start of Bob's URI returns the scheme bitcoin, the path bc1qk2g6u8p4qm2s2lh3gts5cpt2mrv5skcuu7u3e4, which is the address, and the query amount=0.01577764. Characters outside the allowed range in the query are first encoded in UTF-8 and then each byte is written as a percent sign and two hexadecimal digits, so that an apostrophe becomes %27 and a space %20 (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

A URI is text, and text can be forged. A link on a web page can show one thing and contain another, and a malicious page can offer an address that is not the seller's. That is the reason for the rule that a wallet may not act on a URI without the user's authorization, and why the user should compare the address and amount shown by the wallet with what was expected (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

nodes.example: a scheme, a path and a query
nodes.definition: A URI is a text string that names a resource by a scheme such as bitcoin:, a path and optional query parameters; Bitcoin payment requests use the form bitcoin:address?parameters.

nodes.label: QR code
nodes.body: A QR code is a square pattern of black and white dots that serves as a form of barcode: a camera reads it and recovers the text it stores. The book's first chapter describes the code shown on the receive screen of Alice's wallet in this way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Bitcoin, QR codes carry addresses and payment requests from one device to another without any typing.

paras.text: A QR code is a square pattern of black and white dots that serves as a form of barcode: a camera reads it and recovers the text it stores. The book's first chapter describes the code shown on the receive screen of Alice's wallet in this way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Bitcoin, QR codes carry addresses and payment requests from one device to another without any typing.

The code removes the need to type or to copy a long, easily mistyped string, and works between two devices that are not connected to each other at all, just a screen and a camera. For merchants it is the cheapest possible point of sale: a display and a printed or on-screen code. The chapter relies on it when Bob's system creates a QR code that contains an invoice, which Alice scans with her smartphone (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Wallets display codes to receive and scan codes to pay. Hardware signing devices, according to the book, may also connect to a wallet with a camera and QR codes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The size of a code depends on how much it holds and in what mode: the book explains that the mixed-case base58check alphabet requires extra space to encode in QR codes, whereas a bech32 address can be written in capital letters before it is encoded, which allows a special QR encoding mode that uses less space (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); BIP 173 also lists, among its reasons for a new address format, that Base58 needs a lot of space in QR codes, as it cannot use the alphanumeric mode (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

What a QR code stores is a string of characters, and the same text can be packed more or less densely. BIP 173 says that inside QR codes an address in uppercase should be used, as that permits the alphanumeric mode, which is 45 percent more compact than the normal byte mode, and that decoders must not accept strings that mix upper and lower case (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). Bob's address has 42 characters; written in capitals it still consists only of letters and digits, which the short program above confirms. The packing itself is done by the encoder in the wallet or in the shop's software, and a student can treat it as a black box.

A QR code is not secure in itself. What is displayed is whatever someone chose to print, and a printed code that is covered by another one would replace the address without any visible sign. Check the address and the amount that your wallet decodes before you approve the payment, and the book's own tip about the chapter's code is to try to scan it with your wallet to see the address and amount, but not to send money (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a square of black and white dots
nodes.definition: A QR code is a two-dimensional barcode that holds a short text, such as an address or a payment request, which a phone camera reads.

nodes.label: Bitcoin improvement proposal
nodes.body: A Bitcoin improvement proposal, abbreviated BIP, is a design document that provides information to the Bitcoin community or describes a new feature for Bitcoin or its processes or environment. The first of them, BIP 1, says that a BIP should provide a concise technical specification of the feature and a rationale for it, and that BIPs are the primary mechanism for proposing new features, collecting community input on an issue and documenting design decisions (Taaki, 2011). The book's appendix says there are three kinds: standard, informational and process BIPs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A Bitcoin improvement proposal, abbreviated BIP, is a design document that provides information to the Bitcoin community or describes a new feature for Bitcoin or its processes or environment. The first of them, BIP 1, says that a BIP should provide a concise technical specification of the feature and a rationale for it, and that BIPs are the primary mechanism for proposing new features, collecting community input on an issue and documenting design decisions (Taaki, 2011). The book's appendix says there are three kinds: standard, informational and process BIPs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Bitcoin has no company that decides how it changes. The BIP process gives the community a public and traceable way to propose changes and record the reasoning. BIP 1 states that the author of a BIP is responsible for building consensus within the community and documenting dissenting opinions, and that because BIPs are maintained as text files in a versioned repository, their revision history is the historical record of the feature proposal (Taaki, 2011). A BIP is not law: a standards track BIP matters only if the software and its users adopt it.

The chapter meets a BIP when it states that the invoice URI is defined in BIP 21 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's other chapters refer to many more, among them BIP 173 for the bech32 address format, which Bob's address in the invoice uses. The glossary of the book defines a BIP in the same sense, giving BIP 21 as its example (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Each BIP begins with a header that gives its number, title, authors, status and type. BIP 21 has the title URI Scheme, the layer Applications and the type Specification, and its status is now Closed because it has been superseded; BIP 321, assigned in November 2024 and with the status Complete, replaces it. The little program above reads the status from such a header (Schneider and Corallo, 2012) (Corallo, 2024). The documents are plain text, so anyone can read them and quote them, which is how this chapter checks its statements.

A proposal is not a decision. Many BIPs are never adopted, and a status such as proposed or draft says nothing about use. Status also changes: the BIP that the book cites for the invoice format, number 21, is no longer the current document, because it was replaced by a newer one that adds modern address types, and the book's reference is therefore a snapshot of 2023 (Corallo, 2024). Always check the status of the document you cite.

nodes.example: BIP 21 proposes the bitcoin: URI scheme
nodes.definition: A BIP is a design document that proposes or describes a feature of Bitcoin; standards, informational and process proposals are kept as numbered text files in a public repository.
