nodes.label: BIP21 URI
nodes.body: A BIP21 URI is a Bitcoin payment request written as a web link in the format defined by BIP 21. It begins with the scheme bitcoin: and the address, optionally followed by a question mark and parameters such as the amount, a label for the recipient and a message that describes the payment. The chapter shows Bob's invoice in this form and explains its components: a Bitcoin address, the payment amount 0.01577764, a label for the recipient address, Bob's Store, and a description, Purchase at Bob's Store (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A BIP21 URI is a Bitcoin payment request written as a web link in the format defined by BIP 21. It begins with the scheme bitcoin: and the address, optionally followed by a question mark and parameters such as the amount, a label for the recipient and a message that describes the payment. The chapter shows Bob's invoice in this form and explains its components: a Bitcoin address, the payment amount 0.01577764, a label for the recipient address, Bob's Store, and a description, Purchase at Bob's Store (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The format lets a wallet fill in a payment from a single scan and show the payer what is being paid for. The standard says the amount, if given, must be written in decimal bitcoin, with a period as the decimal separator, that the label and message are texts, and that clients must not act on such a URI without getting the user's authorization (Schneider and Corallo, 2012). The separation of address from description also keeps personal information out of the payment: the standard's rationale is that a URI should not represent an exchange of personal information, but a one-time payment (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

Bob's invoice is the example in the chapter, displayed as a QR code on his checkout page (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Wallets register themselves for the bitcoin: scheme so that a link on a page opens the payment. BIP 21 was assigned in January 2012 and has the authors Nils Schneider and Matt Corallo; it is now superseded by BIP 321, which names bech32 and bech32m addresses explicitly and adds parameters for other payment methods, whereas the grammar of the older text names only base58 addresses (Schneider and Corallo, 2012) (Corallo, 2024).

The URI can be taken apart with the standard library. Splitting off the query and parsing it, then percent-decoding the label, returns Bob's Store, since %27 is the apostrophe and %20 a space. The amount 0.01577764 is a decimal number of bitcoin, which as exact decimal arithmetic equals 1,577,764 satoshis. The address, bc1qk2g6u8..., passes the bech32 checksum test of BIP 173, which the concept of the checksum explains.

The invoice in the book is an illustration, not a record of the real payment. The amount 0.01577764 bitcoin is 1,577,764 satoshis, while the real transaction pays 75,000 satoshis to Bob's store, and the 22-byte output script of the real payment holds a different 20-byte program than the one encoded in the invoice's address. Do not conclude from the book's figures that the address in the URI received the payment. The book's own tip says to try scanning the code, but do not send money (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the invoice encoded in the store's QR code
nodes.definition: A BIP21 URI carrying the address, amount, label and message, which the wallet reads so the payer never types an address.

nodes.label: Bitcoin address
nodes.body: A Bitcoin address is a short string of letters and digits that stands for the condition under which a payment can later be spent. The book's glossary describes an address as a string of letters and numbers that is really an encoded form of a hash related to a public key, and says that you ask others to send you bitcoin to one of your addresses much as you ask them to send email to your email address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The address in this chapter, bc1qk2g6u8...uu7u3e4, is written in the newer format defined by BIP 173, which the book calls bech32 (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

paras.text: A Bitcoin address is a short string of letters and digits that stands for the condition under which a payment can later be spent. The book's glossary describes an address as a string of letters and numbers that is really an encoded form of a hash related to a public key, and says that you ask others to send you bitcoin to one of your addresses much as you ask them to send email to your email address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The address in this chapter, bc1qk2g6u8...uu7u3e4, is written in the newer format defined by BIP 173, which the book calls bech32 (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017).

An address exists for the payer's convenience and safety. A payer does not need to know anything about scripts, keys or hashes; the wallet turns the address into the output script that encumbers the payment, and the checksum inside the address catches a mistyped character before any money moves. The book makes the consequence explicit: the checksum prevents a mistyped address from being accepted by the wallet software as a valid destination, an error that would otherwise result in loss of funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The address is the first thing a reader meets in the chapter, as the path component of the invoice's payment link, and the chapter lists it among the components of that link together with the amount, the label and the description (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Block explorers accept an address as a search term, the chapter says, along with a transaction hash, a block number or a block hash. Addresses also appear on receipts, on printed codes in shops and in the course notes for this chapter, where the older style beginning with a 1 is used (Altunel, 2021).

The newer format is readable in three parts. A human-readable prefix, here bc for the main Bitcoin network, is separated by the digit 1 from the data, which encodes a version number and a program of twenty bytes, and ends with six characters of checksum (Wuille and Maxwell, 2017). The program in Bob's address is b291ae1c...9485b1c, and the checksum calculation over the whole string returns the value that BIP 173 requires for a valid address. The small example above reads off the three obvious features: the prefix bc1, the length of 42 characters, and the fact that the address is written entirely in lower case, which the format recommends.

An address is not an account and not an identity. It holds no balance of its own, since a balance is the sum of the unspent outputs that a wallet can spend, and it names no person, which is why following a chain of transactions does not by itself reveal who the parties were. Addresses are also meant to be used once: the book explains that a change address is usually a new address of the sender's wallet for privacy reasons (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Finally, the address in the book's invoice is an illustration: a check of the real transaction shows that its payment output encodes a different twenty-byte program, so the printed address did not receive the printed payment.

nodes.example: bc1qk2g6u8p4qm2s2lh3gts5cpt2mrv5skcuu7u3e4
nodes.definition: A Bitcoin address is a short string, carrying a checksum, that encodes the condition under which a payment may later be spent; it is what a payer is given and what a wallet turns into an output script.

nodes.label: Exchange rate
nodes.body: An exchange rate is the price of one unit of a currency expressed in another currency. In this chapter it is the number that turns a price in United States dollars into an amount of bitcoin. The chapter says that the prices at Bob's store are listed in the local currency, US dollars, but that at checkout customers have the option of paying in either dollars or bitcoin, and that the checkout cart displays the price in dollars and also in bitcoin at Bitcoin's prevailing exchange rate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An exchange rate is the price of one unit of a currency expressed in another currency. In this chapter it is the number that turns a price in United States dollars into an amount of bitcoin. The chapter says that the prices at Bob's store are listed in the local currency, US dollars, but that at checkout customers have the option of paying in either dollars or bitcoin, and that the checkout cart displays the price in dollars and also in bitcoin at Bitcoin's prevailing exchange rate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The rate is where Bitcoin meets the ordinary economy, and it explains a figure that otherwise looks arbitrary. The amount in the invoice, 0.01577764 bitcoin, is not a round number because it is the dollar price of the podcast episode converted at the rate of that moment. It also explains why a merchant who quotes in a local currency carries no currency risk on the listed price while a merchant who quotes in bitcoin does. The chapter earlier notes that people accept a money only if they expect to be able to spend it later, which is a statement about value over time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

You meet the rate on every checkout page that offers bitcoin, in every wallet that shows a fiat equivalent beside an amount, and in the figures of this chapter. The book's first chapter describes the same step from the other side, when Alice buys bitcoins from Joe for cash at an agreed price (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Exchange rates are also what make the chapter's dollar comparisons meaningful, such as the coffee-shop analogy in which card payments below twenty-five dollars are accepted without a signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The arithmetic is a division. If a podcast episode costs twenty-five dollars and one bitcoin is worth 1,584 dollars at that moment, the price in bitcoin is 25 divided by 1584, which rounds to 0.01578283 bitcoin, a figure of the same shape and size as the invoice's amount. The dollar price and the rate here are an illustration chosen to show the calculation, not figures from the book; what the book gives is the converted amount. Converting the other way, an amount in bitcoin multiplied by the rate gives a price in dollars, and the same amount in satoshis is the bitcoin amount multiplied by one hundred million.

A rate is a market price at an instant, and it is the one number in a payment request that goes stale. An invoice that was correct when it was displayed may be worth more or less a few minutes later, which is why merchants normally let a quoted bitcoin amount expire. The rate is also not part of Bitcoin: no rule of the protocol knows about dollars, and the figures printed in the book are a snapshot of 2023. Treat a rate as context for reading the chapter's amounts, never as a constant.

nodes.example: a dollar price shown in bitcoin
nodes.definition: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another; Bob's shop lists prices in dollars and converts them to bitcoin at checkout, so the bitcoin amount of an invoice is only valid for a moment.

nodes.label: Construction
nodes.body: Construction is the work of turning a decision to pay into a valid transaction. In the chapter this is done entirely by Alice's wallet application, which contains all the logic for selecting inputs and generating outputs to build a transaction to Alice's specification (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group describes what the wallet does, in the order in which it does it: find inputs that can pay, create outputs, add a fee and sign.

paras.text: Construction is the work of turning a decision to pay into a valid transaction. In the chapter this is done entirely by Alice's wallet application, which contains all the logic for selecting inputs and generating outputs to build a transaction to Alice's specification (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group describes what the wallet does, in the order in which it does it: find inputs that can pay, create outputs, add a fee and sign.

Construction is where the abstract parts of the first groups come together. A user sees only a destination, an amount and a fee; everything else, from the choice of inputs to the change, is a decision of the software. Understanding it explains why two wallets can build different transactions for the same payment, and why a wallet bug can lose money.

Every wallet does this, for every payment. The book points out that a wallet can construct a transaction even if it is completely offline, if it already knows which inputs it controls, just as one can write a check at home and later send it to the bank in an envelope (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group contains one concept, the construction of a transaction.

The wallet starts from the outputs it controls, which it tracks. If it runs on a full node, it contains a copy of every confirmed transaction's unspent outputs; many user wallets run as lightweight clients that track only their own (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). From these it chooses inputs, creates an output for the receiver, adds a change output when the inputs exceed the payment, leaves a fee, and signs.

The wallet is trusted with decisions the user never sees, so the user must trust its code. That is why the book recommends a design in which wallets are open and reviewed, and why this course returns to wallets in a later chapter. The wallet cannot be trusted to know what has happened on the network if it is offline, either: a transaction built offline is only a candidate until it is sent.

nodes.label: Transaction construction
nodes.body: Constructing a transaction means assembling its inputs and outputs and signing it. The book describes the user's part as small: Alice only needs to choose a destination, an amount and a transaction fee, and the rest happens in the wallet application without her seeing the details (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The wallet finds inputs that can pay the amount, creates the outputs and attaches the signature that proves she may spend the inputs.

paras.text: Constructing a transaction means assembling its inputs and outputs and signing it. The book describes the user's part as small: Alice only needs to choose a destination, an amount and a transaction fee, and the rest happens in the wallet application without her seeing the details (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The wallet finds inputs that can pay the amount, creates the outputs and attaches the signature that proves she may spend the inputs.

A transaction that has been constructed contains, in the words of the book, everything necessary to confirm ownership of the funds and assign new owners, so it can be sent to the network by any route (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is a major reason why Bitcoin needs no trusted intermediary: the proof of authorization travels inside the transaction, and nodes do not need to know who built it or how it reached them.

In the chapter the steps are described in sections of their own. The first is getting the right inputs: the wallet keeps track of the available outputs belonging to the addresses in the wallet, which here includes the output from Joe's transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Next it creates the outputs. The output for Bob is created with a script that says, in effect, that it is paid to whoever can present a signature from the key corresponding to Bob's public address; the book calls this encumbering the output with a demand for a signature from Bob (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second output returns the change, and the fee is not stated: it is implied by the difference between inputs and outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The sums can be rehearsed. With an input of 100000 satoshis, a payment of 75000 and a fee of 5000, the change is 100000 - 75000 - 5000, which is 20000, and the two output amounts are 20000 and 75000, exactly the amounts of Alice's real transaction. The signing step cannot be shown with these numbers, because it requires the private key and a hash of parts of the transaction. The book notes that a transaction does not need to be constructed and signed while connected to the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Four cautions follow. A wallet that has no knowledge of the current state of the network may build a transaction whose inputs have already been spent. A fee that is chosen too low may make the payment wait, and one that is chosen far too high is paid to the miner without any warning from the format. The signature covers the transaction as built, so a wallet cannot adjust the amounts after signing. And, the book adds, a wallet running on a lightweight client has less information than one running on a full node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: from a destination, an amount and a fee to a signed transaction
nodes.definition: A wallet builds a transaction by choosing inputs, creating an output for the receiver and a change output, leaving the fee implied, and signing - even offline.

io.code: (lambda utxo, pay, fee: [utxo - pay - fee, pay])(100000, 75000, 5000)

nodes.label: Wallet
nodes.body: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin. The book's glossary describes it as software that holds all your Bitcoin addresses and secret keys and that you use to send, receive and store your bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In practice it does four things: it keeps the keys, it keeps track of which outputs those keys can spend, it builds and signs transactions, and it presents the result to the user as a balance and a history. In this chapter there are three of them, Alice's, Bob's and, in the figures of the chain, Joe's and Gopesh's.

paras.text: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin. The book's glossary describes it as software that holds all your Bitcoin addresses and secret keys and that you use to send, receive and store your bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In practice it does four things: it keeps the keys, it keeps track of which outputs those keys can spend, it builds and signs transactions, and it presents the result to the user as a balance and a history. In this chapter there are three of them, Alice's, Bob's and, in the figures of the chain, Joe's and Gopesh's.

The wallet is where all the complexity of the chapter is hidden from the user. The book says that Alice's wallet application contains all the logic for selecting inputs and generating outputs to build a transaction to her specification, and that she only needs to choose a destination, an amount and a transaction fee while the rest happens without her seeing the details (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Everything a reader has met so far, coin selection, change, fees, scripts and signatures, is a decision that this program makes, which is why trusting a wallet is as consequential as trusting a bank used to be.

The chapter meets wallets at every step: Alice's wallet reads the payment request and prefills the payment, builds the transaction and sends it; Bob's wallet recognises the incoming payment because it contains an output redeemable by Bob's keys, and can independently verify that the transaction is well formed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book distinguishes wallets that run on a full node, which hold a copy of every confirmed transaction's unspent outputs, from the many user wallets that run as lightweight clients and track only the user's own (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); and it adds that a wallet can build a transaction while completely offline.

The arithmetic a wallet performs for a payment is the subtraction of this chapter. Given the outputs it controls, the amount to pay and the fee to leave, it works out the change: with one output of 100,000 satoshis, a payment of 75,000 and a fee of 5,000, the change is 20,000, which is what Alice's real transaction contains. Around that subtraction sit the steps described elsewhere in this branch: choosing which outputs to spend, writing an output script for the receiver, writing one for the change, and signing each input with the private key that the output being spent demands.

A wallet does not contain bitcoins. It contains keys and a view of the ledger, which is why a backup of the keys restores the funds and a copy of the balance does not. Two further cautions belong here. A wallet that is offline cannot know whether an output it believes it controls has already been spent, so a transaction built offline is only a candidate until the network accepts it. And the user cannot see what the wallet decided, so a defect in the software can overpay a fee or leak a change address without any warning; the book's chapter on fees asks wallets to make an excessive fee rate hard to pay by accident (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the application that holds Alice's keys
nodes.definition: A wallet is the software that keeps a user's keys, tracks the outputs they can spend, builds and signs transactions, and shows balances; it holds keys, not coins.

io.code: (lambda utxos, pay, fee: sum(utxos) - pay - fee)([100000], 75000, 5000)

nodes.label: Network
nodes.body: The Bitcoin network is the set of computers that run the Bitcoin protocol and exchange transactions and blocks with one another. This second branch of the chapter follows Alice's transaction out of her wallet and across that network. The chapter describes the network in two sentences that the whole branch unfolds: it is a peer-to-peer network in which each peer participates by connecting to several other peers, and its purpose is to propagate transactions and blocks to all participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Bitcoin network is the set of computers that run the Bitcoin protocol and exchange transactions and blocks with one another. This second branch of the chapter follows Alice's transaction out of her wallet and across that network. The chapter describes the network in two sentences that the whole branch unfolds: it is a peer-to-peer network in which each peer participates by connecting to several other peers, and its purpose is to propagate transactions and blocks to all participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch matters because the network is what makes the system work without a company in the middle. There is no server that collects payments and no directory that decides who may take part, so a transaction reaches the miners only because independent computers pass it on, and each of them checks it first. That is also what makes the network robust: the chapter notes that it does not matter how or where a transaction is transmitted, since the transaction contains everything necessary for it to be processed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Any route will do, and no single point can block a payment.

A reader meets the network every time a wallet reports that a payment has been sent and a shop reports a few seconds later that it has arrived. The chapter's own account is exactly this: Alice's wallet can send the transaction to any node over any kind of connection, wired, wireless or mobile, or even to another program such as a block explorer that will relay it to a node, and within a few seconds Bob sees it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's chapter on the network adds the scale: about ten thousand listening nodes running various versions of Bitcoin Core and a few hundred running other implementations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch has two groups. The first asks who takes part: the full node that verifies everything, the lightweight client that verifies a little, the peer that is simply another node one is connected to, and the peer-to-peer architecture that these form. The second follows the journey: the transmission of the transaction from the wallet, the gossiping by which each node forwards what it has accepted, the propagation that results, the memory pool in which an unconfirmed transaction waits, the recipient's own check, and the block explorer through which a reader can watch all of it from outside.

Three cautions apply throughout the branch. Reaching the network is not the same as being recorded: the chapter is careful to say that a transaction does not become part of the blockchain until it is included in a block, which belongs to the next branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Being received by many nodes is not a vote either, since each node decides for itself by the rules. And a peer is not a trusted party: everything that arrives from one is checked, which is exactly why a node can safely connect to strangers.

nodes.label: Who takes part
nodes.body: This group names the kinds of program that make up the network and says what each of them can and cannot check. The chapter introduces them in one passage: peers in the Bitcoin peer-to-peer network are programs that have both the software logic and the data necessary to fully verify the correctness of a new transaction, that the connections between peers are often drawn as the edges of a graph whose nodes are the peers themselves, and that for that reason Bitcoin peers are commonly called full verification nodes, or full nodes for short (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group names the kinds of program that make up the network and says what each of them can and cannot check. The chapter introduces them in one passage: peers in the Bitcoin peer-to-peer network are programs that have both the software logic and the data necessary to fully verify the correctness of a new transaction, that the connections between peers are often drawn as the edges of a graph whose nodes are the peers themselves, and that for that reason Bitcoin peers are commonly called full verification nodes, or full nodes for short (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The distinctions in this group decide whom a user has to trust. A program that verifies every rule for itself needs to trust nobody; a program that asks others for answers has to trust what it is told, at least in part. The chapter uses exactly this difference when it describes Bob's situation: his wallet can verify that Alice's transaction is well formed, but only if Bob is using his own full node can his wallet further verify that the transaction spends valid unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same difference runs through the rest of the course.

The kinds differ in what they keep, and therefore in what they can check for themselves. A full node keeps enough of the chain to re-derive every rule: it recomputes each block's identifier, rebuilds the commitment to the block's transactions, and confirms for every input that the output it spends exists and has not been spent, so its verdict depends on nothing it was told. A lightweight client keeps only the chain of block headers, which is small, and asks a full node for the rest; it can confirm that a block exists and that a transaction is committed to it, and it must take on trust that the block obeyed the rules. A peer is simply a node another node has opened a connection to, and because any node may connect to any other and none has a special position, the structure that results is a mesh rather than a hierarchy - which is what makes the network hard to stop and also what makes its behaviour statistical rather than exact (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Resist two tidy pictures. The first is that these kinds are sharp: the book's network chapter explains that a full node may also carry routing, mining and wallet functions, and that some nodes keep a complete archival copy while others do not, so the roles overlap (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is that more participants automatically means more security; what matters is how many independently verify the rules, which is why this group separates the counting of nodes from the question of what each of them actually checks.

nodes.label: Full node
nodes.body: A full node, which the chapter calls a full verification node, is a program that has both the software logic and the data necessary to fully verify the correctness of a new transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's network chapter states the same thing about blocks: full nodes verify every transaction in every block on the valid blockchain with the most proof of work, process every block starting after the genesis block, and can therefore verify any transaction independently and authoritatively (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word node comes from the picture of the network as a graph whose dots are the programs and whose lines are their connections.

The book's network chapter states the same thing about blocks: full nodes verify every transaction in every block on the valid blockchain with the most proof of work, process every block starting after the genesis block, and can therefore verify any transaction independently and authoritatively (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word node comes from the picture of the network as a graph whose dots are the programs and whose lines are their connections.

The full node is the reason the chapter can open by saying that the Bitcoin system does not require trust in third parties, and that each user can run software on their own computer to verify the correct operation of every aspect of the system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A user with a full node accepts a payment because their own program checked it; a user without one accepts it because somebody else said so. The book adds that running a full node gives the pure Bitcoin experience, independent verification of all transactions without the need to rely on, or trust, any other system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter meets a full node three times: when Alice's wallet hands the transaction to any node it can reach, when every node that receives it forwards it only if it is valid, and when Bob's wallet, if it runs on his own full node, checks that the transaction spends valid unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's network chapter says that more than ninety-five per cent of full nodes run some version of Bitcoin Core and that it identifies itself as Satoshi in the version string it sends to its peers, for example as /Satoshi:24.0.1/ (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Verification is the running of a checklist. The book's mining chapter prints the list that a node applies to every transaction it receives, and its items are the ones this chapter has prepared: the syntax and data structure must be correct, neither the list of inputs nor the list of outputs may be empty, the weight must be small enough to fit in a block, each output value and the total must be within the allowed range, the outputs being spent must match outputs in the memory pool or unspent outputs in a block of the best chain, the sum of the inputs may not be less than the sum of the outputs, and the scripts of each input must validate against the corresponding output scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The small example stands for that checklist: a transaction is accepted when every item passes, and the count of items is what was checked.

A full node is not a miner and not a wallet, although one program may do all three. It also does not make a user anonymous or protect their keys, and it does not remove every trust: a user still trusts the software they downloaded, which is why the next chapter of the course is about verifying a release of Bitcoin Core. Finally, a node's view can be briefly out of date, since it learns of a new block only when a peer sends it; what it never does is accept a block or transaction that breaks a rule it enforces.

nodes.example: a program that verifies every rule
nodes.definition: A full node is a program that holds the logic and the data to verify every transaction and block against every rule, so that it needs to trust nobody.

nodes.label: Lightweight client
nodes.body: A lightweight client is a Bitcoin program that does not verify everything. The chapter introduces the kind in a single clause, saying that because full nodes use more resources, many user wallets run lightweight clients that track only the user's own unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's network chapter gives the method a name: such clients download only the block headers, not the transactions in each block, and verify payments by a procedure called simplified payment verification (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A lightweight client is a Bitcoin program that does not verify everything. The chapter introduces the kind in a single clause, saying that because full nodes use more resources, many user wallets run lightweight clients that track only the user's own unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's network chapter gives the method a name: such clients download only the block headers, not the transactions in each block, and verify payments by a procedure called simplified payment verification (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Lightweight clients exist because verification costs resources that a telephone does not have. The book says they are designed to run on space- and power-constrained devices such as smartphones, tablets and embedded systems (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The trade is explicit: the client gets a usable wallet in a pocket and gives up the ability to check everything for itself, relying instead on peers to provide partial views of the relevant parts of the blockchain on demand (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Knowing which of the two kinds a wallet is tells a user exactly how much of the chapter's guarantee applies to them.

This chapter meets the kind twice. When Alice's wallet gets the right inputs, the book contrasts a wallet running on a full node, which contains a copy of every confirmed transaction's unspent outputs, with the many user wallets that run as lightweight clients (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And at the end of the chapter, lightweight clients are said to partially verify payments by confirming that the transaction is in the blockchain and has several blocks mined after it, which gives assurance that miners expended significant effort committing to it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The saving comes from the size of a header. A block header is eighty bytes whatever the block contains, while a full block can hold about four million bytes of transactions, so the chain of headers alone is roughly ten thousand times smaller than the full chain, which is the factor the book gives and which the division above reproduces (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). To check that a particular transaction is in a block, the client asks a peer for a short path of hashes through the block's merkle tree and recomputes the root, as the concepts of the merkle tree and of simplified payment verification explain.

A lightweight client cannot tell by itself whether a transaction obeys the rules; it can only see that it was committed to by work. The book's comparison is a tourist with a street map against a tourist asking strangers for directions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). There is a privacy cost as well, since asking peers which transactions concern you tells them which transactions concern you, and the book devotes a section to that problem (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's warning about block explorers is the same point in another form: looking something up may tell the operator what you are interested in (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a wallet on a telephone
nodes.definition: A lightweight client downloads only block headers and asks peers for the parts of the chain that concern it, so it verifies a payment only partly; this is simplified payment verification.

nodes.label: Peer and connection
nodes.body: A peer is another participant of the network with which a node maintains a connection in order to exchange transactions and blocks. The chapter uses the word in its description of the architecture: the Bitcoin network is a peer-to-peer network, with each peer participating by connecting to several other peers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's network chapter adds that the full nodes that take part are peers to each other, that they can all perform the same functions and that there are no special nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A peer is another participant of the network with which a node maintains a connection in order to exchange transactions and blocks. The chapter uses the word in its description of the architecture: the Bitcoin network is a peer-to-peer network, with each peer participating by connecting to several other peers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's network chapter adds that the full nodes that take part are peers to each other, that they can all perform the same functions and that there are no special nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Peers are how a node learns anything at all. There is no server to ask, so every unconfirmed transaction and every new block reaches a node from a peer, and everything the node has accepted is passed on to its peers in turn. The word also carries a claim about equality: because the participants are of the same kind, no one of them can be removed to stop the network, and the chapter can say that it does not matter how or where a transaction is transmitted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For an operator, each connection is also a small cost in memory and bandwidth.

The chapter meets peers when Alice's wallet sends the transaction to any node it can reach and when that node forwards it to all the other nodes to which it is connected (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's network chapter describes the first thing two peers do, exchanging version messages that state how many blocks each has, and then headers and blocks until the shorter chain has caught up (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A reader who runs a node sees its peers listed with the software each is running.

A connection is a link between two nodes over which messages travel, and a node has several at once; the small example counts a set of three and names the first. The structure matters more than the number: the book describes the nodes as interconnecting in a mesh with a flat topology, with no server, no centralized service and no hierarchy, and says that nodes in such a network both provide and consume services at the same time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A node finds candidates to connect to from addresses it has learned before, a process the book's network chapter calls network discovery.

A peer is not a trusted party, and this is the single most important thing to remember about the word. Everything a peer sends is checked against the rules by the receiving node, which is why connecting to unknown computers is safe for the data. The number of peers is also not a measure of correctness, and a node that is connected to many peers still accepts only what passes its own checks. Finally, peers see what you send them: the book's chapter on lightweight clients and privacy explains that what a program asks its peers for can reveal what it is interested in (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: another node my node talks to
nodes.definition: A peer is another node that a node keeps a connection to in order to exchange transactions and blocks; peers are equals, with no server among them.

nodes.label: Peer-to-peer network
nodes.body: A peer-to-peer network, often abbreviated to P2P, is a network in which the participants are equals: each of them performs the same functions, each both provides and consumes services, and none of them is special. The book states this of Bitcoin directly, adding that the nodes interconnect in a mesh network with a flat topology, that there is no server, no centralized service and no hierarchy within the network, and that such networks are inherently resilient, decentralized and open (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A peer-to-peer network, often abbreviated to P2P, is a network in which the participants are equals: each of them performs the same functions, each both provides and consumes services, and none of them is special. The book states this of Bitcoin directly, adding that the nodes interconnect in a mesh network with a flat topology, that there is no server, no centralized service and no hierarchy within the network, and that such networks are inherently resilient, decentralized and open (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

For Bitcoin the architecture is not a technical preference but a consequence of the goal. The book writes that Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer digital cash system by design, that the network architecture is both a reflection and a foundation of that characteristic, and that decentralization of control can only be achieved and maintained by a flat and decentralized consensus network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nakamoto's paper is titled for the same idea and proposes a solution using a peer-to-peer network in which the participants timestamp transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of proof of work (Nakamoto, 2008). If there were a server, whoever ran it could decide what counts as a payment.

The shape is met in the chapter whenever a transaction travels: Alice's wallet does not have to be connected to Bob's wallet, nor to use the internet connection that Bob offers, though both of those are possible too (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Beyond Bitcoin, the book names the early internet as a preeminent example of the architecture, where the nodes of the network were equal, and file sharing as its largest and most successful application, with Napster as the pioneer and BitTorrent as the most recent evolution (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

What makes the structure work is that every node keeps several connections, so that the whole is connected without any central point. The number of links grows quickly with the number of participants: a group of five nodes in which everyone is connected to everyone has five times four divided by two, that is ten links, as the calculation above shows. A real network does not connect everyone to everyone, because a path of a few hops is enough: the chapter says that a transaction rapidly propagates out across the network, reaching a large percentage of the nodes within a few seconds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Peer-to-peer does not mean that every participant does the same amount of work, nor that there are no services built on top. The book notes that beside the base protocol there are others used for mining and for lightweight wallets, provided by gateway servers that bridge into the peer-to-peer network, and that various companies run nodes as network edge routers on which exchanges, wallets, explorers and payment processors are built (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Those services are centralized even though the protocol beneath them is not, and a user who relies on one of them is relying on its operator.

nodes.example: a mesh with no server
nodes.definition: A peer-to-peer network is one in which every participant is of the same kind and both provides and consumes services, with no server and no hierarchy; Bitcoin is built this way on purpose.

nodes.label: Propagation
nodes.body: Propagation is the spreading of a transaction or a block from the computer that first has it to the rest of the network. This group follows Alice's payment through that spreading, from the moment her wallet transmits it to the moment a reader can look it up from outside. The chapter's three short sections on transmitting the transaction, how it propagates and Bob's view are the backbone of the group, and the memory pool and the block explorer are added so that the whole journey can be described in the words the later chapters use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Propagation is the spreading of a transaction or a block from the computer that first has it to the rest of the network. This group follows Alice's payment through that spreading, from the moment her wallet transmits it to the moment a reader can look it up from outside. The chapter's three short sections on transmitting the transaction, how it propagates and Bob's view are the backbone of the group, and the memory pool and the block explorer are added so that the whole journey can be described in the words the later chapters use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group explains why a payment can be trusted within seconds even though it is not yet recorded. Each node that forwards the transaction has first verified it, so propagation is not mere copying: it is a wave of independent checks. That is also the reason the chapter can say that invalid data does not travel far, and the reason a merchant may make a judgement about an unconfirmed payment, as the security group of the next branch discusses.

A reader meets propagation as the few seconds between pressing Send and seeing the payment appear in the receiver's wallet. The chapter states the figure twice: within a few seconds, about the same amount of time as a credit card authorization, Bob sees the transaction on the register, and even if the transaction goes through other nodes it will reach Bob's wallet within a few seconds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same event can be watched from a third position, in a block explorer, which is why the explorer belongs to this group.

Propagation works by flooding, with each node acting as a filter. A wallet sends its transaction to the few nodes it is connected to; each of those checks it against the rules before doing anything else, and only if it passes does the node announce it to its own connections, which ask for it in turn. Because every hop verifies, an invalid transaction travels no further than the first honest node, and because every hop re-announces, a valid one reaches most of the network in a few seconds without anyone directing it. A node that has accepted a transaction but has not yet seen it in a block keeps it in a memory pool, which is where it waits to be chosen by a miner; the pool is each node's own, so two nodes need not hold the same set. The recipient's own check is the end of the journey and the only one that matters to the recipient, which is the reason the chapter warns about relying on a block explorer instead: asking a third party what happened also tells that party which transaction interests you (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Propagation proves nothing about permanence. A transaction that has reached every node is still unconfirmed, can still be replaced in some circumstances, and is recorded only when a miner includes it in a block that other nodes accept. Speed can also mislead: that a payment appeared in a wallet within two seconds says only that the data arrived, not that the money cannot be taken back, which is the subject of the confirmation concept in the next branch.

nodes.label: Transmitting the transaction
nodes.body: Transmission is the step in which a finished, signed transaction leaves the wallet that built it and is handed to the network. The chapter gives it a section of its own and states the governing principle at once: because the transaction contains all the information necessary for it to be processed, it does not matter how or where it is transmitted to the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). From that moment the wallet's work is over and the network's work begins.

paras.text: Transmission is the step in which a finished, signed transaction leaves the wallet that built it and is handed to the network. The chapter gives it a section of its own and states the governing principle at once: because the transaction contains all the information necessary for it to be processed, it does not matter how or where it is transmitted to the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). From that moment the wallet's work is over and the network's work begins.

This indifference to the route is one of Bitcoin's quietly radical properties. A payment is not a request sent to an institution that may accept or refuse it; it is a self-contained document whose validity any recipient can check. The chapter draws out the practical consequences: Alice's wallet can send the transaction to any Bitcoin node over any type of connection, wired, wireless or mobile, and it can also send it to another program, such as a block explorer, that will relay it to a node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Her wallet does not have to be connected to Bob's wallet directly, and she does not have to use the internet connection offered by Bob, though both of those are possible as well.

The reader meets transmission as the moment of pressing Send. In the chapter, Alice scans the code, sees a payment for the correct amount to Bob's Store, selects Send to authorize the payment, and within a few seconds Bob sees the transaction on the register (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same step is why a transaction can be built on a device that has no network at all: the book compares it to writing a cheque at home and later sending it to the bank in an envelope, and says that a wallet that already knows what inputs it controls can construct transactions completely offline (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mechanism is simply to give the bytes to something that is connected. The small example lists the routes the chapter names, sorted, to make the point that they are interchangeable: a wired link, wireless, mobile, or a program such as a block explorer that will relay the transaction onward. Whatever the route, the receiving node applies its checklist before doing anything else, and only then passes the transaction on, which is the rule that the gossiping concept describes.

Two things are not guaranteed by transmission. The first is arrival: a wallet that sends a transaction to a single node and gets no acknowledgement does not know that the network has it, which is why wallets usually send to several peers and watch for the transaction coming back to them. The second is acceptance: a node that finds the transaction invalid simply drops it, and the chapter's rule is that a node forwards a valid transaction it has not seen before (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Relaying through a third party such as an explorer also tells that party who is paying whom, which is the privacy cost the chapter warns of.

nodes.example: the first hop out of the wallet
nodes.definition: Transmission is the sending of a finished transaction from the wallet to any program that will put it on the network; the route does not matter because the transaction carries everything needed to process it.

nodes.label: Gossiping
nodes.body: Gossiping is the name the chapter gives to the way data spreads through the Bitcoin network. The rule is stated in one sentence: any Bitcoin node that receives a valid transaction it has not seen before will forward it to all other nodes to which it is connected, a propagation technique known as gossiping (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every word of the rule carries weight: valid, so that bad data stops at the first node; not seen before, so that the same transaction is not passed round in circles; and all other nodes, so that no one chooses who hears about it.

paras.text: Gossiping is the name the chapter gives to the way data spreads through the Bitcoin network. The rule is stated in one sentence: any Bitcoin node that receives a valid transaction it has not seen before will forward it to all other nodes to which it is connected, a propagation technique known as gossiping (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every word of the rule carries weight: valid, so that bad data stops at the first node; not seen before, so that the same transaction is not passed round in circles; and all other nodes, so that no one chooses who hears about it.

Gossiping is how a network with no coordinator reaches everybody. Nobody holds a list of participants and nobody decides the route, yet the chapter can say that the transaction rapidly propagates out across the peer-to-peer network, reaching a large percentage of the nodes within a few seconds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The validity condition is what makes this safe rather than reckless: the book's mining chapter explains that every node verifies a transaction before forwarding it, so that only valid transactions are propagated while invalid ones are discarded at the first node that encounters them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets gossiping as the speed of a Bitcoin payment and, from the other side, as the reason a shop can see a payment that was made on the other side of the world. The course notes for this chapter describe the same mechanism under its other common name, flooding, and record the same observation, that a valid transaction is forwarded to the other connected nodes and reaches a large percentage of the network within a few seconds (Altunel, 2021). Blocks spread by the same rule, which is why a new block reaches every miner quickly enough for the competition to restart.

The reach grows multiplicatively. If each node forwards to eight peers, then after one round eight nodes have the transaction, after two rounds sixty-four and after three rounds eight to the third power, that is 512, as the calculation above shows; a handful of rounds is therefore enough for a network of thousands, and each round takes only as long as a message between two computers. The numbers are an idealization, since peers overlap and a node ignores what it already has, but the order of growth is why a few seconds suffice.

Gossiping does not guarantee that every node will hold a given transaction. A node may be offline, may have a full memory pool, or may apply its own relay policy, and the book's chapter on fees notes that nodes limit how many unconfirmed transactions they store (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nor does gossiping record anything: the data is in memory, not in the blockchain. And because what spreads is what a node has accepted, a transaction that one node's policy rejects may travel less widely without being invalid, so wide propagation is evidence of acceptance rather than proof of it.

nodes.example: each node tells all its peers
nodes.definition: Gossiping is the rule that any node receiving a valid transaction it has not seen before forwards it to all the peers it is connected to, so that data spreads without any coordinator.

nodes.label: Transaction propagation
nodes.body: Transaction propagation is the spread of a signed transaction across the network until it has reached, in practice, everyone who cares, including the miners who may record it. It is the composition of the two previous concepts: the wallet transmits the transaction to some node, and then the gossip rule carries it onward hop by hop. The chapter's own summary is that the purpose of the Bitcoin network is to propagate transactions and blocks to all participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Transaction propagation is the spread of a signed transaction across the network until it has reached, in practice, everyone who cares, including the miners who may record it. It is the composition of the two previous concepts: the wallet transmits the transaction to some node, and then the gossip rule carries it onward hop by hop. The chapter's own summary is that the purpose of the Bitcoin network is to propagate transactions and blocks to all participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Propagation is the step that turns a private document into public knowledge, and it is what makes the double-spend check meaningful. If every node sees the transaction that spends an output, a second transaction spending the same output will be rejected by the nodes that already hold the first, so a fraudulent payment has to beat the honest one through the network. Propagation is also what the receiver relies on in the first seconds: before any block exists, the only evidence Bob has is that his own program and everybody else's have seen the payment and found it valid.

The chapter tracks Alice's transaction through exactly this step and gives the timing twice: within a few seconds, about the same time as a credit card authorization, Bob sees it on the register, and even when the transaction goes through other nodes it reaches Bob's wallet within a few seconds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Later the chapter says that the transaction was picked up by the network and included in the pool of unverified transactions, and that once validated by a full node it was included in a candidate block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A block explorer shows the same transaction as unconfirmed during that interval.

The rough arithmetic of the chapter's claim can be done. If a network of about ten thousand listening nodes is reached in about five seconds, that is on the order of two thousand nodes a second, as the division above gives (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nothing coordinates this: each node, on receiving the transaction, applies the verification checklist, stores it in its memory pool and announces it to its own peers, who ask for it if they do not have it. The book's network chapter describes that announcement as the exchange of inventory, in which a node offers what it has and a peer requests what it lacks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Propagation is not confirmation, and this is the misconception the chapter is most careful about: a transaction does not become part of the blockchain until it is included in a block by mining and that block has been validated by full nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A widely propagated transaction can still be dropped if it is never mined, and in some circumstances it can be replaced by another version paying a higher fee, which the book's chapter on fees describes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). What propagation gives is visibility and a first, probabilistic assurance, nothing more.

nodes.example: Alice's payment reaching the network
nodes.definition: Transaction propagation is the spread of a signed transaction across the network by gossip, each node verifying before relaying, until it reaches the miners.

nodes.label: Memory pool
nodes.body: The memory pool, usually shortened to mempool, is the collection of transactions that a node has verified but that are not yet in any block. The book's network chapter says that almost every node on the network maintains such a temporary list of unconfirmed transactions, and uses it to keep track of transactions that are known to the network but not yet included in the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The mining chapter adds how the pool is filled: by independently verifying each transaction as it is received and before propagating it, every node builds a pool of valid but unconfirmed transactions known as the memory pool (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The memory pool, usually shortened to mempool, is the collection of transactions that a node has verified but that are not yet in any block. The book's network chapter says that almost every node on the network maintains such a temporary list of unconfirmed transactions, and uses it to keep track of transactions that are known to the network but not yet included in the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The mining chapter adds how the pool is filled: by independently verifying each transaction as it is received and before propagating it, every node builds a pool of valid but unconfirmed transactions known as the memory pool (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The pool is the waiting room of the system, and it is where the market for block space happens. A miner builds a candidate block out of the pool, and the chapter says that transactions are added to the new block prioritized by the highest fee rate first and a few other criteria (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), so the pool is what the fee rate concept is about. For a user, the pool explains the state a payment is in during the first minutes: verified by everyone, recorded by nobody.

The chapter meets the pool when it says that Alice's transaction was picked up by the network and included in the pool of unverified transactions, and that once validated by a full node it was included in a candidate block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's mining chapter describes the same pool from the miner's side: while searching for a solution, the mining node was also collecting transactions, and by the time the previous block arrived it had collected a few thousand in its memory pool; on receiving and validating that block it removes from the pool any transactions the block contained, and whatever remains is unconfirmed and waiting (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Maintaining the pool is adding and removing. A verified transaction is added and announced to peers; a transaction that appears in a new block is removed, which the small example shows by filtering a pool of three against a block containing one of them and keeping the other two. Some implementations also keep a separate pool for orphaned transactions, whose inputs refer to a transaction the node does not yet know, and move them into the memory pool when the missing parent arrives, a cascade that the book describes as reuniting the orphans with their parents (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The memory pool is local, not global. The book is explicit that the memory pool and the orphan pool represent a single node's local perspective and might vary significantly from node to node depending on when the node was started or restarted, unlike the database of unspent outputs, which represents the emergent consensus of the network and will not usually vary (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). So there is no such thing as the mempool, only each node's own; a transaction in your node's pool may be missing from another's, and nothing in the pool is recorded until it is mined.

nodes.label: The recipient's own check
nodes.body: The recipient's own check is what happens in Bob's wallet when Alice's transaction arrives. The chapter devotes a short section to it, called Bob's view, and makes three statements. Bob's wallet will immediately identify Alice's transaction as an incoming payment because it contains an output redeemable by Bob's keys; his wallet can also independently verify that the transaction is well formed; and if Bob is using his own full node, his wallet can further verify that Alice's transaction only spends valid unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The recipient's own check is what happens in Bob's wallet when Alice's transaction arrives. The chapter devotes a short section to it, called Bob's view, and makes three statements. Bob's wallet will immediately identify Alice's transaction as an incoming payment because it contains an output redeemable by Bob's keys; his wallet can also independently verify that the transaction is well formed; and if Bob is using his own full node, his wallet can further verify that Alice's transaction only spends valid unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

This concept is where the chapter's opening promise becomes concrete for a particular person. Bob does not have to telephone a bank or trust Alice: his own program reads the transaction and recognises the payment. The three statements also form a ladder of assurance that the course returns to again and again. Recognising an output addressed to oneself requires nothing but one's own keys; checking that the data is well formed requires only the rules of the format; checking that the inputs exist and are unspent requires the whole ledger, which is what a full node has.

In the chapter, Bob's wallet may even be the first to receive the transaction if it is connected directly to Alice's, and otherwise receives it within a few seconds through other nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A shop meets the same step as the line on the register that says a payment has arrived. The book's chapter on fees adds the caution that belongs here, discussing merchants that accept unconfirmed transactions and what they should watch for (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Recognition is a search through the outputs for one that the wallet's own keys can spend. The small example does exactly that on the two outputs of Alice's transaction, one belonging to Alice as change and one to Bob, and returns the index 1, which is Bob's payment and the output that the chapter's later figure shows Bob spending as Tx2:1. Checking well-formedness is applying the parts of the verification checklist that need no outside data, such as that the lists of inputs and outputs are not empty and that the amounts are in range; checking the inputs needs the set of unspent outputs, which only a full node keeps.

What the recipient's check cannot establish is that the payment is final. The transaction is unconfirmed at this point, so the assurance is about validity, not permanence, and the chapter moves straight on to mining for that reason. A lightweight wallet is also limited in a way its user may not notice: it will show the incoming payment, but it has not verified that the inputs were unspent, so it is trusting its peers for that part. And recognising an output as one's own is not the same as being able to spend it yet, since an output in an unconfirmed transaction can only be spent further once there is something to build on.

nodes.example: Bob's wallet recognising the payment
nodes.definition: The receiver's wallet recognises an incoming payment because an output is redeemable by its keys, and checks what it can: well-formedness always, and valid unspent inputs only with a full node.

nodes.label: Block explorer
nodes.body: A block explorer is a web application that operates as a Bitcoin search engine: it allows you to search for addresses, transactions and blocks and to see the relationships and flows between them, in the chapter's own words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter uses one throughout, saying that while tracking a transaction through the network to the blockchain it will use a blockchain explorer site to visualize each step, and it provides a link for each transaction and block example so that a reader can look it up and study it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A block explorer is a web application that operates as a Bitcoin search engine: it allows you to search for addresses, transactions and blocks and to see the relationships and flows between them, in the chapter's own words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter uses one throughout, saying that while tracking a transaction through the network to the blockchain it will use a blockchain explorer site to visualize each step, and it provides a link for each transaction and block example so that a reader can look it up and study it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The explorer is what makes this chapter checkable by a reader who has no node. All the data in the blockchain is public, but reading it from the network requires software and a copy of the chain; an explorer does that work and presents the result as a web page. For a course it is also the simplest instrument of the subject: a student can see a real input pointing at a real earlier output, and watch a transaction move from unconfirmed to one confirmation and then to more.

The chapter names three popular explorers, the Blockstream Explorer, Mempool.Space and the BlockCypher Explorer, and says that each has a search function that can take a Bitcoin address, a transaction hash, a block number or a block hash and retrieve the corresponding information from the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It then gives links to the payment made to Bob, to the transaction from Alice to Bob's Store and to the block that includes it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The owner's course notes for this chapter list the explorers of their time, among them blockchain.info and the BlockCypher and Insight explorers, which shows that the set of services changes while the data does not (Altunel, 2021).

An explorer works out from the shape of the query what is being asked for, and the small example shows the idea: a query of sixty-four hexadecimal characters is a transaction or block hash, a string beginning with bc1 is an address of the newer format, and a plain number is a block height. It then looks the item up in its own index of the chain and renders a page, following the links that this chapter has explained, from an input to the output it spends and from a block to its parent. The explorer can also relay a transaction, which is why the chapter lists it among the ways Alice's wallet can reach the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter attaches a warning to the explorer and so should the reader. Searching information on a block explorer may disclose to its operator that you are interested in that information, allowing them to associate it with your address on the internet, your browser details, your past searches or other identifiable information; looking up the transactions in the book is harmless, but looking up your own may let the operator guess how many bitcoins you have received, spent and currently own (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). An explorer is also a third party: what it shows has not been verified by you, which is exactly the trust that running a full node removes.

nodes.example: a web page showing Alice's transaction
nodes.definition: A block explorer is a web application that works as a search engine for the blockchain, taking an address, a transaction identifier, a block number or a block hash and showing what it finds - and learning what you searched for.
