nodes.label: Blockchain
nodes.body: The blockchain is the record in which Bitcoin's transactions are finally written down. The chapter calls it the distributed journal of all transactions and, in its opening overview, the consensus blockchain which is the authoritative journal of all transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's own chapter on the subject is more precise about the shape of the thing: the blockchain is the history of every confirmed transaction, and its data structure is an ordered, back-linked list of blocks of transactions, each block referring to the previous one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This third branch of the chapter is about how a transaction gets into that record and why, once it is there, it becomes progressively harder to remove.

paras.text: The blockchain is the record in which Bitcoin's transactions are finally written down. The chapter calls it the distributed journal of all transactions and, in its opening overview, the consensus blockchain which is the authoritative journal of all transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's own chapter on the subject is more precise about the shape of the thing: the blockchain is the history of every confirmed transaction, and its data structure is an ordered, back-linked list of blocks of transactions, each block referring to the previous one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This third branch of the chapter is about how a transaction gets into that record and why, once it is there, it becomes progressively harder to remove.

The branch answers the question that the first two leave open. A transaction that every node has seen and found valid is still only a proposal: nothing yet says that this payment, and not a competing one spending the same output, is the one that counts. The chapter's answer is computation. Bitcoin's system of counterfeit protection is based on computation: transactions are bundled into blocks whose headers must be formed in a very specific way, requiring an enormous amount of computation to get right but only a small amount to verify as correct (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That asymmetry is what replaces the authority of a bank.

A reader meets this branch as the wait between paying and being sure. In the chapter, about five minutes after Alice's wallet transmitted the transaction a miner finds a solution and announces the block; roughly nineteen minutes later another miner builds on top of it, giving Alice's transaction two confirmations; and the convention the chapter states is that any block with more than six confirmations is considered very hard to change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Below the block containing Alice's payment are hundreds of thousands of earlier blocks, linked all the way back to block number zero, the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch has three groups. The mining group explains who builds blocks and how: the miner, the candidate block, the proof of work that makes a candidate valid, the block and its header, the merkle tree that commits to the transactions, the difficulty that keeps the pace at about ten minutes, the hash rate that measures the search, the consensus rules that every block must obey, the coinbase transaction and the reward it pays, the pool through which small miners take part, and the sudoku analogy from the course notes. The security group explains why the record holds: confirmations, the probability behind them, the best blockchain, the block height, accidental forks and alternative blocks, the double spend that all of this prevents, the genesis block, and the judgements a merchant may make before any confirmation exists. The spending group closes the chapter by letting Bob spend what he received.

Two habits of language should be corrected early. First, a block is not added by anybody's decision: a miner publishes a candidate that satisfies the rules, and each node decides for itself whether to accept it, which the book calls independent validation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Second, nothing in Bitcoin is final in the absolute sense; the book writes that while the protocol always allows a chain to be undone by a longer chain, the probability of such an event decreases as time passes until it becomes infinitesimal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The security of this branch is probabilistic, and saying so precisely is part of understanding it.

nodes.label: Mining
nodes.body: Mining is the process that turns a pool of unconfirmed transactions into the next block of the blockchain. The chapter introduces it in one sentence, saying that Alice's transaction does not become part of the blockchain until it is included in a block by a process called mining and that block has been validated by full nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group gathers everything needed to read that sentence: who does the work, what they build, what makes the result valid, and what they are paid.

paras.text: Mining is the process that turns a pool of unconfirmed transactions into the next block of the blockchain. The chapter introduces it in one sentence, saying that Alice's transaction does not become part of the blockchain until it is included in a block by a process called mining and that block has been validated by full nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This group gathers everything needed to read that sentence: who does the work, what they build, what makes the result valid, and what they are paid.

The group explains Bitcoin's answer to a problem that has no obvious solution: how a network of strangers can agree on an order of events without a referee. The chapter names the two purposes that mining serves. Miners can only receive honest income from creating blocks that follow all of Bitcoin's consensus rules, so they are normally incentivized to include only valid transactions, which allows users to make a trust-based assumption that any transaction in a block is valid; and mining currently creates new bitcoins in each block, almost like a central bank printing new money, in an amount that is limited and diminishes with time following a fixed issuance schedule (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Mining is met in this chapter as the five minutes Alice waits, and in the world as an industry. The chapter describes the mechanism as a decentralized lottery in which each miner creates their own ticket by building a candidate block, feeds it to a hash function, and wins if the output matches a template set by the protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The owner's course notes for this chapter follow the same story and add the history of the hardware, from a fast desktop computer in 2010 through graphics cards to the application-specific integrated circuits that a mining company runs in a warehouse by the thousand (Altunel, 2021).

Mining works as a lottery whose tickets are hash computations. A miner assembles a candidate block from its memory pool, commits to those transactions through a single hash at the top of a tree built over them, and then varies a field of the block's small header, hashing the header again each time, until the result falls below a target that the rules declare. Nothing about that search can be shortened, so the chance of success is proportional to the hashing done, which is what makes the result expensive to produce and cheap to check - any node hashes the header once and compares. The target is adjusted every 2016 blocks so that, whatever hashing power has joined or left, blocks keep arriving about every ten minutes, which is 144 of them a day. The reward is paid by the miner to itself in the block's first transaction, which creates new coins and collects the fees, and a pool exists because a small miner's chance of winning alone is so low that sharing the search and the payment is the only way to be paid regularly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Nakamoto, 2008).

Three warnings belong to the whole group. Mining does not verify transactions on behalf of the network: every full node verifies for itself, and mining decides only the order and the timing. The ten-minute figure is an average and not a schedule, which the security group takes up. And the figures of this group, the reward, the hash rate and the difficulty, change continuously; what is stable is the rule that produces them, so a learner should remember the rule and look up the number.

nodes.label: Miner
nodes.body: A miner is a participant that builds candidate blocks and searches for the proof of work that would make one of them valid. The book's glossary defines a miner as a network node that finds valid proof of work for new blocks by repeated hashing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and its mining chapter describes a concrete one: Jing, who earns bitcoin by running a mining rig, a specialized computer-hardware system designed to mine, connected to a server that runs a full node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A miner is therefore a full node with extra hardware and an extra job, not a different kind of participant.

paras.text: A miner is a participant that builds candidate blocks and searches for the proof of work that would make one of them valid. The book's glossary defines a miner as a network node that finds valid proof of work for new blocks by repeated hashing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and its mining chapter describes a concrete one: Jing, who earns bitcoin by running a mining rig, a specialized computer-hardware system designed to mine, connected to a server that runs a full node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A miner is therefore a full node with extra hardware and an extra job, not a different kind of participant.

Miners exist because somebody has to decide the order of transactions, and Bitcoin pays for that service instead of appointing anybody to it. The chapter describes the balance: mining uses electricity to solve a computational problem, a successful miner collects a reward in the form of new bitcoins and transaction fees, but the reward will only be collected if the miner has included only valid transactions, with the rules for consensus determining what is valid, and this delicate balance provides security for Bitcoin without a central authority (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter meets a miner twice: when Alice's transaction, once validated by a full node, is included in a candidate block, and about five minutes later when a miner finds a solution for the block and announces it to the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's mining chapter adds what the miner's node was doing before that: like every other full node it receives and propagates unconfirmed transactions, and in addition it aggregates them into new blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Outside the chapter, miners are companies with warehouses of hardware, as the owner's course notes describe (Altunel, 2021).

A miner's income is a sum of two parts. The chapter says that each miner includes a special transaction in their candidate blocks, one that pays their own address the block reward plus the sum of transaction fees from all the transactions included in the candidate block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). With the 2023 subsidy of 6.25 bitcoins, which is 625,000,000 satoshis, and fees of 183,000 satoshis from the transactions in the block, the total is 625,183,000 satoshis, as the addition above shows. The work itself is the repeated hashing of the candidate's header, which the proof-of-work concept describes.

A miner cannot cheat by writing itself a larger reward. The book puts the question directly and answers it: an inflated reward would make the block invalid in the eyes of everyone else, wasting the electricity spent on the proof of work, because the miner only gets to spend the reward if the block is accepted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nor is a miner a judge of transactions: it chooses which valid transactions to include, usually by fee rate, but it cannot make an invalid one valid. And mining is not a vote of users: it counts computation, and the nodes that enforce the rules decide what they will accept.

nodes.example: a node that searches for a valid block
nodes.definition: A miner is a node that assembles candidate blocks and searches for a proof of work; it is paid by the new bitcoins of the block and the fees of the transactions it includes.

nodes.label: Candidate block
nodes.body: A candidate block is the block a miner is working on: the transactions it wants to include, a commitment to the previous block, and the other header fields, assembled but without a valid proof of work. The book explains the name, saying that the block is called a candidate block because it is not yet a valid block, as it does not contain a valid proof of work, and that it becomes valid only if the miner succeeds in finding a solution according to the proof-of-work algorithm (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A candidate block is the block a miner is working on: the transactions it wants to include, a commitment to the previous block, and the other header fields, assembled but without a valid proof of work. The book explains the name, saying that the block is called a candidate block because it is not yet a valid block, as it does not contain a valid proof of work, and that it becomes valid only if the miner succeeds in finding a solution according to the proof-of-work algorithm (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The candidate block is where a miner's choices are made, and therefore where the market for block space is settled. The chapter says that transactions are added to the new block prioritized by the highest fee rate transactions first and a few other criteria, and that each miner starts the process of mining a new candidate block as soon as they receive the previous block from the network, knowing that some other miner won that iteration of the lottery (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The candidate is also the lottery ticket in the chapter's own image: each miner can create their own ticket by creating a candidate block that includes the new transactions they want to mine plus some additional data fields (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter meets the candidate when it says that Alice's transaction, once validated by a full node, was included in a candidate block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's mining chapter describes the moment of construction: upon receiving and validating a new block, the mining node compares it against the transactions in its memory pool and removes any that the block contained, and then immediately constructs a new partial block, a candidate for the next block, from what remains (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Miners in a pool are each given a slightly different candidate, so that they do not duplicate one another's work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Assembling a candidate is selection plus commitment. The miner takes transactions from the memory pool in order of what they pay for the space they use, up to the block's limit, which the small example illustrates by taking the first three of five pending transactions and totalling the fees they bring, 470 satoshis. It then writes the coinbase transaction that pays itself the subsidy and those fees, computes the merkle root over the whole list, and fills in the header fields: the hash of the previous block, the merkle root, a timestamp and the target. Only the nonce is then left to vary.

A candidate block is not a block: it has no proof of work, so no node would accept it, and the miner may abandon it at any moment. It is also private until it is solved, which is why two miners can be working on candidates that contain the same transactions without any conflict. And the contents of a candidate are a choice, not a rule: a miner may legally build a block with no transactions at all except the coinbase, which is one of the problems the book describes on the test network, where fees have no value (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a block without a solution yet
nodes.definition: A candidate block is a block that a miner has assembled from its memory pool and committed to the previous block, but which is not yet valid because it has no proof of work.

nodes.label: Proof of work
nodes.body: Proof of work is a piece of data that takes a great deal of computation to find and almost none to check. The chapter builds the idea from the hash function: a miner feeds a candidate block into an algorithm that scrambles the data, producing output that looks nothing like the input; the same input always gives the same output, but nobody can predict the output for a new input; and if the output matches a template determined by the protocol, the block is accepted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter then names the result: the simple verification process probabilistically proves the work was done, so the data necessary to generate that proof, in this case the block, is called proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Proof of work is a piece of data that takes a great deal of computation to find and almost none to check. The chapter builds the idea from the hash function: a miner feeds a candidate block into an algorithm that scrambles the data, producing output that looks nothing like the input; the same input always gives the same output, but nobody can predict the output for a new input; and if the output matches a template determined by the protocol, the block is accepted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter then names the result: the simple verification process probabilistically proves the work was done, so the data necessary to generate that proof, in this case the block, is called proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Proof of work is what makes the record expensive to rewrite, and therefore what makes a confirmed payment reliable. The chapter puts the number on it: as of writing, the number of candidate blocks miners need to try before finding a winning combination is about 168 billion trillion, and that is also how many times the hash function needs to be run; yet once a winning combination has been found, anyone can verify the block is valid by running the hash function just once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Changing a recorded transaction would mean redoing that work and then outpacing everyone else, which is the argument the security group develops.

The reader meets proof of work as the five minutes between Alice's payment and its first confirmation, and as the electricity bill of the mining industry. The book's mining chapter gives a miniature version that can be run by hand: hash the phrase Hello, world! followed by a number and look for a result that begins with a zero. It finds the answer at the number 32 and remarks that although it only takes one hash computation to verify, it took thirty-two to find (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The owner's course notes describe the same mechanism as repeatedly hashing the header of the block with a random number until a solution matching a predetermined pattern emerges (Altunel, 2021).

The search is a loop with one changing field. The example above is the demonstration version used by the interactive page of the practice branch: hashing a block number, a nonce and the text of a payment, and looking for a digest that begins with four zeros, the first nonce that succeeds is 6630. Four leading hexadecimal zeros mean that about one attempt in sixteen to the fourth power, that is one in 65,536, should work, so a few thousand attempts is the expected order. Bitcoin's real condition is the same test with a far smaller threshold: the double hash of the eighty-byte header, read as a number, must be below the target that the difficulty concept explains.

Proof of work proves effort, not honesty and not truth. A block with a perfect proof of work is still rejected if any of its transactions breaks a rule, as the consensus-rules concept explains. The proof is also probabilistic: the chapter's own wording is that the verification process is able to probabilistically prove the work was done, and a lucky miner may find a solution on its first attempt (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Finally, the work is not a puzzle with a meaningful answer; the solution has no use outside the system, which is both the source of its security and the reason its energy cost is debated.

nodes.example: a header hash below the target
nodes.definition: Proof of work is data that is expensive to produce and cheap to check: a block header whose hash is below the target proves that an enormous number of attempts was made.

nodes.label: Block
nodes.body: A block is the unit in which transactions are added to the blockchain. The chapter says that transactions are bundled into blocks, and that blocks have a very small header that must be formed in a very specific way, requiring an enormous amount of computation to get right but only a small amount to verify as correct (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's chapter on the blockchain is exact about the structure: a block is a container data structure that aggregates transactions for inclusion in the blockchain, made of a header containing metadata followed by a long list of transactions that make up the bulk of its size (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A block is the unit in which transactions are added to the blockchain. The chapter says that transactions are bundled into blocks, and that blocks have a very small header that must be formed in a very specific way, requiring an enormous amount of computation to get right but only a small amount to verify as correct (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's chapter on the blockchain is exact about the structure: a block is a container data structure that aggregates transactions for inclusion in the blockchain, made of a header containing metadata followed by a long list of transactions that make up the bulk of its size (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The block is what gives transactions an order and a time. Within a single chain of blocks the position of a transaction defines whether it is earlier or later than another, and a transaction is valid only if it spends outputs of transactions that appeared earlier, which the book says eliminates the problem of double spending (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The block is also the unit in which block space is sold, so its limit is what makes fees necessary, and the unit in which security accumulates, since confirmations are counted in blocks.

The chapter meets the block when the winning block containing Alice's transaction becomes part of the blockchain and counts as one confirmation of it, and it gives a link to the block so that a reader can look it up (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's blockchain chapter lists the fields a stored block has: four bytes of block size, eighty bytes of header, a compact count of the transactions that follow, and then the transactions themselves (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The proportions are worth remembering. The header is eighty bytes whatever the block holds, while the transactions can run to about four million bytes, so a complete block can be almost fifty thousand times larger than its header, as the division above gives and as the book states (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That ratio is the whole reason lightweight clients are possible, since a program that keeps only headers keeps a chain thousands of times smaller than the full one. The link between the small header and the large body is the merkle root, and the identifier of a block is the double hash of the header alone, which the book stresses by calling it more accurately the block header hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two points are easily confused. A block is not a fixed number of transactions: the limit is on size, counted as weight, so a block may hold one transaction or many thousands. And the hash that names a block is not stored inside it; the book notes that the block's hash is computed by each node as the block is received from the network, which is why every node can check the name for itself and nobody can rename a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a header plus a list of transactions
nodes.definition: A block is a container that aggregates transactions, made of an eighty-byte header and a list of transactions that may run to about four million bytes.

nodes.label: Block header
nodes.body: The block header is the small, fixed part of a block that carries its metadata and that mining actually works on. The book's blockchain chapter lists its six fields with their sizes: four bytes of version, thirty-two bytes holding a hash of the previous block, thirty-two bytes holding the merkle root of the block's transactions, four bytes of timestamp in Unix epoch time, four bytes holding a compact encoding of the proof-of-work target, and four bytes of nonce, described as arbitrary data used for the proof-of-work algorithm (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Four plus thirty-two plus thirty-two plus four plus four plus four is eighty bytes.

paras.text: The block header is the small, fixed part of a block that carries its metadata and that mining actually works on. The book's blockchain chapter lists its six fields with their sizes: four bytes of version, thirty-two bytes holding a hash of the previous block, thirty-two bytes holding the merkle root of the block's transactions, four bytes of timestamp in Unix epoch time, four bytes holding a compact encoding of the proof-of-work target, and four bytes of nonce, described as arbitrary data used for the proof-of-work algorithm (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Four plus thirty-two plus thirty-two plus four plus four plus four is eighty bytes.

Everything the chapter claims about the chain follows from this header. Because the header contains the hash of the parent block, any change to a parent requires the child's hash to change, which requires the grandchild to change, and so on; the book concludes that once a block has many generations following it, it cannot be changed without forcing a recalculation of all subsequent blocks, and that because such a recalculation would require enormous computation, the existence of a long chain of blocks makes the blockchain's deep history impractical to change, which is a key feature of Bitcoin's security (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because the header also contains the merkle root, it commits to every transaction without containing any of them.

A reader meets the header's fields in the output of any block explorer or of Bitcoin Core's command for retrieving a block: the chapter's own data for the first block shows a version of 1, a merkle root of 4a5e1e4b...deda33b, a time of 1231006505, a nonce of 2083236893 and a compact target written as 1d00ffff (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The mining hardware of the book's example is given nothing but this header to work on, and it tests trillions of variations of it per second (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The header can be assembled and hashed with the standard library, which is the executed example of this concept. Packing the version as a four-byte little-endian integer, then thirty-two zero bytes for the parent of the first block, then the merkle root with its bytes reversed, then the timestamp, the compact target and the nonce as three more four-byte integers, gives exactly eighty bytes; hashing them twice with SHA-256 and reversing the result produces 00000000...0a8ce26f, the identifier of the genesis block that the book prints (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nothing else is needed: the block hash is a function of the header alone.

Three cautions. The header's version field is no longer simply a version, as the book says its use has evolved over time, and the chapter on Bitcoin Core explains how it came to carry signals for upgrades (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The timestamp is the approximate creation time, set by the miner within limits that the book states as two consensus rules, that no node accepts a block whose time is more than two hours in the future and none accepts a block whose time is not later than the median time of the last eleven blocks, which the book calls the median time past, so a block's time is not a reliable clock (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the nonce is only four bytes, so it is exhausted quickly; miners then change other fields, which the book calls the extra nonce solution (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Merkle tree
nodes.body: A merkle tree, also called a binary hash tree, is a structure for summarizing and verifying the integrity of large sets of data. The book defines it as a tree constructed by hashing paired data, the leaves, then pairing and hashing the results until a single hash remains, the merkle root, and notes that in Bitcoin the leaves are almost always the transactions of a single block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The hash used is SHA-256 applied twice, which the book calls double-SHA256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book defines it as a tree constructed by hashing paired data, the leaves, then pairing and hashing the results until a single hash remains, the merkle root, and notes that in Bitcoin the leaves are almost always the transactions of a single block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The hash used is SHA-256 applied twice, which the book calls double-SHA256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The tree is what lets the eighty-byte header stand for a whole block. The book says that merkle trees are used in Bitcoin to summarize all the transactions in a block, producing an overall commitment to the entire set of transactions and permitting a very efficient process to verify whether a transaction is included in a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also gives the efficiency: with N elements, checking whether any one of them is in the tree takes about the base-two logarithm of N calculations, so proving that one transaction out of the roughly sixteen thousand in the largest possible block is present needs the transaction, the eighty-byte header and 448 bytes of path, which makes the largest possible proof almost ten thousand times smaller than the largest possible block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets the root as a field in every block's data: the first block's merkle root, 4a5e1e4b...deda33b, is equal to the identifier of its single transaction, because a tree with one leaf has that leaf as its root. The tree itself is met by lightweight clients, which the book says use merkle paths extensively: a peer sends the block header together with a path of hashes linking the transaction of interest to the root, and the client recomputes the root and so connects the transaction to the block and the block to the chain, receiving less than a kilobyte instead of a whole block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The construction is a few lines of code, and the executed example performs it. Four pieces of data, A, B, C and D, are each double-hashed to give the four leaves; the first two leaves are joined and double-hashed to give one parent, the last two likewise, and the two parents are joined and double-hashed to give the root, whose first sixteen hexadecimal digits are 59e82c45a3662f55. Because the tree is binary it needs an even number of nodes at each level, so the book explains that if there is an odd number the last hash is duplicated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin's way of doing that duplication has a known flaw, which the book quotes at length from Bitcoin Core's source, where it is logged as a vulnerability about duplicate transaction identifiers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The merkle root commits to the transactions but does not contain them, so a header alone does not let anyone read a block. A merkle path also proves only inclusion: it shows that a transaction is in a block, not that the transaction or the block obeys the rules, which is exactly the limit of simplified payment verification. And the chapter's own text never mentions merkle trees; the concept is brought in here because the chapter's claim that a small header commits to many transactions cannot otherwise be explained.

nodes.label: Difficulty and target
nodes.body: The target is the number that a block header's hash must be below for the block to be valid, and the difficulty is the inverse way of describing the same thing: the book's glossary calls difficulty a network-wide setting that controls how much computation is required to produce a proof of work, and the difficulty target a difficulty at which all the computation in the network will find blocks approximately every ten minutes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book states the relation plainly: a higher target means it is less difficult to find a hash below it, a lower target means it is more difficult, and the target and difficulty are inversely related (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book states the relation plainly: a higher target means it is less difficult to find a hash below it, a lower target means it is more difficult, and the target and difficulty are inversely related (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Without an adjustable target the system would not keep time. The book explains that blocks are generated every ten minutes on average, that this is Bitcoin's heartbeat and underpins the frequency of currency issuance and the speed of transaction settlement, and that it has to remain constant over decades while computer power and the number of miners change, so the difficulty of mining must be adjusted to account for those changes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter touches the same idea when it says that over time, as the height of new blocks increases, so does the computation difficulty for the chain as a whole (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the target in a block's data as a four-byte compact encoding: the first block's is written 1d00ffff and its difficulty is reported as 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Retargeting is met as the event every two weeks when every node recomputes the threshold. The owner's course notes describe the consequence from the hardware side: the difficulty rose so far that mining became profitable only with application-specific integrated circuits, after passing through desktop computers and graphics cards (Altunel, 2021).

The compact form packs an exponent and a coefficient into four bytes. Reading 1d00ffff, the leading byte 0x1d is the exponent, 29, and the remaining three bytes are the coefficient, 0x00ffff, that is 65,535; the target is the coefficient multiplied by two to the power of eight times the exponent minus three, which equals 0xffff times two to the power 208, as the check above confirms. With that target, about two to the power thirty-two attempts, roughly 4.3 billion, are expected per block. The adjustment itself is arithmetic on elapsed time: every 2,016 blocks each node independently computes a new target from the ratio between the time the last blocks actually took and the 20,160 minutes they should have taken, and the book notes that the change is limited to a factor of four in either direction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Three details are often got wrong. Retargeting is not performed by anybody: it occurs automatically and on every node independently, which is why all nodes agree on the result (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The window has an off-by-one error that the book records, since the calculation uses the time of the previous 2,015 blocks rather than 2,016, biasing difficulty upward by about 0.05 per cent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the target is independent of how many transactions a block holds or how much value they move, so the energy spent securing Bitcoin does not depend on how much Bitcoin is used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: The target is the threshold a block hash must fall below; difficulty is the inverse measure of it, adjusted every 2,016 blocks so that blocks keep arriving about every ten minutes.

nodes.label: Hash rate
nodes.body: The hash rate is the speed at which hash computations are performed, counted in hashes per second. It is the natural measure of mining effort, because mining is nothing but repeated hashing, and it is used both for a single machine and for the network as a whole. The chapter gives the figure in a different but equivalent form: the number of candidate blocks miners need to try before finding a winning combination is about 168 billion trillion, and that is also how many times the hash function needs to be run (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The hash rate is the speed at which hash computations are performed, counted in hashes per second. It is the natural measure of mining effort, because mining is nothing but repeated hashing, and it is used both for a single machine and for the network as a whole. The chapter gives the figure in a different but equivalent form: the number of candidate blocks miners need to try before finding a winning combination is about 168 billion trillion, and that is also how many times the hash function needs to be run (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The hash rate is how the cost of rewriting history is quantified, so it is the number behind every security claim in this branch. The book's note on block intervals makes the link: a malicious miner wanting to double spend a transaction would need to do an amount of work equal to ten minutes of the total network hash rate in order to create a chain with equal proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A share of the hash rate is also what defines the attacks the book describes, which it calls hashrate attacks and which succeed with probability depending on that share (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

You meet hash rates in mining advertisements, in charts of the network's growth, and in the book's descriptions of hardware: the mining rigs of its example use application-specific integrated circuits in which hundreds of thousands of circuits run the double SHA-256 algorithm in parallel, testing trillions of variations of the header per second (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book also records the history of growth: the hashing power has increased exponentially every year of Bitcoin's existence, through the move from processors to graphics cards and then to purpose-built chips (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The network's rate follows from the chapter's own number by one division. If about 168 billion trillion attempts, that is 1.68 times ten to the twenty-third, are expected for each block, and a block is expected every ten minutes, that is 600 seconds, then the network is running about 2.8 times ten to the twentieth hashes a second, which the calculation above gives as 280,000,000,000,000,000,000. In the units the industry uses that is about 280 exahashes a second. A single pool miner's contribution is measured the same way, and a pool estimates it by counting shares, as the mining-pool concept explains.

A hash rate is an estimate, not a measurement: nobody counts the hashes of the world's miners, so the figure is inferred from the difficulty and the observed block times, which is why published values differ and fluctuate. It also measures only this one kind of computation, so comparing it with the speed of a general-purpose computer is meaningless. And a higher network hash rate does not make payments faster; the difficulty adjusts to keep the pace at ten minutes, so extra hash rate buys security, not speed.

nodes.example: hashes per second across the network
nodes.definition: The hash rate is the number of hash computations performed per second; dividing the attempts expected per block by six hundred seconds gives the rate the whole network is running at.

nodes.label: Consensus rules
nodes.body: The consensus rules are the rules by which a full node decides whether a block and the transactions in it are acceptable. The book's glossary defines them as the block validation rules that full nodes follow to stay in consensus with other nodes, and separately defines consensus itself as the situation in which most nodes have the same blocks in their locally validated best blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter introduces the term through the miner's incentive, saying that miners can only receive honest income from creating blocks that follow all of Bitcoin's consensus rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The consensus rules are the rules by which a full node decides whether a block and the transactions in it are acceptable. The book's glossary defines them as the block validation rules that full nodes follow to stay in consensus with other nodes, and separately defines consensus itself as the situation in which most nodes have the same blocks in their locally validated best blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter introduces the term through the miner's incentive, saying that miners can only receive honest income from creating blocks that follow all of Bitcoin's consensus rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The rules are what makes a decentralized record possible at all. Because every node applies the same rules, no miner can profit from breaking them: the book explains that an invalid coinbase transaction would make the entire block invalid, so the block would be rejected and the transaction would never become part of the blockchain, and that the miners therefore have to construct a block based on the shared rules that all nodes follow and mine it with a correct solution, expending electricity that is wasted if they cheat (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter draws the consequence for users: because miners are incentivized to include only valid transactions, users may optionally make a trust-based assumption that any transaction in a block is a valid transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the rules as the list of checks a node performs. The book names the functions in Bitcoin Core that contain them and gives the items: the block data structure must be syntactically valid, the block header hash must be less than the target, the timestamp must lie between the median time past, which the book defines as the median time of the last eleven blocks, and two hours in the future, the weight must be within acceptable limits, the first transaction and only the first must be a coinbase transaction, and all transactions in the block must be valid by the transaction checklist (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter also refers to the rules when it limits an output's value, which Bitcoin Core fixes in its source as at most 21,000,000 times one hundred million satoshis (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Validation is the conjunction of independent checks, which the small example renders as a set of five that must all hold; the count is how many were applied and the verdict is whether every one passed. The order matters in practice, since cheap checks come first, but logically a block is valid only if nothing fails. The book calls this independent validation and names it the third step of Bitcoin's consensus mechanism, after independent verification of transactions and the aggregation of transactions into blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Consensus rules are not the same as consensus, and the book warns against confusing the two: the rules are what nodes check, while consensus is the agreement that results (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The rules also change, but only in careful ways: the book devotes a long section to how they are altered, distinguishing a soft fork, which tightens them compatibly, from a hard fork, which does not (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the rules are enforced by nodes, not by miners; a block with a perfect proof of work that breaks a rule is simply discarded.

nodes.label: Coinbase transaction
nodes.body: The coinbase transaction is the special first transaction of every block, by which the miner pays itself. The book's glossary calls it the first transaction in a block, always created by a miner, and the mining chapter adds the distinguishing property: unlike regular transactions the coinbase transaction does not consume unspent outputs as inputs, but has only one input, called the coinbase input, which implicitly contains the block reward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter describes it without naming it, as a special transaction that pays the miner's own Bitcoin address the block reward plus the sum of transaction fees from all the transactions included in the candidate block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The coinbase transaction is the special first transaction of every block, by which the miner pays itself. The book's glossary calls it the first transaction in a block, always created by a miner, and the mining chapter adds the distinguishing property: unlike regular transactions the coinbase transaction does not consume unspent outputs as inputs, but has only one input, called the coinbase input, which implicitly contains the block reward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter describes it without naming it, as a special transaction that pays the miner's own Bitcoin address the block reward plus the sum of transaction fees from all the transactions included in the candidate block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

This transaction is where new bitcoins enter the world, so it is the only place in the system where money is created rather than moved. It is also what ties the miner's income to the validity of the whole block: the fees it claims are the differences between the inputs and outputs of the other transactions, so an error anywhere in the block makes the coinbase transaction wrong and the block invalid. The chapter's statement that a successful miner receives the reward after the block is added to the blockchain and the reward transaction becomes spendable refers to this transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets a coinbase transaction in every block, including the very first: the genesis block contains a single transaction whose coinbase input holds the text about the Chancellor on the brink of a second bailout for banks, which the book says was intended as proof of the earliest date the block could have been created (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book notes that in 2023 it was common for a coinbase transaction to have two outputs, one a zero-value output committing to the witnesses of the block's segregated-witness transactions and the other paying the miner (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The interactive demonstration of the practice branch has a page devoted to coinbase transactions.

The arithmetic of the coinbase transaction is the miner's income statement: it spends nothing, and it pays out the subsidy plus the total fees, as the small example shows with zero inputs spent and 625,183,000 satoshis paid. The book gives the formula for the fee part, the sum of the inputs of all the other transactions minus the sum of their outputs, and the function in Bitcoin Core that computes the subsidy part from the block height (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because the coinbase input spends nothing, it is free space, and the book says the coinbase field provides up to one hundred bytes for arbitrary data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Three traps. The output of a coinbase transaction cannot be spent immediately: the book's verification checklist requires at least a hundred confirmations, the constant it calls COINBASE_MATURITY, and its blockchain chapter explains that after a hundred blocks there is so much stability that the reward can be spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The term is also overloaded: the glossary warns that the coinbase, a field, is not to be confused with the coinbase transaction, and neither has anything to do with a company of a similar name (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Finally, the miner cannot write any amount it likes, because every node recomputes the permitted total.

nodes.definition: The coinbase transaction is the first transaction in a block; it spends no earlier output and pays the miner the new bitcoins of the block plus the fees of the other transactions.

nodes.label: Block reward
nodes.body: The block reward is what a miner earns for a block: the newly created bitcoins, which the book calls the subsidy, together with the transaction fees of everything in the block. The chapter states the first half as a fact about money, saying that mining currently creates new bitcoins in each block, almost like a central bank printing new money, and that the amount created per block is limited and diminishes with time following a fixed issuance schedule (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's mining chapter gives the schedule: bitcoins are minted during the creation of each block at a fixed and diminishing rate, and every 210,000 blocks, or approximately every four years, the issuance rate is decreased by fifty per cent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter states the first half as a fact about money, saying that mining currently creates new bitcoins in each block, almost like a central bank printing new money, and that the amount created per block is limited and diminishes with time following a fixed issuance schedule (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's mining chapter gives the schedule: bitcoins are minted during the creation of each block at a fixed and diminishing rate, and every 210,000 blocks, or approximately every four years, the issuance rate is decreased by fifty per cent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reward is the engine of the whole system. It pays for the computation that secures the record, and because it diminishes on a schedule that nobody can change, it also defines Bitcoin's monetary policy. The book draws the conclusion: the finite and diminishing issuance creates a fixed monetary supply that resists inflation, and unlike a fiat currency, which can be printed in infinite numbers by a central bank, no individual party has the ability to inflate the supply (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also tells the miner's future: after the subsidy reaches zero, blocks will contain no new bitcoins and miners will be rewarded solely through transaction fees (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the figure whenever a block is inspected. For the first four years of the network each block contained fifty new bitcoins; the first halving occurred at block 210,000; the subsidy was 6.25 bitcoins when the book was written in 2023; and the book predicted the next halving at block 840,000, in April or May of 2024, which takes it to 3.125 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The owner's course notes, written in 2021, give the then-current figure of 6.25 newly created bitcoins per block, which is the same era (Altunel, 2021).

The rule is a halving, which in whole numbers is a right shift. Bitcoin Core computes the subsidy by dividing the block height by the halving interval of 210,000 to get the number of halvings, starting from fifty times one hundred million satoshis and shifting that right once per halving, returning zero once there have been sixty-four of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the 2023 era, three halvings had occurred, so the subsidy was fifty times ten to the eighth shifted right three times, that is 625,000,000 satoshis or 6.25 bitcoins, as the expression above evaluates. Summing 210,000 blocks of each successive subsidy gives 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis in total, which is the figure the book's own script prints and just under 21 million bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Any particular reward figure goes stale, so learn the rule and not the number; the book's own glossary still says the reward is currently 12.5 bitcoins, which was true two halvings earlier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Note also that the maximum is an upper limit rather than a promise: the book remarks that a miner may intentionally mine a block taking less than the full reward, and that such blocks have already been mined, so the total issued may end up lower (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the reward is not paid immediately in a usable form, because the coinbase output must mature for a hundred blocks.

nodes.label: Mining pool
nodes.body: A mining pool is an arrangement in which many miners search for the same block together and share whatever is found. The chapter describes it in one sentence: miners who participate in a mining pool have set up their software to create candidate blocks that assign the reward to a pool address, and from there a share of the reward is distributed to the members of the pool in proportion to the amount of work they contributed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's glossary calls the practice pooled mining and defines it in the same terms (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A mining pool is an arrangement in which many miners search for the same block together and share whatever is found. The chapter describes it in one sentence: miners who participate in a mining pool have set up their software to create candidate blocks that assign the reward to a pool address, and from there a share of the reward is distributed to the members of the pool in proportion to the amount of work they contributed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's glossary calls the practice pooled mining and defines it in the same terms (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Pools exist because mining alone has become a lottery with very long odds. The book says that in this highly competitive environment individual miners working alone do not stand a chance, that the likelihood of finding a block to offset electricity and hardware costs is so low that it represents a gamble, and that by participating in a pool miners get a smaller share of the overall reward but typically get rewarded every day, reducing uncertainty (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its example is concrete: a miner with a ten-thousandth of one per cent of the network's hash rate would find a block about once every twenty years alone, and in a pool holding one per cent of the rate would average more than one block a day and earn the same amount, only far more evenly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets pools as the names that appear beside blocks in an explorer, and as the services that small miners sign up to. The book describes the arrangement: miners configure their equipment to connect to a pool server after creating an account, their hardware stays connected while mining, successful blocks pay the reward to a pool address rather than to individual miners, and the server periodically pays the miners once their share of the rewards passes a threshold, usually charging a percentage fee for the service (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The pool measures contributions with Bitcoin's own proof of work at an easier setting. The book explains that the pool sets a higher target, typically more than a thousand times easier than the network's, so that each time a pool miner finds a header hash below the pool target they prove they did the hashing work and earn a share; each miner is given a slightly different coinbase template so that no effort is duplicated, and the shares measure the work done without any possibility of cheating (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Payment is then proportional, which the small example computes: with shares of fifty, thirty and twenty, a reward of 625,000,000 satoshis splits into 312,500,000, 187,500,000 and 125,000,000.

Pools change who controls what. A pool member runs the hardware but the pool decides what goes into the candidate block, so hash rate concentrates in the hands of pool operators, and the book's section on hashrate attacks notes that a pool with a large share can attempt them while its participants might remain blissfully unaware (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A share is also not a bitcoin: it is a unit of accounting inside the pool, worth nothing outside it. And a pool is a counterparty, so its members trust it to measure and to pay.

nodes.example: many small miners sharing one reward
nodes.definition: A mining pool combines the hash rate of many miners, measures each one's contribution with an easier target, and shares the reward in proportion to the shares earned.

nodes.label: Sudoku analogy
nodes.body: The sudoku analogy is a teaching picture, taken from the owner's course notes for this chapter, in which mining is described as a giant competitive game of sudoku. The notes list the features that make the comparison work: the puzzle is large, several thousand rows and columns in size; it resets every time someone finds a solution; its difficulty adjusts automatically so that a solution takes approximately ten minutes; and if someone shows you a completed puzzle you can verify it quite quickly (Altunel, 2021). The notes conclude that Bitcoin's puzzle, based on a cryptographic hash, is asymmetrically hard to solve, easy to verify and adjustable in difficulty, and so exhibits similar characteristics (Altunel, 2021).

paras.text: The sudoku analogy is a teaching picture, taken from the owner's course notes for this chapter, in which mining is described as a giant competitive game of sudoku. The notes list the features that make the comparison work: the puzzle is large, several thousand rows and columns in size; it resets every time someone finds a solution; its difficulty adjusts automatically so that a solution takes approximately ten minutes; and if someone shows you a completed puzzle you can verify it quite quickly (Altunel, 2021). The notes conclude that Bitcoin's puzzle, based on a cryptographic hash, is asymmetrically hard to solve, easy to verify and adjustable in difficulty, and so exhibits similar characteristics (Altunel, 2021).

The analogy is useful because it captures the one property that makes proof of work possible, the asymmetry between solving and checking, in an everyday object. A student who has filled in a sudoku knows from experience that finding the answer is laborious while checking a finished grid is quick, and that a larger grid is harder without being harder to check. Those are exactly the properties the chapter claims for the hash search: an enormous amount of computation to get right, only a small amount of computation to verify as correct (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The analogy is met in the course notes of this chapter and in many introductory presentations, and it is kept here as a bridge for a first reading. It is not in the third edition of the textbook, which prefers a different picture: the chapter calls mining a decentralized lottery in which each miner creates a lottery ticket, and the mining chapter uses a game of dice in which players try to throw less than a falling target (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A learner meets all three pictures and should be able to say what each one gets right.

The comparison can be made quantitative, which is also where it breaks down. An ordinary sudoku has nine times nine, that is eighty-one cells, and a solver explores a search space that a computer clears in a moment; Bitcoin's search needs about 168 billion trillion attempts per block, a number vastly larger than eighty-one, as the comparison above states (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The notes handle this by enlarging the puzzle to several thousand rows and columns and by resetting it after every solution, which mirrors the retargeting of the difficulty and the start of a new round after each block (Altunel, 2021).

The analogy must be labelled as one. A sudoku has a unique solution reached by reasoning, whereas a proof of work has very many possible solutions and no reasoning helps: the only method is trial, because the hash function's output cannot be steered. A sudoku also has no reward, no competition between solvers for the same grid and no chain of earlier grids, so the analogy says nothing about incentives, about confirmations or about why a long chain is hard to rewrite. Use it to understand the asymmetry and then put it down.

nodes.example: mining as a giant competitive sudoku
nodes.definition: An analogy from the course notes: mining is like a huge sudoku that is hard to solve, quick to check, adjustable in size, and restarted whenever somebody finds a solution.

nodes.label: Soft fork and hard fork
nodes.body: A rule change is an alteration of the consensus rules, and it comes in two kinds. The book explains that while the consensus rules are invariable in the short term and must be consistent across all nodes, they are not invariable in the long term, because in order to evolve the system the rules can change from time to time to accommodate new features, improvements or bug fixes, and that upgrades to a consensus system are much more difficult than ordinary software upgrades and require coordination between all participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A change that older nodes still accept is a soft fork; one they reject is a hard fork.

paras.text: A rule change is an alteration of the consensus rules, and it comes in two kinds. The book explains that while the consensus rules are invariable in the short term and must be consistent across all nodes, they are not invariable in the long term, because in order to evolve the system the rules can change from time to time to accommodate new features, improvements or bug fixes, and that upgrades to a consensus system are much more difficult than ordinary software upgrades and require coordination between all participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A change that older nodes still accept is a soft fork; one they reject is a hard fork.

The distinction decides whether an upgrade can happen without splitting the network, so it is the practical reason Bitcoin can change at all. The book states the rule precisely: a soft fork is a forward-compatible change to the consensus rules that allows unupgraded clients to continue to operate in consensus with the new rules, and it adds the consequence that is not immediately obvious, that soft forks can only be used to constrain the consensus rules and not to expand them, because transactions and blocks created under the new rules must be valid under the old rules too but not the other way round (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader has already met a rule change in this chapter without being told. The two extra fields at the front of Alice's transaction, and the witness structure at its end, were added as part of the segregated witness change to the consensus rules, and the book notes that the obvious way of implementing that change would have required a hard fork, with all the challenges that brings, so an alternative approach was found that worked as a soft fork (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's glossary describes the other kind as a permanent divergence that commonly occurs when non-upgraded nodes cannot validate blocks created by upgraded nodes following newer rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The test is a comparison of what each version of the rules accepts. If the set of things the new rules accept is contained in the set the old rules accept, then nothing new offends an old node and the change is a soft fork, which the small example decides for a new rule set that is a subset of the old one; if the new rules accept something the old ones reject, old nodes will reject those blocks and the chain splits, which is a hard fork. The book adds that the term soft fork does not name a particular method but a family of them, all sharing the property that they do not require every node to upgrade or force unupgraded nodes out of consensus, and it describes two implemented in Bitcoin by reinterpreting opcodes that previously did nothing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Three cautions. The word fork here is not the accidental fork of the security group, which is two blocks at the same height, and the book remarks that in practice a soft fork is not a fork at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A soft fork is compatible but not free: an unupgraded node keeps accepting blocks yet no longer verifies the new rule itself, so a user who wants the new protection must upgrade. And compatibility is a property of the rules, not of intentions: a change that was meant to be gentle is still a hard fork if any old node would reject a block that a new one accepts.

nodes.example: segregated witness, deployed as a soft fork
nodes.definition: A soft fork is a change that only narrows what is valid, so unupgraded nodes stay in consensus; a hard fork widens what is valid and is not compatible with older nodes.
