nodes.label: Security
nodes.body: Security, in this chapter, means the confidence that a payment already recorded will stay recorded. This group collects the concepts that make that confidence precise. It explains the confirmation, the unit in which the confidence is counted; the probability that lies behind the counting; the rule by which nodes choose between competing chains, the best blockchain; the block height that positions a block in the record; the accidental fork and the alternative block that a dishonest miner would have to produce; the double spend that all of this is designed to prevent; the genesis block at the bottom of the chain; and the judgement a merchant may make when there is no confirmation at all.

paras.text: Security, in this chapter, means the confidence that a payment already recorded will stay recorded. This group collects the concepts that make that confidence precise. It explains the confirmation, the unit in which the confidence is counted; the probability that lies behind the counting; the rule by which nodes choose between competing chains, the best blockchain; the block height that positions a block in the record; the accidental fork and the alternative block that a dishonest miner would have to produce; the double spend that all of this is designed to prevent; the genesis block at the bottom of the chain; and the judgement a merchant may make when there is no confirmation at all.

The group matters because the honest answer to the question is probabilistic, and students are owed the honest answer. The chapter does not say that a confirmed payment cannot be reversed; it says that as the blocks pile on top of each other it becomes harder to reverse the transaction, thereby giving Bob more and more confidence that Alice's payment is secure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The reason is an argument about cost: the chapter shows that a miner conspiring with Alice would have to produce two blocks where an honest miner produces one, and that the high cost of doing so for a small additional payment is normally much less profitable than honest mining (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets this group as the advice that merchants follow: nothing for a cup of coffee, a few confirmations for an ordinary purchase, six or more for something valuable. The chapter gives the convention, that any block with more than six confirmations is considered very hard to change because it would require an immense amount of computation to recalculate six blocks plus one new block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and the book's mining chapter gives the reasoning behind the harder cases, including an example in which a gallery hands over paintings after one confirmation and loses both the paintings and the payment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group is read from the unit upward. A confirmation is one block built on top; the probability concept quantifies what each one buys, using the table in Nakamoto's paper; the best blockchain is the rule that decides which chain those blocks belong to; the height is where a block sits; a fork is what happens when two blocks claim the same height, and an alternative block is what an attacker would need; the double spend is the attack itself; the genesis block is the anchor that makes heights and chains well defined; and the acceptance of a small payment without confirmation shows that the right number of confirmations is a business decision and not a protocol rule.

Guard against two opposite errors. One is to treat six confirmations as a magic number: the chapter calls it a convention, and the book's own advice for high-value items is to wait longer, mentioning twenty-four hours, which is about 144 confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The other is to treat the system as fragile because nothing is absolute; the same arithmetic that denies certainty shows that the probability of reversal falls away very quickly, and the book's figure of a probability of about two in ten thousand after six confirmations against an attacker with a tenth of the hash rate is the concrete form of that (Nakamoto, 2008).

nodes.label: Confirmation
nodes.body: A confirmation is a block that commits to a transaction, counted once for the block that contains it and once more for each block built on top. The chapter defines it as it happens: the winning block containing Alice's transaction became part of the blockchain, and the block containing Alice's transaction is counted as one confirmation of that transaction; each block mined on top of the one containing Alice's transaction counts as an additional confirmation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's glossary says the same and adds the common rule of thumb, that six or more confirmations is considered sufficient proof that a transaction cannot be reversed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A confirmation is a block that commits to a transaction, counted once for the block that contains it and once more for each block built on top. The chapter defines it as it happens: the winning block containing Alice's transaction became part of the blockchain, and the block containing Alice's transaction is counted as one confirmation of that transaction; each block mined on top of the one containing Alice's transaction counts as an additional confirmation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's glossary says the same and adds the common rule of thumb, that six or more confirmations is considered sufficient proof that a transaction cannot be reversed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Confirmations are how the chapter turns a vague feeling of safety into a number that a merchant can act on. Each additional block multiplies the work an attacker would have to redo, because the attacker must not only replace the block containing the transaction but also outpace the honest chain that has grown in the meantime. The chapter spells the arithmetic out: after a second block is mined on top, Alice's transaction can only be changed if two alternative blocks are mined plus a new block on top of them, a total of three blocks, for Alice to take back the money she sent Bob (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets confirmations in every wallet and explorer, usually as a small counter beside a payment. In the chapter, Alice's transaction gets its first confirmation about five minutes after it was transmitted and its second about nineteen minutes later (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The owner's course notes record the same figures and the misconception they create, noting that waiting for a full six confirmations may take up to sixty minutes (Altunel, 2021). Bitcoin Core reports the count directly; the chapter's own data for the first block shows a confirmations field with a very large value.

The counting is addition, and the small example performs it: a transaction whose block has two blocks on top has three confirmations. The reason each one matters is the chain of header hashes. Because each header commits to its parent, the book explains that any change to a parent block requires a child's hash to change, which requires a change in the grandchild, and so on, so that once a block has many generations following it, it cannot be changed without forcing a recalculation of all subsequent blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cost of that recalculation is what a confirmation measures.

A confirmation is not a guarantee and six is not a law. The chapter calls the six-block figure a convention, and the book's mining chapter describes a hashrate attack in which an attacker with enough power invalidates six or more blocks in a row, so that transactions considered immutable become invalid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the other direction, the number of confirmations says nothing about whether the transaction was correct, only about how hard it now is to remove; a payment to the wrong address is just as irreversible as a payment to the right one.

nodes.example: one block on top is one confirmation
nodes.definition: A transaction has one confirmation when it is in a block, and one more for each block built on top; reversing it means redoing all of them and one more.

nodes.label: Probability of reversal
nodes.body: The probability of reversal is the chance that a transaction already in the blockchain is removed, because somebody builds a competing chain that excludes it and that other nodes come to prefer. The chapter states that such a probability exists without quantifying it, saying that normally the high cost of dishonestly creating two blocks for a small additional payment is much less profitable than honestly creating a new block, making it unlikely that a confirmed transaction will be deliberately changed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nakamoto's paper quantifies the same event, calculating the probability that an attacker ever catches up from a given number of blocks behind (Nakamoto, 2008).

paras.text: The probability of reversal is the chance that a transaction already in the blockchain is removed, because somebody builds a competing chain that excludes it and that other nodes come to prefer. The chapter states that such a probability exists without quantifying it, saying that normally the high cost of dishonestly creating two blocks for a small additional payment is much less profitable than honestly creating a new block, making it unlikely that a confirmed transaction will be deliberately changed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nakamoto's paper quantifies the same event, calculating the probability that an attacker ever catches up from a given number of blocks behind (Nakamoto, 2008).

Without a number, the advice to wait for confirmations is folklore. With one, it becomes engineering: a merchant can weigh the value of the goods against the chance of losing them and choose how long to wait. The paper's own conclusion is the one the chapter repeats in words, that the probability of a successful attack drops exponentially as blocks are added, and that the receiver therefore becomes safer by waiting (Nakamoto, 2008). The book's blockchain chapter puts the same thing as a picture of geological layers, in which the topsoil may blow away while the deeper strata have been undisturbed for ages (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets these numbers in the appendix of the book, which reproduces Nakamoto's paper, and in the research record of this course, where the figures were recomputed: for an attacker controlling a tenth of the hash rate the probability of catching up falls from 0.2045873 at one confirmation to 0.0002428 at six, and a transcription of the paper's own procedure reproduces that table exactly (Nakamoto, 2008). The chapter's own figures of five minutes and nineteen minutes are the time axis of the same table.

Two calculations are worth doing. The simple one is the paper's own expression for an attacker who is already a given number of blocks behind and must close the gap: with a share of a tenth of the hash rate the chance is the ratio of the attacker's share to the honest share raised to the number of blocks, which for six blocks is 0.1 divided by 0.9, to the sixth power, about 1.882 in a million, as the expression above gives. The paper's full formula also allows for the attacker's progress during the waiting time, which raises the figure for six confirmations to about 0.0002428; both numbers were executed for this chapter, and both fall away quickly as blocks are added (Nakamoto, 2008).

These probabilities rest on assumptions, and the assumptions matter more than the digits. They assume the attacker has a minority of the hash rate, and the book's section on hashrate attacks shows that with a majority the arithmetic changes qualitatively, since success becomes almost certain given enough patience (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They also describe only this one attack: they say nothing about a stolen key, a faulty wallet or a payment sent to the wrong place, which are far more common ways to lose money than a reorganization of the chain.

nodes.example: about two chances in ten thousand after six blocks
nodes.definition: The chance that an attacker with a minority of the hash rate catches up from behind falls very fast with each confirmation, which is what makes confirmations worth counting.

nodes.label: Best blockchain
nodes.body: The best blockchain is the valid chain of blocks that carries the most cumulative proof of work, and it is the chain that a node treats as the record. The chapter states the rule in its account of why a confirmed payment is hard to change: when there are multiple alternative blocks to choose from, Bitcoin full nodes choose the chain of valid blocks with the most total proof of work, called the best blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's mining chapter repeats it as the final part of the consensus mechanism, the assembly of blocks into chains and the selection of the chain with the most proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The best blockchain is the valid chain of blocks that carries the most cumulative proof of work, and it is the chain that a node treats as the record. The chapter states the rule in its account of why a confirmed payment is hard to change: when there are multiple alternative blocks to choose from, Bitcoin full nodes choose the chain of valid blocks with the most total proof of work, called the best blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's mining chapter repeats it as the final part of the consensus mechanism, the assembly of blocks into chains and the selection of the chain with the most proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

This single rule is what produces agreement without agreement being negotiated. Every node applies it to the blocks it has, so nodes that have seen the same blocks reach the same conclusion, and nodes that have seen different blocks converge as soon as the missing blocks arrive. The book says so directly: by selecting the greatest-cumulative-work valid chain, all nodes eventually achieve network-wide consensus, and temporary discrepancies between chains are resolved eventually as more work is added (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is also the rule that sets the price of rewriting history, since an attacker must produce more work than everyone else combined over the period in question.

The reader meets the rule in the chapter's argument about Alice and Bob: for the entire network to accept an alternative block, an additional new block would need to be mined on top of the alternative, which is simply the statement that the alternative chain must accumulate more work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's mining chapter adds what a node does with the chain it did not choose: the losing blocks are valid but not part of the best chain, and are kept for future reference in case one of those secondary chains later becomes primary (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Choosing is comparing two sums. The small example models two chains by the work in each of their blocks and picks the one whose total is larger, which is chain B. A real node does the same with the work implied by each block's target, keeping a running total that Bitcoin Core reports as the chain work. The book describes the procedure on arrival of a block: the node looks at the previous block hash to find the parent, usually the tip of the best chain, and if the new block does not extend the best chain it attaches the header to a secondary chain and compares the work; if the secondary chain is now the best, the node reorganizes its view of confirmed transactions and available unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Three corrections to common wording. The rule is most work, not longest chain: a chain of fewer blocks mined at a higher difficulty can carry more work, which is why the book speaks of cumulative proof of work. The rule applies only among valid chains, so a chain with more work that breaks a rule is not a candidate at all. And the choice is each node's own, made independently; there is no vote and no announcement, which is exactly why no authority is needed.

nodes.example: the chain with the most total work
nodes.definition: When several valid chains exist, every node independently chooses the one with the most cumulative proof of work; that chain is the record.

nodes.label: Block height
nodes.body: The height of a block is its position in the chain, counted as the number of blocks below it. The book's blockchain chapter explains that the genesis block is at block height zero and that each subsequent block added on top is one position higher, like boxes stacked one on top of the other (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter itself uses the word when it says that over time, as the height of new blocks increases, so does the computation difficulty for the chain as a whole (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The vertical language comes from the habit of drawing the chain as a stack, with the first block as the foundation and the newest block as the top or tip (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book's blockchain chapter explains that the genesis block is at block height zero and that each subsequent block added on top is one position higher, like boxes stacked one on top of the other (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter itself uses the word when it says that over time, as the height of new blocks increases, so does the computation difficulty for the chain as a whole (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The vertical language comes from the habit of drawing the chain as a stack, with the first block as the foundation and the newest block as the top or tip (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Heights are how people and programs talk about where something is in the record. A height is short, ordered and human-readable, where a block hash is thirty-two bytes and says nothing about position, so explorers accept a height as a search term and rules are written in terms of heights: the subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks, the difficulty is retargeted every 2,016 blocks, and a coinbase output matures after a hundred. The chapter's own picture of hundreds of thousands of blocks below the one containing Alice's transaction is a statement about height (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets heights everywhere a block is identified: the first block is height 0, and the book notes that height 800,000 was reached during the writing of the book in mid-2023, meaning there were 800,000 blocks stacked on top of the first, created in January 2009, which the addition above records (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's links to the block containing Alice's transaction and the book's examples of a node at height 277,314 receiving a block that takes it to 277,315 are the same convention at work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Counting is addition, but the subtle part is that the number is derived rather than stored. The book explains that in early blocks the height was not part of the block's data structure and that each node identified a block's position dynamically when it was received, and that a later protocol change began including the height in the coinbase transaction, although its purpose was to ensure that each block had a different coinbase transaction, so nodes still have to determine the height themselves in order to validate that field (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A height is not a unique identifier. The book is emphatic: although a single block always has a specific and invariant height, the reverse is not true, because two or more blocks might have the same height while competing for the same position in the chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Only the block hash always names exactly one block. A height is therefore the right way to speak about the record and the wrong way to refer to a particular block when forks matter, which is the subject of the next concept.

nodes.example: the genesis block is height 0
nodes.definition: The height of a block is its distance from the first block; heights are how blocks are counted, but a height does not always name a single block.

nodes.label: Fork and alternative block
nodes.body: A fork, in the sense used here, is the temporary situation in which two or more valid blocks claim the same height, so that the chain briefly has two tips. The book's glossary calls it an accidental fork and says it typically occurs when two or more miners find blocks at nearly the same time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The blockchain chapter explains the same thing from the shape of the data: although a block has just one parent it can have several children, each committing to the same parent, and eventually only one child becomes part of the chain accepted by all full nodes and the fork is resolved (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). An alternative block is one of those competing blocks.

The book's glossary calls it an accidental fork and says it typically occurs when two or more miners find blocks at nearly the same time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The blockchain chapter explains the same thing from the shape of the data: although a block has just one parent it can have several children, each committing to the same parent, and eventually only one child becomes part of the chain accepted by all full nodes and the fork is resolved (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). An alternative block is one of those competing blocks.

The concept matters for two reasons, one benign and one not. The benign one is that forks happen by themselves, because the network takes time to carry a block to everybody, and a reader who does not expect them will be puzzled when a block briefly disappears from an explorer. The book says that forks are almost always resolved within one block, and that the ten-minute interval is a design compromise between fast confirmation times and the probability of a fork (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The other reason is that a deliberate fork is exactly what a reversal needs, which is the argument the chapter makes about Alice and Bob.

The chapter meets the alternative block in its central security argument. It says that after the block containing Alice's transaction has propagated, creating an alternative block with a different version of Alice's transaction, such as one that does not pay Bob, would require performing the same amount of work as it will take all Bitcoin miners to create an entirely new block, and that for the whole network to accept that alternative block an additional new block would have to be mined on top of it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's glossary gives the name of a block that loses such a race: a stale block, successfully mined but not on the best chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Detecting a fork is comparing heights, which the small example does: if a new block claims the same height as the current tip there is a fork, and either way the next block will be one higher. Resolving it is the best-chain rule: nodes keep both branches, and whichever branch the next block extends carries more work and wins, after which the node reorganizes its view of confirmed transactions and available unspent outputs if it had preferred the other branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book adds that an accidental fork can occasionally extend to two blocks, when two blocks are found almost simultaneously by miners on opposite sides of a previous fork, but that the chance is low (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The word fork is badly overloaded and the book warns about it repeatedly. The accidental fork of this concept is not the same as a soft fork or a hard fork, which are changes to the consensus rules, and neither is the same as a software fork of a source repository (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nor is a stale block the same as an orphan block, which the glossary defines as a block whose parent has not yet been processed by the local node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And an accidental fork is not an attack: it is the ordinary consequence of a network with delays.

nodes.example: two blocks claiming the same height
nodes.definition: An accidental fork occurs when two valid blocks appear at the same height; it is normally resolved by the next block, and a deliberate alternative block is what a reversal would require.

nodes.label: Double spend
nodes.body: A double spend is the attempt to spend the same money twice. The book's glossary defines it as the result of successfully spending some money more than once, and adds how Bitcoin prevents it: by verifying each transaction added to the blockchain to ensure that the inputs had not previously already been spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the vocabulary of this chapter, a double spend is two transactions whose inputs name the same outpoint, of which at most one can be recorded.

paras.text: A double spend is the attempt to spend the same money twice. The book's glossary defines it as the result of successfully spending some money more than once, and adds how Bitcoin prevents it: by verifying each transaction added to the blockchain to ensure that the inputs had not previously already been spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the vocabulary of this chapter, a double spend is two transactions whose inputs name the same outpoint, of which at most one can be recorded.

This is the problem Bitcoin was invented to solve, and the chapter's opening sentences are about it: the system does not require trust in third parties, and software on a user's own computer can verify every aspect of its operation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nakamoto's paper puts it at the centre, proposing a solution to the double-spending problem using a peer-to-peer network that timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of proof of work (Nakamoto, 2008). Digital data can be copied, so a purely digital coin can be offered to two people at once; only an agreed order of events can decide which offer counts.

The reader meets the prevention in three places in this chapter and the next. A node's verification checklist requires that the outputs being spent match outputs in the memory pool or unspent outputs in a block of the best chain, so a second spend is refused on arrival (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The set of unspent outputs is the record that makes the check cheap. And the chapter's security argument is about the remaining case, where the first spend is already in a block and a miner would have to build an alternative chain to replace it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's mining chapter gives a worked attack of exactly that kind, in which a buyer and a friendly pool operator replace a payment for paintings with one that pays the buyer back (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The check itself is a membership test, which the small example performs: if the outpoint named by a new transaction's input is already in the set of spent outputs, the transaction is rejected. Doing this reliably is what the whole branch is for. Within one chain of blocks the order is unambiguous, and the book says that the enforcement of that order ensures no two valid transactions can spend the same output, eliminating the problem of double spending (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The hard case is not within one chain but between two competing chains, and that is resolved by the best-chain rule.

A double spend of a confirmed transaction is not impossible, only expensive, and the book notes that it can only be done on the attacker's own transactions, for which the attacker can produce a valid signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Replacement of an unconfirmed transaction is a different and much cheaper matter: the book's chapter on fees explains that an unconfirmed transaction can be replaced by one paying a higher fee rate, and warns the receiver of an unconfirmed transaction accordingly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And a double spend is not the same as a fork: a fork is two blocks, a double spend is two conflicting transactions.

nodes.example: spending the same output twice
nodes.definition: A double spend is the attempt to spend one output in two transactions; nodes reject the second, and the blockchain's order is what makes the rejection unambiguous.

nodes.label: Genesis block
nodes.body: The genesis block is the first block of the blockchain, the one with no parent. The chapter introduces it at the bottom of the stack, saying that below the block containing Alice's transaction are hundreds of thousands of blocks linked to each other in a chain all the way back to block number zero, known as the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's blockchain chapter adds that it was created in 2009 and is the common ancestor of all blocks, so that if you start at any block and follow the chain backward in time you will eventually arrive at it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The genesis block is the first block of the blockchain, the one with no parent. The chapter introduces it at the bottom of the stack, saying that below the block containing Alice's transaction are hundreds of thousands of blocks linked to each other in a chain all the way back to block number zero, known as the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's blockchain chapter adds that it was created in 2009 and is the common ancestor of all blocks, so that if you start at any block and follow the chain backward in time you will eventually arrive at it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The genesis block is what makes the chain's security well founded rather than circular. Every other block is trusted because of the work piled on top of it, but the first block has nothing below it, so it is fixed in the software instead. The book explains the consequence: every node always starts with a blockchain of at least one block because the genesis block is statically encoded within Bitcoin Core so that it cannot be altered, every node always knows its hash and structure, the fixed time it was created and even the single transaction within, and thus every node has a secure root from which to build a trusted blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets the genesis block as the block at height zero in any explorer, with the hash 00000000...0a8ce26f, and in the chapter's own data, where Bitcoin Core reports its height as 0, its version as 1, its merkle root equal to the identifier of its one transaction, its time as 1231006505, its nonce as 2083236893 and its compact target as 1d00ffff (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is also where Bitcoin's one famous piece of prose lives: the book says its coinbase input contains the text about the Chancellor on the brink of a second bailout for banks, taken from the headline of a British newspaper, which was intended to offer proof of the earliest date the block could have been created (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Every claim about the block can be recomputed from its fields. Its timestamp, 1231006505, is a count of seconds since the start of 1970, and converting it gives the third of January 2009, which is the executed example of this concept and the date the book gives for the start of the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Assembling the eighty bytes of its header from the same fields and hashing them twice reproduces the published hash, as the block-header concept shows. And because the block contains one transaction, its merkle root equals that transaction's identifier, 4a5e1e4b...deda33b.

The genesis block is special in ways that break general rules, so it should not be used as an example of an ordinary block. Its previous-block field is all zeros because it has no parent; its reward was never spendable in the usual way; and its presence in the software means that a node does not verify it in the way it verifies every later block, which the book describes by saying that full nodes validate every block after the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Note also that the test networks have genesis blocks of their own, which is why the book shows a different first hash for each of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: block number 0, mined in January 2009
nodes.definition: The genesis block is the first block, height 0, with no parent; it is built into the software, so every node starts from the same trusted root.

nodes.label: Unconfirmed transaction
nodes.body: An unconfirmed transaction is one that has been verified and propagated but is in no block. The book's network chapter uses exactly that word for the contents of a node's memory pool, transactions that are known to the network but not yet included in the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's own framing is the complement: Alice's transaction does not become part of the blockchain until it is included in a block by mining and that block has been validated by full nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An unconfirmed transaction is one that has been verified and propagated but is in no block. The book's network chapter uses exactly that word for the contents of a node's memory pool, transactions that are known to the network but not yet included in the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's own framing is the complement: Alice's transaction does not become part of the blockchain until it is included in a block by mining and that block has been validated by full nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

This state is where most of the practical confusion about Bitcoin lives, because it looks like a completed payment and is not yet one. A merchant sees the money arrive in a few seconds and must decide whether to act. The chapter is careful about the two different intervals: within a few seconds Bob sees the transaction on the register, and approximately five minutes after the transaction was first transmitted a miner finds a solution for the block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Those two sentences describe propagation and confirmation, and treating them as the same thing is the error this concept exists to prevent.

The reader meets unconfirmed transactions in a wallet as a pending payment, in an explorer as a transaction without a block, and in the chapter as the pool of unverified transactions that Alice's payment joined before being included in a candidate block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The owner's course notes for this chapter treat the same point under the heading of the ten-minute misconception, observing that transactions must be confirmed, that confirmations ensure the transaction has been accepted by the network, and that waiting for a full six confirmations can take up to sixty minutes (Altunel, 2021).

The arithmetic behind that figure is a multiplication: six blocks at an average of ten minutes each is sixty minutes, as the expression above gives. The important word is average. The book explains why the interval is ten minutes and that blocks are generated every ten minutes on average, with the difficulty adjusted to keep that pace, but nothing makes any particular block arrive on time: a block may follow the previous one within a minute or after half an hour, and the book's own example has a miner finding a solution almost eleven minutes after starting (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). So the waiting time for a confirmation is a random quantity with a known mean.

Three cautions. An unconfirmed transaction can be replaced, not only ignored: the book's chapter on fees describes replacement by a version paying a higher fee rate and advises the receiver of an unconfirmed transaction accordingly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It can also simply never be mined, if its fee rate is too low for the current market, in which case it may eventually be dropped from the memory pools that hold it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And the number of nodes that have seen it is not a measure of safety, because propagation is not confirmation.

nodes.example: a payment seen by everyone and recorded by nobody
nodes.definition: An unconfirmed transaction has propagated and been verified but is in no block; blocks arrive about every ten minutes on average, which is not a timetable.

nodes.label: Accepting a small payment unconfirmed
nodes.body: Accepting a small payment unconfirmed is the practice of treating a transaction as paid as soon as it has propagated, without waiting for a block. It is not a rule of Bitcoin but a judgement about risk. The book's mining chapter describes it in the setting of this very chapter: Bob, the seller, is willing to accept payment without waiting for confirmation because the risk of a double spend on a small item is low in comparison with the convenience of rapid customer service (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Accepting a small payment unconfirmed is the practice of treating a transaction as paid as soon as it has propagated, without waiting for a block. It is not a rule of Bitcoin but a judgement about risk. The book's mining chapter describes it in the setting of this very chapter: Bob, the seller, is willing to accept payment without waiting for confirmation because the risk of a double spend on a small item is low in comparison with the convenience of rapid customer service (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The practice matters because it shows that the number of confirmations to require is an economic question, not a technical one. The book offers the comparison that makes it intuitive: it is similar to the practice of coffee shops that accept credit card payments without a signature for amounts below twenty-five dollars, because the risk of a chargeback is low while the cost of delaying the transaction to obtain a signature is comparatively larger (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same chapter draws the opposite conclusion for expensive goods, warning that selling a more expensive item runs the risk of a double-spend attack in which the buyer broadcasts a competing transaction that spends one of the same inputs and cancels the payment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets the practice in shops, at vending machines and in the chapter itself, where Bob sees the transaction on the register within a few seconds and the sale proceeds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The owner's course notes record the same reasoning: a merchant may accept a valid small-value transaction with no confirmations, for something like a cup of coffee, where a ten-minute delay is unnecessary, accepting that it is riskier than a card payment (Altunel, 2021). The book's counter-example is the gallery that hands over paintings after a single confirmation and loses them to a pool-assisted double spend (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The decision is a comparison, which the small example renders: a value below the threshold is accepted at once, a value at or above it waits. Setting the threshold means weighing the value of the goods, the chance of a reversal, which the probability concept quantifies, and the cost of delay. The book's guidance at the other end of the scale is explicit: a merchant selling large-value items must wait at least six confirmations before handing over the product, may reasonably wait for more, and for high-value items may wait twenty-four hours, which corresponds to about 144 confirmations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Do not read this practice as a claim that unconfirmed payments are safe. They can be replaced by a version paying a higher fee, as the book's chapter on fees explains, and they can be deliberately double spent by a buyer who is willing to try (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Note also what is being accepted: a payment whose validity has been checked, so the risk is reversal and not forgery. And the threshold is nobody's recommendation; the twenty-five dollars in the comparison is about credit cards, not about Bitcoin, and each merchant must set its own.

nodes.example: selling a coffee without waiting
nodes.definition: A merchant may accept a small payment with no confirmation because the loss if it is reversed is smaller than the cost of making the customer wait; the threshold is a business decision.

nodes.label: Spending the transaction
nodes.body: This last group of the branch follows what happens after Alice's payment has been recorded: Bob spends it. The chapter gives the step a section of its own and begins it by saying that now that Alice's transaction has been embedded in the blockchain as part of a block, it is visible to all Bitcoin applications, and each full node can independently verify the transaction as valid and spendable (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group has two concepts, the onward spending itself and the weaker verification that a lightweight client can perform.

paras.text: This last group of the branch follows what happens after Alice's payment has been recorded: Bob spends it. The chapter gives the step a section of its own and begins it by saying that now that Alice's transaction has been embedded in the blockchain as part of a block, it is visible to all Bitcoin applications, and each full node can independently verify the transaction as valid and spendable (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group has two concepts, the onward spending itself and the weaker verification that a lightweight client can perform.

The group closes the circle of the chapter. It began with Alice spending an output that Joe had created and ends with Bob spending the output that Alice created, which shows that there is only one mechanism in Bitcoin and that every participant uses it in turn. The chapter says exactly this in its summary: it saw how transactions build a chain that moves value from owner to owner, and tracked Alice's transaction from the moment it was created in her wallet, through the network, to the miners who recorded it on the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The first concept follows Bob, who can now pay a contractor or a supplier by transferring value from Alice's podcast payment to these new owners, and who in doing so extends the chain of transactions; the chapter's last figure shows the chain running from Joe through Alice and Bob to Gopesh, Bob's web designer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second concept is the verification that a wallet without a full node can do, which the chapter describes as confirming that the transaction is in the blockchain and has several blocks mined after it, and which the book calls simplified payment verification (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Being spendable is not the same as being spent, and being in the blockchain is not the same as being in a wallet's control: Bob can spend the output only because his wallet holds the key that the output's script demands. Note also the one exception to onward spending that this chapter has met, the coinbase output, which must wait a hundred blocks before it can be spent at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Spending onward
nodes.body: Spending onward is the use of a received output as the input of a new transaction. It is the same operation that the chapter began with, seen from the other side: Alice spent an output that Joe's transaction created, and now Bob spends the output that Alice's transaction created. The chapter says that Bob can now spend the output from this and other transactions, for example by paying a contractor or a supplier, transferring value from Alice's podcast payment to these new owners, and that as he spends the payments received from Alice and other customers he extends the chain of transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Spending onward is the use of a received output as the input of a new transaction. It is the same operation that the chapter began with, seen from the other side: Alice spent an output that Joe's transaction created, and now Bob spends the output that Alice's transaction created. The chapter says that Bob can now spend the output from this and other transactions, for example by paying a contractor or a supplier, transferring value from Alice's podcast payment to these new owners, and that as he spends the payments received from Alice and other customers he extends the chain of transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

This step is what makes the word money appropriate. A payment that could be received but not spent again would be a receipt, not a currency; because every received output can become an input, value circulates and the chain of ownership that the chapter opened with continues indefinitely. It is also the step that makes the whole history auditable, since each spending leaves a link that anyone can follow backward to the block in which the bitcoins were first created.

The chapter's own example is Bob paying his web designer Gopesh for a new website page, and its final figure shows Alice's transaction as part of a transaction chain from Joe to Gopesh (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The earlier figure of the chain gives the numbers: Bob creates a transaction, labelled Tx3, that spends the output he received in Tx2, pays 67,000 satoshis in a single output and therefore pays a fee of 8,000, and because it has only one output the book calls it a changeless transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The arithmetic is the same subtraction as before. Bob received 75,000 satoshis and pays 67,000, so the difference of 8,000 satoshis is the fee, which the expression above computes and confirms against the figure the book prints (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). His transaction's input is the outpoint Tx2:1, the second output of Alice's transaction, and his wallet must supply whatever the output's script demands, which here is a signature made with the key for the address Alice paid. No change output is needed because the amount he is paying is close to what he has.

Two cautions. Spending onward needs the key, not just the record: the output is public, but only the holder of the key that satisfies its script can spend it, which is why losing a key loses the funds. And a changeless transaction like Bob's is only practical when the amount to be paid is roughly the amount available minus the fee, as the book says; otherwise the surplus would be handed to the miner (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: Bob paying Gopesh from Alice's payment
nodes.definition: Once recorded, an output can be spent by its owner in a new transaction, which extends the chain; Bob's payment of 67,000 satoshis out of Alice's 75,000 leaves a fee of 8,000.

nodes.label: Simplified payment verification
nodes.body: Simplified payment verification is the method by which a program that does not hold the whole blockchain can still gain assurance about a payment. The chapter describes what it achieves without naming it: lightweight clients can partially verify payments by confirming that the transaction is in the blockchain and has several blocks mined after it, thus providing assurance that the miners expended significant effort committing to it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's network chapter gives the name, saying that for space- and power-constrained devices a simplified payment verification method is used to let them operate without validating the full blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Simplified payment verification is the method by which a program that does not hold the whole blockchain can still gain assurance about a payment. The chapter describes what it achieves without naming it: lightweight clients can partially verify payments by confirming that the transaction is in the blockchain and has several blocks mined after it, thus providing assurance that the miners expended significant effort committing to it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's network chapter gives the name, saying that for space- and power-constrained devices a simplified payment verification method is used to let them operate without validating the full blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The method is what makes a Bitcoin wallet possible on a telephone, and it is the clearest example in the course of a deliberate trade between cost and trust. What the client gives up is stated plainly by the book: lightweight clients cannot construct a full picture of all the unspent outputs available for spending because they do not know about all the transactions on the network, and they rely instead on peers to provide partial views of relevant parts of the blockchain on demand (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). What they keep is the ability to tell that work was done committing to their payment, which is the guarantee that this whole branch is about.

The reader meets this method in the chapter's closing section, where it is contrasted with what a full node does, namely validating every transfer of the funds from the moment the bitcoins were first generated in a block through each subsequent transaction until they reach Bob's address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's blockchain chapter describes the mechanics: the client receives a message containing the block header and a merkle path linking the transaction of interest to the merkle root, uses the path to connect the transaction to the header and the header to the rest of the chain, and so receives less than a kilobyte instead of a whole block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The efficiency comes from the shape of the merkle tree. Proving that one of N transactions is in a block needs about the base-two logarithm of N hashes of thirty-two bytes each, so for the roughly sixteen thousand transactions of the largest possible block that is fourteen hashes, 448 bytes, as the calculation above gives and as the book states (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The client then recomputes the pairwise hashes along the path and compares the result with the root in the header it already has; if they match, the transaction was in that block.

The limits of the method must be stated as clearly as its benefit. It proves inclusion and work, not validity: a lightweight client has not checked that the transaction's inputs existed and were unspent, so it is trusting the miners and its peers for that. It also leaks information, since asking peers about particular transactions reveals an interest in them, and the book devotes a section to lightweight clients and privacy for that reason (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The honest summary is the chapter's own word, partially: the client verifies part of what a full node verifies, and knowing which part is the point.

nodes.example: checking inclusion with a short path of hashes
nodes.definition: A lightweight client confirms that a transaction is in a block and that blocks were mined after it, using a merkle path of about log2(N) hashes instead of the whole block.

nodes.label: Semantics
nodes.body: This branch reads the chapter with the eyes of the course rather than of the book. A transaction chain, as the first branch described it, is a record of what came from what: each output exists because a transaction consumed earlier outputs, and each transaction happened because somebody who held a key authorized it. That is precisely the subject matter of provenance, for which the World Wide Web Consortium has published a standard vocabulary, the PROV Ontology (Lebo et al., 2013). The branch shows that the chapter's own structure can be expressed in that vocabulary, which is why this course treats Bitcoin as a case study in semantic modelling as well as a payment system.

paras.text: This branch reads the chapter with the eyes of the course rather than of the book. A transaction chain, as the first branch described it, is a record of what came from what: each output exists because a transaction consumed earlier outputs, and each transaction happened because somebody who held a key authorized it. That is precisely the subject matter of provenance, for which the World Wide Web Consortium has published a standard vocabulary, the PROV Ontology (Lebo et al., 2013). The branch shows that the chapter's own structure can be expressed in that vocabulary, which is why this course treats Bitcoin as a case study in semantic modelling as well as a payment system.

The branch matters for two reasons. The first is academic honesty about what the course is doing: every chapter of this material is turned into an ontology, and a student is entitled to see why the subject suits that treatment. The second is practical. Once a transaction chain is described in a standard vocabulary, questions about it can be asked in a standard query language and answered by a general tool, instead of by a program written for Bitcoin; and the same description can be joined to descriptions of other things, which is what makes a vocabulary worth standardizing.

The branch has one group with three concepts. The ontology is the general idea of writing down the concepts of a domain and their relations in a form a machine can use. The triple is the unit in which such descriptions are written, a subject, a predicate and an object, and the graph is what a set of triples forms. The provenance graph is the application to this chapter: Alice's transaction as an activity, the outputs as entities derived from one another, and the key holders as the agents responsible.

Two things this branch does not claim. It does not claim that the Bitcoin software uses any of these standards; it does not, and the description here is a model of the chapter's content, built for teaching and for querying. And it does not claim that provenance in this sense identifies anybody: the agents of the model are key holders, and a key holder is not a person until some evidence outside Bitcoin connects them, which is the same caution the first branch gave about addresses.

nodes.label: Provenance model
nodes.body: A provenance model is a description of where things came from: which things existed, which processes made or changed them, and who was responsible. This group introduces the vocabulary in which such a description is written and then applies it to the chapter. The standard it uses is the PROV Ontology, a World Wide Web Consortium Recommendation of April 2013, which the specification describes as a set of classes, properties and restrictions, expressed in the OWL2 Web Ontology Language, which is the World Wide Web Consortium's standard language for writing ontologies, that can be used to represent and interchange provenance information generated in different systems and under different contexts (Lebo et al., 2013).

paras.text: A provenance model is a description of where things came from: which things existed, which processes made or changed them, and who was responsible. This group introduces the vocabulary in which such a description is written and then applies it to the chapter. The standard it uses is the PROV Ontology, a World Wide Web Consortium Recommendation of April 2013, which the specification describes as a set of classes, properties and restrictions, expressed in the OWL2 Web Ontology Language, which is the World Wide Web Consortium's standard language for writing ontologies, that can be used to represent and interchange provenance information generated in different systems and under different contexts (Lebo et al., 2013).

The group is the bridge between this chapter and the method of the course. Bitcoin's blockchain is unusual among records in that its provenance is complete and public: for any output one can follow the chain back to the block in which the bitcoins were created, which is exactly what the chapter says a full node does when it validates every transfer of the funds from the moment the bitcoins were first generated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A record with that property is the ideal case study for a vocabulary designed to express where things came from.

The model works by committing to a small number of kinds of thing and then saying only what can be said with them. The standard this course borrows offers three starting points - something that exists, something that happens, and someone responsible - and every statement is written as a triple, a subject, a property and a value, so that statements from different sources join simply by sharing a subject. Describing Bitcoin with it means choosing which of its objects fall under which kind: an output is something that exists, a transaction is something that happens, and the holder of a key is someone responsible, after which the links the chapter already describes - that this transaction consumed that output, that this output was created by that transaction - are ordinary provenance relations rather than Bitcoin-specific ones. The gain is that a question about the origin of a coin becomes the same kind of question as a question about the origin of any other record, and can be asked in the same language (Lebo et al., 2013).

Keep the model and the thing modelled apart. The triples described here are written by this course, not by Bitcoin, and a different modeller could reasonably choose differently: an output might be modelled as an entity or as a state of an entity, and a transaction as one activity or as several. A model is a tool for answering particular questions, so it is judged by whether it answers them, not by whether it is the only possible description.

nodes.label: Ontology
nodes.body: An ontology, in computing, is an explicit description of the concepts of some area of knowledge and of the relations among them, written in a form that a machine can process. It names the classes of thing that exist, arranges them in a hierarchy of more and less general, gives properties that relate them, and states which individuals belong to which class. The PROV Ontology is one: the specification says it provides a set of classes, properties and restrictions that can be used to represent and interchange provenance information, and that it can be specialized to create new classes and properties for different applications and domains (Lebo et al., 2013).

paras.text: An ontology, in computing, is an explicit description of the concepts of some area of knowledge and of the relations among them, written in a form that a machine can process. It names the classes of thing that exist, arranges them in a hierarchy of more and less general, gives properties that relate them, and states which individuals belong to which class. The PROV Ontology is one: the specification says it provides a set of classes, properties and restrictions that can be used to represent and interchange provenance information, and that it can be specialized to create new classes and properties for different applications and domains (Lebo et al., 2013).

For this course the ontology is the form in which each chapter is recorded, so that the material can be queried, checked and reused rather than only read. Three benefits follow. Terms are defined once and used consistently, which is why this chapter insists that every technical word it uses is itself a concept. Questions can be stated in advance as competency questions and the description tested against them. And because the vocabulary is standard, the result can be joined to other descriptions, as this branch does by borrowing the provenance vocabulary of the Web consortium.

The reader meets an ontology as the structure of the page they are reading: the branches, groups and concepts of this chapter are the classes of an ontology, the worked examples are individuals, and the explanations are the documentation. Outside this course, ontologies are used for medical terminologies, product catalogues, scientific data and the descriptions that search engines read from web pages. The World Wide Web Consortium's provenance work is itself an example published as a Recommendation (Lebo et al., 2013).

The smallest useful description is a list of classes with their parents, which is what the example computes: four classes of which two have no parent, and therefore two roots and a hierarchy below them. A real ontology adds properties, such as the relation between a transaction and the outputs it spends, and constraints, such as that every concept must have a definition. The ontology of this chapter is generated from the text you are reading and is checked before it is published: every number quoted in it is executed, and shapes are applied to the result.

An ontology is not a database and not a program. It says what kinds of things there are and how they relate, not how to store them efficiently or what to do with them, and a statement in an ontology is a claim about the world that may be wrong. Nor is one ontology ever the ontology of a subject: the same chapter could be modelled with different classes, and this one is organized around how a learner meets the material, which is a pedagogical choice and not a discovery.

nodes.example: the concept list of this chapter
nodes.definition: An ontology is an explicit, machine-readable description of the concepts of a domain, their hierarchy and their relations, against which questions can be asked and answers checked.

nodes.label: Triple and graph
nodes.body: A triple is the unit in which these descriptions are written: a subject, a predicate and an object, read as a single sentence. The statement that Alice's transaction used Joe's output is a triple whose subject is the transaction, whose predicate is the relation used and whose object is the output. A set of triples forms a graph, in which the subjects and objects are nodes and each triple is a directed edge labelled with its predicate. The same structure that this chapter has already used to picture the network, nodes joined by edges, is the structure of the description itself.

paras.text: A triple is the unit in which these descriptions are written: a subject, a predicate and an object, read as a single sentence. The statement that Alice's transaction used Joe's output is a triple whose subject is the transaction, whose predicate is the relation used and whose object is the output. A set of triples forms a graph, in which the subjects and objects are nodes and each triple is a directed edge labelled with its predicate. The same structure that this chapter has already used to picture the network, nodes joined by edges, is the structure of the description itself.

Triples are chosen because they combine without planning. Two descriptions written by different people, about different things, can simply be put together, and anything they have in common joins up; nothing has to be merged, because there are no tables and no columns. This is why the provenance standard can be reused here: its predicates for derivation, generation and attribution can be applied to this chapter's outputs and transactions without changing anything in the standard.

The reader meets triples in every file this course publishes, where they are written in a compact text form, and in the query language that is used to ask questions of them. Outside the course, the same form carries product and event descriptions on web pages, open government data and scientific catalogues. The provenance standard lists the starting-point predicates of its vocabulary, among them was derived from, was attributed to and was generated by, each of which is the middle element of a triple (Lebo et al., 2013).

Counting a small graph shows how a description grows. The three triples of the example mention four distinct things in all, Alice's transaction, the output it spent, the output it created and Alice herself, because the transaction is the subject of two of them; so three statements already describe a connected fragment with a path from Joe's output through the transaction to Bob's. Adding Bob's onward transaction extends the same graph without altering what is already there, which is the property that makes the form useful for a chain that grows block by block.

Triples are a notation, not a guarantee of truth: a graph records what somebody asserted, so the question of who asserted it, which is itself a provenance question, is always worth asking. A graph is also not a hierarchy, although hierarchies can be expressed in it, and the absence of a triple means only that nothing was said, not that the opposite is true. Finally, the graph of this chapter is a description of the record and not the record: the blockchain itself is a sequence of bytes, and these triples are what this course says about it.

nodes.example: Alice's transaction used Joe's output
nodes.definition: A triple is a statement of the form subject, predicate, object; a set of triples forms a graph whose nodes are the things and whose edges are the statements.

nodes.label: Provenance graph
nodes.body: A provenance graph of this chapter is the transaction chain written in the vocabulary of the provenance standard. The standard's three starting-point classes fit the chapter's parts closely. An entity, which the specification defines as a physical, digital, conceptual or other kind of thing with some fixed aspects, is a transaction output. An activity, which it defines as something that occurs over a period of time and acts upon or with entities, including consuming, processing, transforming and generating them, is a transaction. An agent, which it defines as something that bears some form of responsibility for an activity taking place or for the existence of an entity, is the holder of the key that authorized the spending (Lebo et al., 2013).

paras.text: A provenance graph of this chapter is the transaction chain written in the vocabulary of the provenance standard. The standard's three starting-point classes fit the chapter's parts closely. An entity, which the specification defines as a physical, digital, conceptual or other kind of thing with some fixed aspects, is a transaction output. An activity, which it defines as something that occurs over a period of time and acts upon or with entities, including consuming, processing, transforming and generating them, is a transaction. An agent, which it defines as something that bears some form of responsibility for an activity taking place or for the existence of an entity, is the holder of the key that authorized the spending (Lebo et al., 2013).

Reading the chain this way makes the course's theme visible in the chapter's own material. The chapter says that each input spends an earlier output, that anyone can follow a payment back through the chain of ownership, and that a full node validates every transfer from the moment the bitcoins were first generated in a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Those are statements about derivation, and the provenance vocabulary exists to express exactly them, so Bitcoin's ledger becomes an example of a complete and public provenance record rather than a special case needing its own language.

The chapter supplies the graph twice in picture form: the figure of three transactions in which the output of one is the input of the next, and the closing figure of Alice's transaction as part of a chain from Joe through Alice and Bob to Gopesh, Bob's web designer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A block explorer draws the same graph interactively, and a reader who follows the links from an input to the output it spends is walking it by hand.

The translation is mechanical, which is what the executed example shows: a chain of outputs becomes a list of derivation triples, each saying that one output was derived from the one before, so the chain Tx1:0, Tx2:1, Tx3:0 yields two statements. A fuller description adds, for each transaction, that it used the outputs it spent and generated the outputs it created, and that it was attributed to the agent who signed it; the standard's predicates for those are used, was generated by and was attributed to (Lebo et al., 2013). The fee needs no special treatment, since it is the difference between what was used and what was generated.

The model has limits worth stating. Attribution is to a key holder, not to a named person, so the graph does not identify anybody; the chapter's own remark that the change address is often new, for privacy reasons, shows that even the grouping of outputs by owner is a guess (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The activity has a time only once the transaction is in a block, and even then the timestamp is approximate. And derivation here is between whole outputs, not between amounts: an output derived from two inputs does not tell you which satoshi came from where, because the protocol does not record that.

nodes.example: the chain from Joe to Gopesh as a graph
nodes.definition: The chapter's transaction chain is a provenance graph: outputs are entities derived from earlier entities, transactions are the activities that derive them, and key holders are the agents responsible.
