nodes.label: Practice
nodes.body: The last branch of this chapter is about trying things out. The concepts of the earlier branches are all mechanical, which means that a learner can operate them rather than only read about them, and a small number of interactive pages have become the standard way to do that in teaching. This branch describes the ones the owner's course notes point to: the demonstration pages of Anders Brownworth's Blockchain Demo, which the notes link under the address of its hash page (Altunel, 2021) (Brownworth, n.d.). The branch exists so that the pages are part of the chapter's record and not an unexplained link at the end of a slide.

paras.text: The last branch of this chapter is about trying things out. The concepts of the earlier branches are all mechanical, which means that a learner can operate them rather than only read about them, and a small number of interactive pages have become the standard way to do that in teaching. This branch describes the ones the owner's course notes point to: the demonstration pages of Anders Brownworth's Blockchain Demo, which the notes link under the address of its hash page (Altunel, 2021) (Brownworth, n.d.). The branch exists so that the pages are part of the chapter's record and not an unexplained link at the end of a slide.

The branch matters because the central claim of the chapter, that a chain of hashes makes a record expensive to change, is far more convincing when a student breaks a chain with their own hands and watches every block after the change turn invalid. The pages also make the asymmetry of proof of work physical: mining a single demonstration block takes a perceptible moment, and verifying it is instant. For a course this is the cheapest possible laboratory, since the pages run in a browser and risk nothing.

The branch has one group, the interactive demonstration, with five concepts, which follow the pages of the demonstration in its own order: the hash page, which computes a digest as you type; the block page, which adds a nonce and a mining button; the blockchain page, which links five blocks and shows the cascade of invalidity; the distributed page, which gives three peers their own copies; and the coinbase page, which puts transactions and a block reward inside the blocks. Each concept says what the page shows, which concept of the earlier branches it demonstrates, and what it simplifies away.

A demonstration is not the system. The pages use a single hash, a difficulty of four leading zeros and a handful of blocks, where Bitcoin uses a double hash, a difficulty astronomically higher and hundreds of thousands of blocks; they have no network, no signatures, no scripts and no fees. Their value is that every simplification is a point of comparison: a student who can say what the page leaves out has understood the chapter.

nodes.label: Interactive demonstration
nodes.body: An interactive demonstration, in the sense of this group, is a web page that implements a small part of the chapter's mechanics and lets a reader change the inputs and watch the outputs. The group describes the five pages of the Blockchain Demo, whose navigation names them Hash, Block, Blockchain, Distributed and Coinbase, in that order, each page building on the one before (Brownworth, n.d.). The owner's course notes for this chapter give the address of the first of them as the application with which to experience the subject (Altunel, 2021).

paras.text: An interactive demonstration, in the sense of this group, is a web page that implements a small part of the chapter's mechanics and lets a reader change the inputs and watch the outputs. The group describes the five pages of the Blockchain Demo, whose navigation names them Hash, Block, Blockchain, Distributed and Coinbase, in that order, each page building on the one before (Brownworth, n.d.). The owner's course notes for this chapter give the address of the first of them as the application with which to experience the subject (Altunel, 2021).

The group is included because the chapter's claims are of exactly the kind that a demonstration can settle. That a hash changes completely when one character of the input changes, that a block is valid only when its hash matches a template, that changing an old block invalidates every later one, and that different peers can hold different chains are all statements that can be seen rather than believed. The pages are also a shared reference: a class can be asked to do the same thing and compare results.

The pages work the same way throughout. Each block is a box with fields, the contents of the box are hashed as you type, and the box turns from red to green when its hash satisfies the difficulty. The script of the demonstration sets that difficulty to four leading zeros and limits the search to five hundred thousand attempts, with a note that because a hexadecimal digit has sixteen values, each extra digit of difficulty makes the puzzle sixteen times harder (Brownworth, n.d.). The later pages add fields, a previous-hash field to make a chain, a column per peer to make a network, and transaction rows to make a ledger.

Treat the pages as illustrations of single ideas, not as a model of Bitcoin. Their hash is a single SHA-256 rather than the double hash Bitcoin uses, their blocks have no merkle root and no timestamp, their mining is a button rather than a competition, and the amounts in the coinbase page are written as plain numbers with no keys or signatures behind them. The group names these differences for each page so that a learner can translate in both directions.

nodes.label: Hash page
nodes.body: The hash page is the first and simplest page of the demonstration. Its content is two fields, labelled Data and Hash, under the heading SHA256 Hash, and the page recomputes the digest of whatever is in the data field as the reader types (Brownworth, n.d.). Nothing else happens on the page: there is no block, no chain and no mining, so the only thing on show is the behaviour of the hash function itself.

paras.text: The hash page is the first and simplest page of the demonstration. Its content is two fields, labelled Data and Hash, under the heading SHA256 Hash, and the page recomputes the digest of whatever is in the data field as the reader types (Brownworth, n.d.). Nothing else happens on the page: there is no block, no chain and no mining, so the only thing on show is the behaviour of the hash function itself.

The page is the right place to start because every later concept of the chapter rests on this one function. The two properties that the chapter attributes to it are both visible within a few keystrokes: that the same input always produces the same output, which the reader sees by typing a text, clearing it and typing it again, and that nobody can predict the output for a new input, which the reader sees by changing a single character and watching the whole digest change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The fixed length is equally visible, since the digest stays sixty-four characters long however much is typed.

The owner's course notes for this chapter end with a link to exactly this page, offered as the application with which to experience the subject (Altunel, 2021). Inside this chapter the same function is met three times over: the identifier of a transaction, the identifier of a block and the proof of work are all results of applying it, twice in a row in each case. Outside the chapter a reader meets it whenever a downloaded file is checked against a published digest, and whenever a password is stored in a form that cannot be read back. The page is useful precisely because it isolates that one function from everything else, so a learner can satisfy themselves about its behaviour before meeting it inside a block.

The page computes, for a text, the same value that the standard library computes: the digest of the sentence Alice pays Bob 75000 begins 320a22eeeb9c0391, which is the executed example of this concept and can be compared with what the page shows for the same input. A reader should then try the chapter's own test case, the phrase that the book hashes, and the experiment of changing one letter: the course's check for the hash-function concept measures that changing the exclamation mark to a question mark changes sixty-one of the sixty-four digits.

Three differences from Bitcoin should be noted while using the page. It applies SHA-256 once, where Bitcoin's identifiers and proof of work apply it twice. It hashes text as typed, where Bitcoin hashes exact binary structures, so a reader cannot reproduce a real transaction identifier by pasting its hexadecimal form into the data box. And a digest on this page is only a digest: it is not a commitment to anything until something refers to it, which is what the next pages add.

nodes.example: a digest that changes as you type
nodes.definition: The first page of the demonstration shows a data box and its SHA-256 digest, recomputed at every keystroke, so the unpredictability and the fixed length of a hash can be seen.

nodes.label: Block page
nodes.body: The block page puts the hash of the previous page inside a box that has to satisfy a condition. Its fields are a block number, a nonce, a data field and the hash, with a Mine button beside them (Brownworth, n.d.). The box is shown in one colour when the hash begins with the required number of zeros and in another when it does not, so the reader can see at a glance whether the block is valid; pressing Mine makes the page try nonce after nonce until the condition is met.

paras.text: The block page puts the hash of the previous page inside a box that has to satisfy a condition. Its fields are a block number, a nonce, a data field and the hash, with a Mine button beside them (Brownworth, n.d.). The box is shown in one colour when the hash begins with the required number of zeros and in another when it does not, so the reader can see at a glance whether the block is valid; pressing Mine makes the page try nonce after nonce until the condition is met.

This page is where proof of work stops being a phrase. The reader has already seen that a digest cannot be steered, so the only way to satisfy the condition is to try, and the page does the trying in front of them. The asymmetry that the chapter describes, an enormous amount of computation to get right and only a small amount to verify as correct, is experienced as the difference between the pause after pressing Mine and the instant recolouring of the box when the answer is in (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets the same mechanism in the chapter's account of the lottery, in which a miner feeds a candidate block to the hash function and makes a small change and tries again if the output does not match the template (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's own miniature version, hashing a phrase with a number until the digest begins with a zero, is the same experiment with an easier target and a found nonce of 32 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The page's rule can be reproduced exactly. Its script fixes the difficulty at four leading zeros and limits the search to five hundred thousand attempts, and it hashes the concatenation of the block's fields (Brownworth, n.d.). Doing the same here, for block number 1 and the data Alice pays Bob 75000, the first nonce whose digest begins with four zeros is 6630, which is the executed example of this concept. The expected number of attempts for four hexadecimal zeros is sixteen to the fourth power, that is 65,536, so 6630 was a lucky run; the script's own note is that each extra digit of difficulty makes the puzzle sixteen times harder, and that a difficulty of six needs a limit well above five hundred million (Brownworth, n.d.).

The differences from real mining are large and instructive. There is one miner and no competition, so no block is ever lost to a faster rival. The difficulty is fixed by the page instead of being retargeted every 2,016 blocks. The threshold is expressed as leading zeros rather than as a number below a target, which is a good approximation but not the real rule. And the nonce here is unbounded, whereas Bitcoin's is four bytes and must be supplemented by changing other fields.

nodes.example: a nonce searched until four zeros appear
nodes.definition: The second page adds a block number, a nonce and a Mine button, so that the asymmetry of proof of work can be felt: a search of thousands of attempts, then an instant check.

io.code: (lambda h: next(n for n in range(500000) if h(('1' + str(n) + 'Alice pays Bob 75000').encode()).hexdigest().startswith('0000')))(__import__('hashlib').sha256)

nodes.label: Blockchain page
nodes.body: The blockchain page shows five blocks in a column, each with the fields of the block page and one more, labelled Prev, which holds the hash of the block before it (Brownworth, n.d.). Because a block's hash is computed over its own fields including that one, the blocks are chained: the hash of block two depends on the hash of block one, the hash of block three on that of block two, and so on. The page recomputes the whole column whenever anything is typed.

paras.text: The blockchain page shows five blocks in a column, each with the fields of the block page and one more, labelled Prev, which holds the hash of the block before it (Brownworth, n.d.). Because a block's hash is computed over its own fields including that one, the blocks are chained: the hash of block two depends on the hash of block one, the hash of block three on that of block two, and so on. The page recomputes the whole column whenever anything is typed.

This page demonstrates the single most important claim of the chapter's third branch. The book states it as a chain of consequences: any change to a parent block requires a child block's hash to change, which requires a change in the pointer of the grandchild, which in turn changes the grandchild, and so on, so that once a block has many generations following it, it cannot be changed without forcing a recalculation of all subsequent blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the page this is not an argument but an observation: edit the data of block two and blocks two to five all turn invalid at once.

The reader meets the same structure in the chapter, which describes hundreds of thousands of blocks linked to each other in a chain of blocks all the way back to block number zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and in the book's blockchain chapter, which calls the structure an ordered, back-linked list of blocks and compares its stability to the layers of a geological formation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The owner's course notes end with a slide titled Chain of Blocks and the link to this demonstration (Altunel, 2021).

The cascade is a simple consequence of dependency, which the small example renders: editing the block at position one invalidates it and every position after it, here the positions one to four of a five-block chain. To repair the chain the reader must mine each affected block again, in order, and each one takes its own search, which is the page's way of showing what the chapter means when it says that recalculating six blocks, plus one new block, would require an immense amount of computation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The work grows with the depth of the change, which is the reason confirmations are counted.

Note what the page cannot show. There is only one chain and one editor, so there is no competition and no best-chain rule, and nothing stops the reader from patiently remining all five blocks, which in Bitcoin would mean outpacing the entire network while it keeps extending the honest chain. The page also has no transactions, so the thing being protected is only a text; the coinbase page adds a ledger, and the distributed page adds the other participants.

nodes.example: changing block 2 reddens blocks 2 to 5
nodes.definition: The third page links five blocks by a previous-hash field, so that editing an early block invalidates it and every block after it until each is mined again.

io.code: (lambda chain, edited: [i for i in range(len(chain)) if i >= edited])(['b1', 'b2', 'b3', 'b4', 'b5'], 1)

nodes.label: Distributed page
nodes.body: The distributed page repeats the five-block chain of the previous page once for each of three peers, labelled Peer A, Peer B and Peer C (Brownworth, n.d.). Each peer has its own column of blocks with its own fields and its own Mine buttons, and the page recomputes each column independently. Nothing is sent between the peers: the point of the page is that each of them holds a copy, and that a reader can compare the copies by eye.

paras.text: The distributed page repeats the five-block chain of the previous page once for each of three peers, labelled Peer A, Peer B and Peer C (Brownworth, n.d.). Each peer has its own column of blocks with its own fields and its own Mine buttons, and the page recomputes each column independently. Nothing is sent between the peers: the point of the page is that each of them holds a copy, and that a reader can compare the copies by eye.

The page adds the dimension that the chapter's second branch is about. A chain that only one person holds proves nothing about agreement, whereas three chains that agree show what consensus looks like in the simplest possible case. Tampering with one peer's block two makes that peer's chain disagree with the other two from block two onward, which is the picture behind the chapter's statement that full nodes choose the chain of valid blocks with the most total proof of work when several alternatives exist (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the idea in the chapter's description of the network, in which every participant holds and verifies the same data and no participant is special (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and in the book's network chapter, which says that the nodes interconnect in a mesh with a flat topology and that there is no server and no hierarchy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The page is the smallest possible version of that: three equals, each with the whole record.

Comparison is the operation the page invites, and the small example performs it: three peers whose latest hashes are collected, two of which agree and one of which does not, so the set of distinct values has more than one element and the peers are not in consensus. On the page the same comparison is done by eye, reading the last hash of each column. Repairing the tampered peer means remining its blocks until its column matches again, which is the demonstration's version of a node catching up with the network.

The page leaves out everything about how peers learn from one another: there are no messages, no propagation, no gossip and no rule for choosing between chains, so a reader must supply those from the second and third branches. Nor is there any notion of cumulative work, so the page cannot show why a longer or heavier chain wins; it can only show that disagreement is visible. Three peers are also a very small network, and the chapter's figure of about ten thousand listening nodes is a different order of magnitude (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: three peers with their own chains
nodes.definition: The fourth page gives three peers, A, B and C, each a full copy of the five-block chain, so a reader can tamper with one peer and see that the others disagree with it.

nodes.label: Coinbase page
nodes.body: The coinbase page is the last of the demonstration and the one closest to Bitcoin. Each block of each peer now has a line labelled Coinbase, which pays an amount to somebody, followed by transaction rows that each move an amount from one name to another, and then the previous hash and the hash of the block (Brownworth, n.d.). The heading of the page is Coinbase Transactions, and the three peers of the previous page are kept, so the reader sees a small ledger replicated three times.

paras.text: The coinbase page is the last of the demonstration and the one closest to Bitcoin. Each block of each peer now has a line labelled Coinbase, which pays an amount to somebody, followed by transaction rows that each move an amount from one name to another, and then the previous hash and the hash of the block (Brownworth, n.d.). The heading of the page is Coinbase Transactions, and the three peers of the previous page are kept, so the reader sees a small ledger replicated three times.

The page closes the circle of the chapter by putting payments inside the blocks whose security the earlier pages demonstrated. It shows the two things the mining group explains: that new money enters only through the coinbase line, and that everything else is a transfer from one party to another. It also makes tampering meaningful, because changing an amount in an early block now changes who owns what, and the cascade of invalid hashes is the reason that change cannot pass unnoticed.

The reader meets the same arrangement in the chapter, where each miner includes a special transaction that pays their own address the block reward plus the fees, and in the book's mining chapter, which calls that the coinbase transaction and notes that it does not spend any earlier output (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The genesis block of Bitcoin is the extreme case, a block whose only transaction is its coinbase (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Balances on the page are read by adding and subtracting along the chain, which the small example does for one block: a coinbase of one hundred paid to a first party, who then sends thirty to a second and twenty to a third, leaves that party with fifty. Doing this for every block of a peer's column gives every name's balance, and comparing the columns of the three peers shows whether they agree about it. The reader should then try the experiment the chapter warns about: spend the same amount twice in one column and see that nothing in the page prevents it.

That last experiment is the page's most useful limitation. There are no keys and no signatures, so anybody can move anybody's money, and there is no check that a sender has what they send, so a double spend is not rejected; Bitcoin prevents both with the scripts and signatures of the first branch and the verification checklist of the second. The amounts are plain numbers rather than outputs, so there are no unspent outputs, no change and no fees. And the coinbase amount here never halves, where Bitcoin's subsidy is cut in half every 210,000 blocks.

nodes.example: a block reward and transactions in each block
nodes.definition: The last page adds a coinbase line and transaction rows to every block of every peer, so that a chain of hashes becomes a ledger whose balances can be read off.

findings: Chapter 2 follows one real transaction - Alice paying Bob's Store - through wallet, network and blockchain: transactions as double-entry lines of inputs and outputs with an implied fee, transaction chains, change and coin selection, common transaction forms, constructing and propagating a transaction, mining that bundles transactions into blocks, and confirmations that make a payment harder to reverse as blocks pile up.

The chapter's claim that a payment becomes harder to reverse with each confirmation is quantified in Nakamoto's paper: for an attacker with a tenth of the hash power the probability of catching up falls from 0.2045873 at one confirmation to 0.0002428 at six, and a Python transcription of the paper's own procedure reproduces that table exactly.

For the course theme, a transaction chain - each input spending an earlier output - is a provenance graph, and W3C's PROV Ontology offers the vocabulary to describe it: entities derived from entities by activities, attributed to agents.
The Bitcoin Core software that full nodes run to verify every rule has continued to release after the book; its releases page lists 31.1 as the newest.

The owner's course notes for this chapter (2021, after the 2nd edition) surfaced topics now added to the deck, each checked against the 3rd edition: the invoice as a BIP21 URI, which the 3rd edition prints in full with a bech32 address where the notes had the older format; why ten minutes is an average and six confirmations a convention, with small payments accepted unconfirmed at low double-spend risk as coffee shops accept small card payments, from the 3rd edition's chapter 12; the notes' own analogy of mining as a giant competitive sudoku, kept and labelled as an analogy because the 3rd edition does not use it; and the Blockchain Demo the notes link to, verified reachable.

Known limit of the chapter page. The quality gate that governs this chapter's ontology is a SHACL shape file, sen0401_ch02_domain_shacl_v1_1_1.ttl, which states 3 node shapes: that every individual carries a label, that anything defined cites its source, and that a worked example carries exactly one input and one output. The chapter builder applies those shapes to the TBox and the ABox before it writes them, and the build fails if they are violated, so the gate does run; what it does not do is reach the student. The interactive page embeds the chapter's TBox, ABox, document and this research record as Turtle, and the shape file is not among them, so a reader who opens the page can read the ontology it teaches from but cannot read, query or re-run the gate that admitted it, and the page's own list of the triples in each corpus file never mentions the shapes. The limit is recorded here rather than repaired here because the list of files the page embeds is set by the page build chain, which this chapter does not own; repairing it means adding the shape file to that chain's corpus list, after which this finding should be revised to say that the gate is shipped.
Quantities of the mining and security sections, recomputed

Every figure the chapter states about mining and confirmations was reproduced from a primary source or from arithmetic. The chapter's 168 billion trillion attempts per block divide by 600 seconds to a network hash rate of 2.8 times ten to the twentieth hashes a second. The first block's compact target 1d00ffff expands to 65,535 times two to the power 208, which implies about 4.295 billion attempts at difficulty one, and its eighty-byte header, assembled from the published version, merkle root, time, target and nonce, hashes to the published block hash 000000000019d668...0a8ce26f, whose timestamp 1231006505 is the third of January 2009. The subsidy rule of Bitcoin Core's GetBlockSubsidy gives 6.25 bitcoins for the 2023 era and 3.125 after block 840,000, and summing 210,000 blocks of each successive subsidy gives the book's total of 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis. Nakamoto's own procedure for an attacker with a tenth of the hash rate reproduces 0.2045873 at one confirmation and 0.0002428 at six. The demonstration page's difficulty of four leading zeros was reproduced by finding the nonce 6630 for a sample block, against an expected 65,536 attempts.

An audit of the 1.1.0 explanations listed every technical term they use and checked each against the concept list of this chapter and of chapter 1. Sixty-five terms were used without a concept of their own: the cryptographic and computing foundations (hash function, key pair, public key, public-key cryptography, elliptic curve, digital signature, checksum, entropy, nonce, encryption, bit, byte, hexadecimal notation), the remaining parts of a transaction (script, double-entry ledger, transaction size, weight, virtual byte, fee rate, unspent transaction output, transaction identifier, serialization, byte order, outpoint, witness), the pieces of a payment request (URI, QR code, improvement proposal, Bitcoin address, exchange rate), the wallet and the construction of a transaction, the participants and stages of the network (full node, lightweight client, peer, peer-to-peer network, transmission, gossiping, memory pool, the recipient's own check), and the whole vocabulary of mining and of security (miner, candidate block, proof of work, block header, merkle tree, difficulty and target, hash rate, coinbase transaction, block reward, mining pool, soft and hard fork, probability of reversal, best blockchain, block height, fork and alternative block, double spend, spending onward, simplified payment verification) together with the ontology, the triple and the five pages of the interactive demonstration. Version 1.2.0 adds a concept for each of them, so that a second run of the same audit over the new text reports no term that is not a concept of this chapter or of chapter 1. Two terms are explained inside the concept that quotes them rather than as concepts of their own, because the chapter needs them only in one sentence each: the median time past, glossed where the block's timestamp rule is stated, and the OWL2 Web Ontology Language, glossed where the PROV Ontology is introduced.
The book's illustration against the real transaction

The chapter's figures and its printed invoice do not all describe the same payment, and every difference was located in the bytes of the real transaction that the book prints in chapters 3 and 6. The invoice asks for 0.01577764 bitcoin, which is 1,577,764 satoshis, while the transaction of the figures pays 75,000 satoshis; the twenty-byte program encoded in the invoice's bech32 address is b291ae1c...9485b1c, which is not the program in the real payment output; the figure labels Alice's input Tx1:0 while the stored output index is 1; and the order of Alice's two outputs in the real transaction is change first, at 20,000 satoshis, then the payment of 75,000, which is why the later figure has Bob spending Tx2:1. The amounts of the figures are consistent in themselves: 100,000 in, 75,000 plus 20,000 out, a fee of 5,000, and a fee of 8,000 on Bob's onward transaction of 67,000. Bitcoin Core's reported size, virtual size and weight for that transaction, 194, 143 and 569, were all recomputed from its 194 bytes.

stories.title: Nine pages, one table of probabilities
stories.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, announcing on the metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list
stories.story: On 31 October 2008 a pseudonymous author posted nine pages to a cryptography mailing list. Section 11 does something unusual for a systems paper: it computes the attacker's odds. Modelling the race between an honest chain and a secret one as a binomial random walk, it tabulates the probability that an attacker with a share q of the hash power ever catches up from z blocks behind. This deck does not quote that table - it reruns the paper's own procedure and draws the result.
stories.lesson: A confirmation is a probability statement, and you can compute it
stories.source: Nakamoto, 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' (2008), section 11; announcement of 2008-10-31 on the metzdowd.com cryptography list. The chapter research record reproduced the paper's q=0.1 column - 0.2045873 at one confirmation, 0.0002428 at six - to seven decimal places (examples group AttackerSuccess reruns it for this deck).

stories.title: Five free bitcoins for every visitor
stories.who: Gavin Andresen, the developer Satoshi later handed the project to
stories.where: freebitcoins.appspot.com, announced on the bitcointalk forum
stories.story: In June 2010 there was almost nowhere to buy bitcoin, so a developer in Massachusetts stocked a website with 1,100 of his own coins and gave five to anyone who asked - solving a CAPTCHA was the only price. Thousands of people got their first bitcoin from Gavin Andresen's faucet. The giveaway seeded the user base the first exchanges and the first payments then grew from, and Andresen went on to lead Bitcoin's development when Satoshi withdrew in 2011.
stories.lesson: Before price discovery, distribution itself had to be invented
stories.source: Andresen's own announcement thread, bitcointalk.org topic 141, 2010-06-11: 'Get 5 free bitcoins from freebitcoins.appspot.com', initially stocked with 1,100 BTC. Photo: Web Summit 2014, CC BY 2.0.

stories.title: The day someone printed 184 billion bitcoin
stories.who: An unknown attacker; spotted by developer Jeff Garzik; patched by Satoshi Nakamoto
stories.where: block 74,638, discussed live on the bitcointalk forum
stories.story: On 15 August 2010 block 74,638 contained a transaction paying out about 184,467,440,737 BTC - thousands of times the 21 million cap. Two outputs were so large that, summed as 64-bit integers, they overflowed to a small number and slipped past the checks. Jeff Garzik flagged the 'strange block' on the forum within the hour; Satoshi shipped version 0.3.10 with a corrected rule about five hours after the block, and the honest chain, rebuilt without the forged coins, overtook the bad one. The 184 billion bitcoins ceased to exist.
stories.lesson: Validation by every node is the immune system - and it worked
stories.source: en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Value_overflow_incident: block 74,638 of 2010-08-15 (two outputs of 92,233,720,368.54 BTC each), Garzik's 'Strange block 74638' thread, Satoshi's 0.3.10 patch ~5 hours later, good chain ahead by block 74,691.
